Katalog Berita (Halaman 40/57)

#3570. Scott Colom's Mississippi Is the One You Should Know

“Mississippi is not who you think we are.”

This is what an older Black woman said to MS NOW’s Nnamdi Egwuonwu as he interviewed Scott Colom supporters on the Tougaloo College campus Thursday night. The crowd was waiting for Colom to speak after his historic victory, becoming the first Black Mississippian elected to statewide office since Reconstruction, and its first Democratic senator in nearly a half century. The woman did not give her name, but her simple statement has tattooed itself inside my brain.

“To understand the world, you must first understand a place like Mississippi” is a more famous cautionary quip that scratches at the same sentiment. If you’ve known anyone from Mississippi, you’ve probably heard it. Everyone cites William Faulkner, even though nobody has definitively sourced it. But as the world looks with fresh eyes on my home state, the wisdom checks out.

Onlookers, including longtime national political strategists, seem surprised by Colom’s win. Mississippians are not. The extremes of the moral universe have always been duking it out down there, which makes Mississippi not strange or anomalous, but illustrative.

There’s no avoiding the facts: Human beings have committed the most brutal violence imaginable against their fellow humans in Mississippi, as a matter of law and legacy. One of the consequences of that horror is that it has become prophecy. It is impossible not to feel a sense—from within the state and from without—of frustration and dread that it is taking way too long to emerge from a racism that has raptured the entire culture.

But to people who do not know Mississippians, who do not understand Mississippi—to those who suggest any right-minded or good people simply up and leave, or think the rest of the country should abandon all hope, or worse, look away entirely—you are missing one of the most important threads in the future of American politics and culture. Colom got at this rub when he said that outlets like Cook Political Report, who prognosticate a “solid R” conclusion, are destructive. “They made it much more difficult to fundraise and are part of the reason the South has been neglected for so long,” he wrote. And if you dismiss possibility in Mississippi, you are compounding the neglect. You are part of the destruction.

You think John McCain was a maverick? Scott Colom is a maverick.

During the race, he drew national attention not only for his prospect of flipping the unflippable, but also because he was doing so through one of the most vivid, creatively engaged, and original campaigns in modern politics. He built a coalition virally, with his twin brother, Andrew Robert Colom, as collaborator, offering “Sheeeeit” to the world (yes, that’s how many white Mississippians really talk), along with a Hollywood-worthy Sinners send-up, and Andrew’s searing spoken-word poem set to the strains of Fannie Lou Hamer. Colom even stood in line at a Trump rally to speak earnestly with voters who would otherwise be against him—I guarantee he won some of them over.

His entire strategy was built on making people recognize Mississippi, in all its underdog idiosyncrasies. He asked Kamala Harris to campaign with him, even as his advisers reportedly told him it would be an error, because he knew she would draw media attention to underfunded hospitals. And he took the phone call informing him that he’d won while wearing a Richard Pryor hoodie. Because we like to laugh in Mississippi, okay?

As Kiese Laymon, novelist, memoirist, and modern-day Mississippi bard, told me, “Once I saw the protein ad, I knew he’d win.”

History doesn’t echo in Mississippi; it rhymes. You can draw a straight line from the murders of Medgar Evers, or those of James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner, to the killings of Jorge Gomez or Renee Good or Alex Pretti. You can draw a straight line from Theodore Bilbo to Tate Reeves to Donald Trump.

As Kiese wrote in this magazine in 2020, Mississippi politics flow from its culture. (Incidentally, Kiese and Colom both attended Millsaps College, about 10 years apart, and had the same thesis adviser.) In “Mississippi: A Poem, in Days,” Kiese describes how he got into “an altercation with two fraternities on Bid Day”—when the students who want to be in the Greek system receive offers from frat and sorority houses. “Some fraternity members wore Confederate capes, Afro wigs, and others blackened their faces.” They called Kiese and his girlfriend the N-word.

I have never written about the heartbreak of seeing the future governor of Mississippi in that group of white boys, proudly representing the Kappa Alpha fraternity and its confederate commitment to Black suffering. I have never admitted that after playing basketball against Tate all through high school, and knowing that he went to a public school called Florence, not a segregation academy, like so many other white boys we knew, it hurt my feelings to see Tate doing what white boys who pledged their identities to the Old South ideologies were supposed to do.

When I saw Tate in that confederate cacophony of drunken white boyhood, doing what they did, I knew he could one day be governor of Mississippi and president of the United States.

That is still the most damning thing I can ever say about a white boy from Mississippi.

Damning things still happen, and will again. Just days ago, as the votes continued to stack up for Colom, the old ugliness reared its head. White women in my hometown, students at the University of Mississippi, were captured on video making racist gestures—gesturing and making sounds like monkeys—at their Black neighbors’ video doorbell. The school, still embarrassingly insistent on calling itself “Ole Miss,” continues to investigate, while the offenders get so much more grace than they deserve from the victims and their families, as you can see in their CBS interview. I feel deep shame in these moments, because I know this is what so many people think Mississippi is. There is no excuse for it, and no explanation beyond the obvious. The shame should be obvious, too, but a white person from Mississippi is compelled to express it.

The women are not from Mississippi, according to a source familiar; one, Alaina Kunes, is from Wisconsin, where a car dealership that bears her family’s name is now being sued for a separate allegation of racist actions. This is not an excuse, but rather a fear: that Mississippi’s reputation for the worst parts of history continues to attract the worst sorts of people.

But this is partly what Faulkner, or whoever it was, meant by understanding the world through the lens of Mississippi: Everywhere we must hope our better angels prevail.

I was born and raised in Mississippi among a large, politically engaged family who have wanted change for generations. When Sargent Shriver turned up unexpectedly at my grandparents’ house for dinner one night, on a swing through the South in a failed presidential bid, my grandmother whispered the urgent directive of “FHB”—“family holdback”—so her five sons would leave enough food for Shriver. This story, and that guest, was a point of pride her whole life. She was an unforgiving George McGovern campaigner; in our family photo album, among the pool parties and Christmas mornings, are pages of Polaroids she snapped of Richard Nixon’s televised resignation.

Local private schools, as I understood them, were inherently racist. Public school was a choice of one, and I got a world-class education in the Oxford school system. (Hyde-Smith attended Lawrence County Academy and she sent her own child to Brookhaven Academy, both segregation academies.) My class of 2000—I came up with the same kids from kindergarten through high school—was roughly half Black and half white, with the skinniest pie slivers of anything else. I left for college and never moved back, but my parents, brother, and extended family are still there. Today, Mississippi’s public-school students are doing better than most of their peers across the nation; my own children in the New York City school system are getting a more segregated, less excellent education than I did.

My father, a green-energy mayor and a Barack Obama appointee to the Tennessee Valley Authority (fired by Trump amid a Republican board takeover), pushed throughout my childhood to take the Confederate flag off the state flag and to remove the Confederate monument that still mars the Oxford Square. I was about eight years old when someone keyed “LIBERALS” into the trunk of our Honda Civic, probably because of the Ray Mabus for Governor bumper sticker. I recall being worried about it, until I saw that my parents were amused.

As white Southern liberals, we were in a tiny minority. And though the mantle was worn proudly, it was more existential than that—you were proud to be a Democrat not because it was one party over another, but because it was a stand-in for compassion, common good, and humanity. And nowhere could this be truer, or more necessary, than in Mississippi. (By way of disclosure, I see no conflicts in telling you all this. As former Time editor Rick Stengel says, “You should be non-partisan, but not neutral. Journalists must be biased in favor of the truth and facts. Biased in favor of democracy itself.” And this is the truth, in favor of democracy.)

Scott Colom and I were born a year apart in the earliest 1980s, during a sort of second-wave new New South rebranding. More jobs were coming into the state thanks to manufacturing; more national attention was being paid to Black Mississippians’ cultural contributions (the Delta Blues Museum was established in 1979). William Winter was governor the years of our respective births, and he gave us free kindergarten. William Allain, whose moment was virtually destroyed by a racist, homophobic GOP slander campaign, followed. And Allain was succeeded by Mabus—who won on the slogan “Mississippi will never be last again.” Now, with the exception of Ronnie Musgrove, the governor has been a Republican since 1992. We’ve never had a Black person, or a woman for that matter. Have you had many good thoughts about Mississippi in all this time? I don’t think you have.

Heavy, Kiese’s devastating and raw memoir of coming of age as a Black boy in Mississippi, written in address to his activist and educator mother, gives his own view into 1980s and ’90s Mississippi: “You worked on Governor Mabus’s campaign and kept talking about how much was possible politically in Mississippi because it was the blackest state in the nation,” he writes. And his mother says to him: “Do you understand what’s possible if we actually get effective radical politicians in place down here?” Kiese responds, “I’m glad Mabus won but hearing about it every day is just kinda mee-guh.” Meager. It was not enough then, and we have plenty far to go.

Heavy was published in October 2018, just before Stacey Abrams turned Georgia purple, signaling to the rest of the country that it was time to take notice of the deeply disenfranchised Southern states.

When I reached out to Mabus, who went on to become Bill Clinton’s ambassador to Saudi Arabia and then Obama’s Secretary of the Navy, he identified the dominoes that knocked toward Colom’s win: the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, rampant corruption, a welfare scandal featuring Brett Favre, and “office holders taking constituents for granted” over decades. Mabus was a young man working for Winter when Colom and I were little, and this election, he said, “brings hope for the future.”

It doesn’t really matter which party you’d like to claim. Repulsive policies will eventually push everyone away. Mississippi Republicans are not moderate, are not descended of gentle governance. (See: Bilbo et al.) This is the state that put “personhood” on the ballot as part of a national antiabortion strategy; fortunately for all y’all, Mississippians rejected the idea of life beginning at conception. Lynn Fitch, the current attorney general, not only effortfully attempted to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election, but she is the signed counsel for the petitioners in the Dobbs brief, which ultimately reversed Roe v. Wade. (Because I keep underscoring to you the infinite refractions of Mississippi, Fitch also went after Colom for one of his ads that used AI; he removed it.) Even the affidavit ballots that have taken so long to count are a result of strident, generational attempts by Republicans to disenfranchise Black voters. Which is why Mississippians knew, as the Colom–Hyde-Smith race came down to those affidavits, exactly in whose favor they would tally up. Were it not for the dedication of young Black canvassers—especially Black women—and homegrown mobilization efforts, things would have gone differently.

“There is a radical history of Black academics, activists, lawyers, and judges who have really been working to see a Mississippi where this was possible,” Kiese emailed me over the weekend. “I am thankful that someone like Leslie McLemore, who was a young member of Hamer’s Mississippi Democratic Party, can see what they worked and died for.”

What does Colom’s win mean for Kiese? “It means that the people, not any party, get what they organize and fight for,” he replied. “Our state taught the world that again last week.”

My privileged position occluded my own understanding of Mississippi’s true potential until I was older. Growing up, I mostly just clocked defeat—every presidential election, every midterm, Mississippi was red as red could be, as Mississippi’s poverty levels ratcheted toward a 21st-century high of 24%. In 2008, John McCain beat Barack Obama in the state by a 13% margin (the two staged a debate in Oxford). In 2016, Trump bested Hillary Clinton by almost 18 points.

After Trump won in 2024, an old childhood friend who’d gone MAGA texted me a GIF of a penis ejaculating stars that reconstituted in the shape of a patriotic eagle. Flash forward a year later, he’s angry about gas prices, and, more striking to me, horrified by the war in Gaza. Colom’s protein ad is for him, and that nerve of enthusiasm it struck is going to keep firing.

Colom didn’t run on pronouns or any numerical strain of woke. He has said he is a fan of Trump’s border security, agrees with him on certain tax policies, and supports the Second Amendment. When asked about improving wages for government employees, he has said he wants to take care of teachers—and cops. As Colom told Jen Psaki in a televised interview, “We gotta be a party that represents our whole country, that understands all parts of the country.”

Now that people outside Mississippi are waking up to Colom, leftists may find his centrism irritating or even offensive. You may find a new reason to look down your noses at Mississippi. It all but promises to provide an opportunity.

So I will just leave you with the brothers Colom.

“They lied about Mississippi. Said that evil lived in one state, but the cotton cow fed the nation. Europe eating off the same plate. They lied about Mississippi. Said the torture was only here, but the banker’s desk in northern mills still dripping blood from hostage tears. They lied to us all. That’s propaganda machine on both sides, running on slander…. Denying the nation condoned it, denying the nation owned it, denying the nation fed off pain…. They lied about Mississippi. Said that evil lived in one state.”

He says, invoking Hamer, “Mississippi Freedom Party began again.”

And the vision of Scott: “There is nothing wrong with Mississippi that can’t be fixed by what’s right.”

#3569. Some Of The Olsen Twins’ Iconic Movies Are Finally Streaming, But I’m Still Hoping Another Film Gets Added

Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen may be best known for their shared role as Michelle Tanner on Full House, but the child actors -- who eventually left Hollywood -- also launched their own cinematic universe of sorts. In the '90s and early 2000s, the duo starred in several TV and direct-to-video movies. For the longest time, most of these movies were only available to fans who owned the hard copies, but that’s starting to change as a handful of their movies have popped up on Prime Video (though one of my favorite titles hasn't been added).

Unlike most movies that are released, the highly successful Olsen twins managed to retain all the rights to a majority of their films after buying out the co-founder and former manager of their entertainment company, making them their own bosses. This allowed Mary-Kate and Ashley to control how their films were distributed and thus kept them off streaming services. It’s unclear what has changed, but it seems like the Olsens have realized how sought-after these films are to their millennial fans and have started to loosen the reins. As a fan of the Mary-Kate and Ashley Cinematic Universe, I’m ecstatic.

As of writing this, eight Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen movies are currently available to stream for Prime Video subscription holders. Four of them are from the early days of the twins’ career and were filmed while Full House was still airing new seasons. The titles include To Grandmother’s House We Go, a Christmas movie and the first of their television films; the Halloween flick Double Double Toil and Trouble; It Takes Two, a loose book-to-screen adaptation of Mark Twain’s The Prince and the Pauper; and How the West Was Fun.

There are also four films from the twins’ post-Full House days, including Passport to Paris, Billboard Dad, Switching Goals and one of my personal favorites and their final movie, New York Minute. Needless to say, this is a sweet lineup, but can I just take a moment to highlight one flick that's not present?

While the rest of us were being "normal kids," the Olsen twins were busy producing and starring in a total of fourteen movies between 1992 and 2004. Eight films aren't a bad start, but there are still a lot that need to be added to complete the Mary-Kate and Ashley Cinematic Universe. However, there is one movie that I need to be added ASAP: the 2001 flick Holiday in the Sun.

In the film, Mary-Kate and Ashley play the Stewart twins, whose parents surprise them with a trip to Atlantis Resort in the Bahamas over their winter break. I vividly remember being in awe, listening to “Island in the Sun” play as the twins jet off to the Caribbean. And if Prime Video needs another reason to get the rights to Holiday in the Sun ASAP, it also serves as Megan Fox’s film debut.

As bummed as I and several other Olsen twin fans are that Holiday in the Sun isn’t one of the eight featured on Prime Video (as of now), it doesn’t put too much of a damper on the reveal. After all, we’ve waited years for even one of their films to hit streaming services, and now we have access to half their filmography.

Despite there being no official word from Prime Video, news of the release did travel fast on social media, with fans sharing their joy on X:

I guess it’s time for me to pause my marathon of watching all the new and upcoming Christmas movies and head over to Prime Video to revisit some of these gems. Maybe if enough of us watch, the streamer will add Holiday in the Sun or any of the other Olsen twins movies!

Danielle Bruncati is a writer and pop culture enthusiast from Southern California. She earned a Master of Fine Arts degree in Television Writing and Producing from a top film school. #3568. Critical Role Returns With the Mighty Nein Season 2 in 2027, but Fans Aren’t Happy

More Mighty Nein is never a bad thing, but this latest news has left Critters despondent

It's always a great time to be a Critical Role fan, and 2027 will be no different, with several new live-play shows and series planned. However, things are about to get even better, thanks to a new announcement made by Critical Role during TwitchCon 2026: The Mighty Nein season 2 will arrive on Prime Video on March 24, 2027.

The news was announced during a special live Lord of the Rings one-shot, when Game Master Liam O’Brien asked fans to raise a cup to celebrate The Mighty Nein’s return.

However, the good news came with a worrying catch. According to the official news release, the episode release schedule for The Mighty Nein will be very different from that of its first season — and Critters are concerned about what this could mean for the show's future.

Season 2 of The Mighty Nein will consist of eight episodes, all of which will be released at once when the season debuts on Mar. 24, 2027. This contrasts sharply with the release schedule for season 1, which released its first three episodes on Nov. 19, 2025, followed by weekly episodes through Dec. 22, 2025.

The change has left Critters speculating whether Prime Video — the publisher and partner behind The Mighty Nein and Critical Role’s other animated series, The Legend of Vox Machina — has lost faith in Critical Role’s animated tales set in Exandria.

“God, I hope not,” one user posted on social media platform X, referring to all episodes of The Mighty Nein dropping at once. “Publishers have to know by now that dropping everything at once instantly kills a series online presence?”

“[It] makes me sad and I hope also isn't a choice that's at all indicative of Amazon's faith in the series or a sign s1 underperformed,” another user posted. “Really hope it means nothing at all and they just thought it'd do better bc tm9 is genuinely so good so far.”

It’s impossible to know what Prime Video is thinking about its binge release of The Mighty Nein, but Critters aren’t wrong. This type of release rarely sparks discussion the way a week-to-week release does.

Primve Video’s news release for season 2 of The Mighty Nein included a plot summary, which you can read below.

“In Season Two, The Mighty Nein set off on a pirate adventure across the high seas as they face their complicated pasts and hurtle toward a treacherous future. While Fjord’s burgeoning powers tempt him down a dark path, the Beacon reveals its own enticing possibilities, and the group must choose between newfound magic and their friendship.”

The first season of The Mighty Nein already featured plenty of changes, including a revised backstory for Aasimar barbarian Yasha (Ashley Johnson). There seem to be even more changes this time around, with the group’s pirate arc taking center stage earlier than expected. We wonder whether this means certain characters will stick around longer than they were originally established in the actual-play Dungeons & Dragons campaign from which The Mighty Nein is adapted. Only time will tell.

The Mighty Nein airs exclusively on Prime Video. Season 1 is available to watch now, with season 2 set to debut on Mar. 24, 2027.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3567. Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Makes a Weak Case for His Post-Trial Comeback

For weeks, Los Angeles has been plastered with posters of a malevolent-looking man in a top hat and gray sideburns. It always takes me a few minutes to process that this elderly curmudgeon is Johnny Depp, doing his Hollywood walk of shame in Ebenezer.

“It’s good to be back,” Depp gurgles in the movie’s trailer. He’s either reveling in his return from infamy or trolling the audience, depending on your point of view.

I adored Johnny Depp back in his Edward Scissorhands/Gilbert Grape/Ed Wood heyday; he probably would’ve been my hall pass if I’d known about the concept back then. Now, though, it feels as if the once chiseled-cheeked heartthrob has found a character that suits him: a monstrous figure seeking redemption.

“Grant me the grace to prove that I am no longer the man that I once was,” Ebenezer Scrooge begs one of the ghosts haunting him in this rather plodding new version of Charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol, directed by horror auteur Ti West. Scrooge is trying to make up for a lifetime of stinginess and cruelty, whereas Depp seeks to win back mainstream audiences after the ugly, drawn-out brawl that was his marriage and divorce from Amber Heard.

Heard alleged that he was an abusive addict. Depp denied abusing her and filed two defamation suits. He aimed one at the British tabloid The Sun for calling him a wife-beater (which he lost, since the court found the characterization to be “substantially true”). The other was leveled at Heard for describing herself in a Washington Post op-ed as “a public figure representing domestic abuse.” What started as a defamation trial ended up as a livestreamed referendum on post-#MeToo gender politics.

The saga spawned organized smear campaigns soaked in misogyny. Social media erupted with vile memes, hashtags, and videos targeting Heard, bearing hashtags like #AmberHeardIsAPsychopath and #DontBelieveAllWomen. One men’s group launched a “Ditch the Witch” protest in support of Depp. It seemed to echo one of Depp’s texts about Heard, released during the trial, in which he proposed to a friend: “Let’s drown her before we burn her!!!…I will fuck her burnt corpse afterwards to make sure she is dead.” And it wasn’t just ordinary guys taking up arms for Depp. Moments after the verdict was announced, the GOP’s House Judiciary tweeted a GIF of Depp in Pirates of the Caribbean from its official account, showing support for him.

“The craziness [aimed at Heard] was a kind of pent-up anger at women,” a film producer suggested to me back in 2022. “I think it really stirred up a lot of deep-seated resentment that hasn’t been allowed expression since #MeToo.”

Depp didn’t come out of the crucible with his career intact. He was asked to resign from the Fantastic Beasts franchise—though Warner Bros. still paid Depp his full $16 million salary—and his former agent claimed Disney dropped him from the next Pirates of the Caribbean movie. Still, he never really went away. In fact, like so many guys who have been supposedly “canceled,” he wormed his way back in quite easily. In 2023, he got a standing ovation at Cannes for his role as Louis XV in the French film Jeanne du Barry. The next year, he directed the movie Modì, Three Days on the Wing of Madness. Meanwhile, producer Jerry Bruckheimer confirmed in 2025 that he’s been talking to Depp about a sixth Pirates film after all. All the while, Depp has also kept his massive brand deal as the face of Dior’s Sauvage.

“I don’t feel boycotted by Hollywood because I don’t think about Hollywood,” Depp announced imperiously a few years back. “I don’t have much further need for Hollywood.” Enter Ebenezer, his official return to…Hollywood. Which he doesn’t need or think about. At all.

Call it Christmas-washing: What could be more wholesome and uncontroversial than A Christmas Carol? According to Variety, Paramount paid Depp just $5 million—a big drop-off from the days when he could reportedly command $50 million for a single film—and only spent $38 million to produce the movie, hedging its bets. Still, this film is a pretty warm welcome back to American movie screens, major marketing campaign and all.

Unfortunately, Depp’s mediocre performance in Ebenezer doesn’t dispel the sour scent of desperation that hangs over his career. Scrooge is one of the most unlovable characters in all of literature, and Depp’s charm does not shine through the gnarled facial prosthetics. He plays the archetypal miser in the broadest of ways, spending much of the nearly two-hour movie alternating between exaggerated expressions of cantankerousness and horror. Depp’s inspiration for the role might as well have been Oscar the Grouch, though one with less educational value who’s hollow at his core. At various points, the actor campily throws himself into physical comedy that is at odds with the horror-soaked vibe of West’s production.

Knowing this is a test run for Depp’s uncanceling, viewers will find it hard not to see Ebenezer as a wink-filled plea for absolution. “I’m not the man I was!” his character screams over and over. “Allow me my redemption.” To which the answer—or my answer, at least—is simple: Bah, humbug.

#3566. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

#3565. Model Kathy Ireland Reveals Husband Escaped a Burning Boat After Explosion

Former swimsuit model Kathy Ireland revealed her husband, Greg Olsen, narrowly escaped danger after his boat burst into flames due to an engine exploding.

“Engine exploded and a fire quickly melted all navigation equipment and survival raft! My heart is both heavy and full. Heavy because I know the love, sweat and life you poured into this vessel,” Ireland, 63, wrote via Instagram on Sunday, November 15. “Full because of the outpouring of love and support. I’m so thankful God gifted you with a brilliant mind to navigate this disaster so seamlessly.”

Ireland added that Olsen, a former physician who retired to pursue commercial fishing, was “out alone” while she was “on the road for business.”

Footage accompanying her message showed the boat, named The 4th Watch, rocking out at sea as a blazing fire and thick black smoke gushed from atop.

A subsequent Instagram post shared by Ireland also revealed what her husband found in the aftermath of the incident. “Greg went to the harbor to assess the damage. The boat and all its contents are no more. Besides our commercial fishing licenses, the only thing on the boat that survived is his Bible,” she captioned three photos from Olsen’s return to the scene. “Completely unscorched! My heart is overflowing full!”

The former Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover girl and Olsen married in August 1988 and share three children: son Erik, 32, and daughters Lily, 27, and Chloe, 23.

Ireland evolved her modeling career into a lifestyle brand, launching clothing lines, operating events spaces and writing children’s books over the years. In 2012, Celebrity Net Worth named her the richest supermodel in the world. Forbes magazine also reported at the time that she had sold “an astounding $2 billion worth of licensed products” at retail to make her as big as Martha Stewart.

Us reported in March that Ireland and Olsen were suing their former business managers amid allegations of negligence, theft, intentional representation, constructive fraud and more.

The lawsuit, obtained by Us at the time, stated, “This case is about trust betrayed on a staggering and unconscionable scale. For over 35 years, defendants Jason Winters and Erik Sterling held themselves out to Kathy and Greg, not only as their managers, but as their family. … But in fact, they concealed and misrepresented information from Kathy and Greg to hide their predatory misdeeds.”

Ireland had claimed the defendants were liable for damages “in the tens of millions of dollars, if not exceeding $100 million.”

After the lawsuit attracted headlines, Kathy Ireland Worldwide (kiWW) chair and chief executive officer Brittany Duncan shared a statement via LinkedIn slamming the suit. “Kathy Ireland may be spiritually broken, but she is not financially ‘broke,’” Duncan wrote at the time. “I have known this woman my entire life. This situation is deeply sad. … What is being done is beneath the dignity of this firm.”

Us reached out to Ireland’s attorney for comment on the LinkedIn post but did not hear back.

#3563. See Bruce Springsteen, Martin Scorsese, and Surprise Guest Tom Cruise Honor Steven Spielberg at MoMA

Bruce Springsteen and Steven Spielberg are good friends. They’ve vacationed together a number of times on the director’s yacht, the Seven Seas. They went to Portofino in 2019, Sicily in 2017, and to Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat in 2024—the latter time with Bono and The Edge. But when Springsteen took the stage at MoMA Thursday night to toast Spielberg at the museum’s annual Film Benefit, he had a bone to pick with the director.

“In June of 1975, I went to a small theater directly across from the Atlantic Ocean and I saw Jaws. I was 25 years old,” Springsteen said. “Now, one of the great pleasures on the Jersey Shore in 1975 was night swimming, preferably naked, on one of those 90-degree, 80% humidity August nights, preferably with someone you wanted to have sex with. There was nothing like after the bars closed, you had a few drinks in you—naked night swim.”

“Steven Spielberg fucked that up,” Springsteen continued. “He fucked it up good. Now, many times over the years, I asked myself, Why? Why would a nice man like that—why would he do that?”

Here at MoMA, a guitar slung around his back, Springsteen then attempted a bit of playful psychoanalysis. He recalled his trips on the Spielberg family yacht. Maybe, thought the guy who wrote “Born to Run,” the guy who directed Jaws is scared of swimming.

“I’ve been on that boat many times and I can tell you: Steven Spielberg does not go in that water— ever. Steven’s boat is so fucking big it has water on it. There’s a pool on it. Steven Spielberg does not go in that fucking pool—and I mean ever,” Springsteen said. “I’m not sure I’ve seen him in a bathing suit. So the reason night swimming is fucked—not just on the Jersey Shore, but every fucking place in the world—is because that nice man, Steven Spielberg, is very afraid of the water.”

“The name of that boat is the Seven Seas,” Springsteen finished. “And I guarantee you, Steven Spielberg has not been in any of the water on any of those fucking seven seas.”

Springsteen added, of course, that he loves Spielberg and his wife, the filmmaker and artist Kate Capshaw. And he wanted to sing a song for them. So he broke into “Dancing in the Dark.”Ch

The whole night was like this. I’ve been to the MoMA Film Benefit a number of times, and it’s always a celebrity-stuffed evening at the museum, always sponsored by Chanel, a highlight of the season. But this was on another level. The museum was honoring a director synonymous with the modern era of blockbuster movies: the avatar of American celluloid excellence, the closest thing Hollywood has to a Michael Jordan. What’s more, there’s a true connection between the art institution and the director. His first theatrical feature, The Sugarland Express, had its New York premiere at MoMA, in 1974, as part of a series called New Directors/New Films.

“This is where it all began, here at MoMA,” Spielberg said. “Why did you wait so long to invite me back?”

He went on to praise the institution’s herculean efforts to restore films and add them to the collection. He also thanked Chanel for dressing him in a look way fancier than his usually quite casual (but fawned over) director ’fits, and for supporting the benefit over nearly two decades.

“MoMA’s dedication, since 1935, to curation, preservation, and restoration is what makes this honor so deeply personal for me, for all of us who love film,” Spielberg said.

Earlier in the night, Spielberg caught up with Amy Sherald, showing the artist some pictures on his phone, as Jeff Goldblum, who played Dr. Ian Malcolm in a little movie called Jurassic Park, pulled up to his table. Nearby, Christopher Walken—who had a great turn in Spielberg’s Catch Me If You Can—was wandering toward his seat, looking a bit lost, when another slightly older man came up to say hello. It was Robert De Niro.

The artist Taryn Simon and her husband, Jake Paltrow, were chatting with Christy Turlington Burns at the bar when Stephen Colbert went up to get a drink. Studio Museum director Thelma Golden was chatting with MoMA board president Sarah Arison, and Jennifer Lawrence strolled in with her husband, the art dealer Cooke Maroney. Michael Ovitz, the collector and MoMA board member for nearly four decades, who happens to also have a long history with Spielberg—“Michael Ovitz, my former agent from a long time ago!” Spielberg said onstage—invited the artist Nicolas Party and the novelist Sarah Blakley Cartwright to his table, with Larry Gagosian sitting nearby.

Lorne Michaels was chatting with collector Ray McGuire—though when everyone sat for the opening remarks, the seat across from Michaels remained mysteriously empty. Soon, a montage of iconic Spielberg clips filled the room. As the lights came up, a figure walked across the stage, mouthing the word “wow” over and over. Surprise: It was Tom Cruise. A MoMA rep, sitting near me, confirmed that Spielberg had no idea that the star of Minority Report and War of the Worlds would be attending the event.

“Since I was a young man, you were very generous with me, always on movie sets—and at your home with Kate, the meals that we had together, the hours that you shared talking about your films and what inspired making them,” Cruise said from the stage. “The stories about you as a young boy with that eight-millimeter camera. You were gracious enough to listen to my stories about the jobs that I took, so that I could buy the tickets to go see your movies.”

Cruise later waded into the crowd to hug his director and take that empty seat across from Michaels. MoMA director Christophe Cherix then got up to gush about his favorite Spielberg movies before introducing the next speaker: Martin Scorsese.

“The films he has made have changed the world. So art does matter. It always will,” Scorsese said. “We’re here tonight surrounded by art in the museum, and it’s really the appropriate setting all the more to honor Steven. And so Steve, I don’t want to… Listen, we’ve known each other since 1972, and how do we get to be in our 80s? What happened?”

To introduce Spielberg himself, the museum managed to rope in Steve Martin and Martin Short, who have never been in a Spielberg-directed movie. Actually, they have no obvious connection to the honoree, except for the fact that they’re two of the funniest people alive.

“You know Steven is very proud that he has never used AI in any of his films. By the way, AI is Steven’s nickname for us,” Steve Martin said.

“I’ll never forget the first time I saw Saving Private Ryan,” Martin Short said. “I found the film so mesmerizing that, halfway through, I whispered into my phone, ‘I’m going to have to call you back.’”

Spielberg was dying in his seat, just losing it laughing, and then had to follow up Martin and Short, which he compared to playing after a Taylor Swift concert. “Marty and Steve, I’d happily follow you anywhere, except up here,” the director joked.

Michelle Pfeiffer, Steven Spielberg, and Michelle Williams

He looked even more moved as Springsteen ripped through a no-bullshit, full-throated performance of “Dancing in the Dark,” which is not something you usually get to see at a museum that’s got The Starry Night and Les Demoiselles d’Avignon hanging upstairs. And then it was time to leave the museum, to go back to the reality of a stormy New York where you can’t catch a cab. In the coat check line, Spike Lee turned to Donna Langley, the studio head at Universal, for whom he’s made a number of pictures.

Then Lee bounced outside, giving a fist bump to every single security guard working the door at MoMA, greeting each of them with what’s going to be a lifelong mantra: “Knicks in five.” “Knicks in five.” “Knicks in five.”

#3561. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3560. A Look Inside the Scorpion Ball, Princess Grace Kelly’s Scorpio-Themed 40th Birthday Party

Grace Kelly always had a deep passion for astrology. Born on November 12, 1929, she was a Scorpio, and very proud of it. To celebrate her 40th birthday on November 15, 1969, the Princess of Monaco organized a party themed by her astrological sign, resulting in the extravagant Scorpio Ball, held at the Hôtel de l’Hermitage in Monte Carlo. For the occasion, she only invited celebrities who were also Scorpios. Among the 60 or so guests were Swedish actress Hjördis Paulina Genberg, American actor Rock Hudson, and Italian actress Virna Lisi.

Actor Richard Burton was also in attendance, accompanied by his wife Elizabeth Taylor, even though she was born under the sign of Pisces. An exception was made for the actress, who was granted special permission thanks to her husband’s astrological sign—Scorpio, born on November 10. For the occasion, Taylor chose to dazzle, wearing a Cartier diamond necklace with an estimated value of $1 million around her neck—a gift from Burton two weeks earlier. She also wore a spectacular evening cape by Tiziani, made of black velvet and adorned with two rhinestone scorpions on the front and a third on the hood.

Guests were required to adhere to a dress code devised by Kelly, inspired by the colors associated with the sign of Scorpio. Red, black, and white were therefore strongly recommended. The princess, for her part, opted for an off-the-shoulder black velvet dress by Balenciaga from the fall-winter 1967 couture collection. Two ruby brooches set with diamonds—a wedding gift from Prince Rainier III—completed her ensemble.

The decor also reflected the evening’s theme. Red candles, portraits of famous Scorpios, and a lavish cake adorned with golden scorpions set the tone. No detail had been left to chance: The waiters, wearing powdered 18th-century wigs, dressed in velvet suits embroidered with sparkling stars and held silver candelabras adorned with red candles.

Princess Grace was seen on numerous occasions alongside Carroll Righter, an astrologer and Hollywood columnist nicknamed “the astrologer to the stars.” According to People magazine, the princess’s birth chart also revealed a Scorpio ascendant, while her Midheaven was in Leo. In astrology, the Midheaven is associated with career, public image, and reputation. Some attributed her commanding presence and magnetism in the spotlight to this configuration.

Kelly embodied the mysterious aura that her admirers associated with her astrological sign. Unfortunately, that light was extinguished on September 14, 1982, when the Princess of Monaco lost her life in a tragic car accident on the hills above the principality.

#3559. Michael J. Fox's 3 Daughters, Wife Join Actor on Parkinson's Gala Red Carpet

Michael J. Fox had the support of his family during his latest Parkinson’s gala.

Stepping out together at the Saturday, November 14, event’s red carpet, the Back to the Future star posed for photos with wife Tracy Pollan and their three daughters: twins Aquinnah and Schuyler, 31, and Esmé, 25. (The couple are also parents to son Sam, 37, who did not appear to be in attendance.)

The Michael J. Fox Foundation’s A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to Cure Parkinson’s event at the Waldorf Astoria in New York City saw Fox, 65, opt for a black jacket and black pants with a navy tee, while Pollan, 66, and their daughters wore long gowns and had their hair styled in soft waves.

The actor, who was diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s disease in 1991 when he was 29, also posed for additional photos beside Pollan as the pair grinned for the cameras.

Pollan said in an interview with People at the event, which marked its 26th year, that the gala and wider foundation continues to raise vital funds for the scientists who need it. “Just the huge and amazing amount of money that’s been raised that goes directly into the scientists’ pockets, and they can just do all the work that’s necessary [to finding a cure],” she told the magazine. “We really are seeing so much progress.”

Pollan also spoke about the family’s mindset as they continue to navigate Fox’s diagnosis. “I think you just have to do it day by day,” the actress, who married the actor in 1988 after meeting him on the set of Family Ties, told People. “You have to look at what’s in front of you … and you have to stay in the moment, and if the moment is OK, that’s where you are.”

Fox stepped out with his son at March’s SAG-AFTRA’s 2026 Actor Awards for a rare public appearance. During an address to the cameras, Fox spoke directly about Sam, who was seated beside him. “Sometimes I like to remind them, ‘If I weren’t an actor, they wouldn’t be here.’ By the way, he’s not an actor — he’s my date,” the Shrinking star quipped while gesturing to his son. “I’m Michael J. Fox. I’m a dad and I’m an actor.”

In addition to fatherhood and acting, Fox’s contributions to Parkinson’s disease research were also recognized publicly this year. While receiving the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award at September’s Emmy Awards, Fox spoke on stage about how far his attitude toward his disease had come over time.

“I [later] understood that accepting Parkinson’s didn’t mean I had to surrender to it,” he told the crowd, who gave Fox a standing ovation once his speech had wrapped. “It just meant doing everything I could for everyone living with this disease … I’m proud of the progress we’ve made.”

#3558. Jensen Huang’s Potentially Seismic Art Retreat

Welcome to True Colors. I’m in Manhattan. Lots to get into this week. There’s the matter of what to do about a major new San Francisco arts institution that was set to be named after Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang. Understandably, it’s a question whether that renaming will still happen given…everything. There’s my ode to the death of the Cybertruck. And there’s all the details from the star-studded MoMA Film Benefit honoring Steven Spielberg. Tom Cruise shocked the crowd with surprise remarks, and Bruce Springsteen roasted the director. It was a whole night.

MENTIONED IN THIS ISSUE: Donald Trump, Jason Calacanis, Brendan Dugan, Siniša Mačković, David Zwirner, Lorenzo Amos, Kate Capshaw, Zohran Mamdani, Jessica Craig-Martin, Dean & DeLuca, Indochine, Stanley Whitney, Marina Adams, Will Whitney, The Beverly Hills Hotel, Elon Musk, Lana Del Rey, Grimes, Travis Scott, Pharrell Williams, 21 Savage, Tyler, the Creator, Bad Bunny, Julia Wachtel, Todd von Ammon, Frieda Toranzo Jaeger.

The major arts institution named for Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori, appears to be—shocker!—very much in jeopardy.

Just months ago, Huang was getting a phone call from President Trump while onstage at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles. “I’m here with the besties, Mr. President,” a laughing Huang said, putting his phone up to the mic. “Tell him I say hi!” said All-In cohost Jason Calacanis.

But Huang’s recent weeks have not been marked by good times with the besties. First, the Democrats took over Congress, throttling all the goodwill he built with the administration. Then he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by the US to be a Chinese spy—and then news of another affair, this time allegedly with a subordinate, came via a shocking New York Times bombshell. Amid rumors that yet another affair would soon break, he stepped down as CEO and, according to Forbes, has watched nearly $20 billion of his estimated net worth vaporize since Monday.

What’s unknown is the current state of his relationship with his wife, Lori Huang—and their ambitious plans for an arts organization that was set to bear their name. Earlier this year, the Huangs pledged $75 million to Vanderbilt University in order to help transform the soon-to-be-closed legendary San Francisco art school California College of the Arts into part of Vanderbilt’s SF campus. Vanderbilt announced that it planned to name a portion of its SF campus the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design.

Which is now a bit awkward, given the multiple alleged affairs, and the whole Chinese-spy thing. Plus, Huang is no longer affiliated with Nvidia, which teamed up with CCA in 2025 to form the CCA-Nvidia Incubator for Creative Intelligence. Will Jensen and Lori Huang still put their names together on arts organizations after all that’s happened? And if there is no Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design, what will happen to Vanderbilt’s SF campus when it opens next year?

The CCA was started in 1907, and Huang and his wife were expected to support its transition to a new chapter. It would be a shame if this is how it ends. Reps at Vanderbilt didn’t get back to me.

It’s a new era in Tribeca. Tonight, Karma, a burgeoning mega-gallery with spaces in New York’s Chelsea and LA’s Hollywood, opens its new gallery at 38 White Street. Founder Brendan Dugan and director Siniša Mačković took me on a tour earlier this week, and it’s easily one of the most generous spaces anywhere in the neighborhood. Plus, an outpost of Karma Bookstore—a much needed bookstore for a neighborhood shockingly lacking in one—is coming in right across the street.

This will be the latest big-tent blue chipper to take a space in the Triangle Below Canal, as they used to call this neighborhood. Something to consider: In the last few years, mega-galleries such as David Zwirner and Hauser & Wirth have shut their uptown townhouses and opened downtown.

Also opening tonight is a White Street outpost of Gratin gallery, which has a roster of incredibly exciting young stars, including Lorenzo Amos (whom we wrote about a year ago). I’m hearing about other younger dealers grabbing spaces in the neighborhood. The art market isn’t exactly on fire, but dealers are betting on one thing: the enduring power and capital of New York City.

Speaking of New York, guess who’s lived here full-time for almost a year? Steven Spielberg, that’s who. On New Year’s Day 2026, the GOAT American director—who is married to the artist Kate Capshaw—moved his official residence from California to New York, and has made the apartment in the San Remo his home base. You will not be surprised to hear that, post-move, Spielberg is doing extremely cool stuff in town. He’s walking around with a script and a Tracy Kidder book while slugging down an iced McCafé. He’s getting lunch at Benvenuto Cafe. He’s having Mayor Zohran Mamdani over to the crib.

The only thing left was for one of the city’s great museums to throw a big party for the Hollywood-royalty-gone-Gotham. Last night, Spielberg got just that: He was honored at the MoMA Film Benefit, sponsored by Chanel. I was there. Read the full report—with fun pictures!—here.

Also on VF this week: an exclusive excerpt from an uproarious new memoir by artist Jessica Craig-Martin, I Regret I am Able to Attend. Craig-Martin is a real treasure of the art world, a great photographer—and, as it turns out, a hell of a writer. The whole book is a compulsively readable blast. The chapter where Craig-Martin recalls working as an extremely inexperienced, occasionally larcenous teller at Dean & DeLuca is one of the funniest, most satisfying New York vignettes I’ve read this year. And of course, all the scuttlebutt from the ’80s art scene is fabulous. Read the excerpt, in which our narrator spills all the tea—and, um, stuff stronger than tea—about working as a waitress when Indochine opened.

Happy 80th birthday to the great painter Stanley Whitney. His wife, the artist Marina Adams, and son, dealer Will Whitney, threw Stanley a party to celebrate his octogenarian status on Nine Orchard’s roof, overlooking Dimes Square. Writers, artists, dealers, old heads, everyone was there. A fabulous Wednesday night.

This year’s celebrity Halloween costumes were well worth talking about. From Zendaya channeling a 2000s Halle Berry to Carmen Electra going full Catwoman, the creativity that went into each costume was truly impressive. But even though Halloween is over, actress Jessica Chastain has taken it upon herself to dress up as Jessica Rabbit. I’ve got to say, I’m surprised this is happening shortly after the spooky season, but I'm not mad at it.

In many of Chastain’s best movies, she takes on a variety of looks. Whether it’s early 20th-century garb in Crimson Peak or portraying a blonde ‘60s housewife in The Help, each film's costume really adds to her transformative performances. But I have to say that even though the Oscar winner didn't dress as Jessica Rabbit for a movie, this costume is still quite impressive. It's unclear if her Flaunt Magazine photoshoot actually happened after Halloween, but the photographer is sharing pics on his Instagram now:

A post shared by Greg Swales (@gregswalesart)

Whoa, baby! I can’t believe it’s taken this long for the Zero Dark Thirty actress to dress as this sultry animated character. That shiny, silk red dress is the perfect way to show the femme fatale character’s seductive qualities. This has always been a perfect fit for her, as she’s already got the Who Framed Roger Rabbit character’s first name and her signature red locks. Now, we just need to hear Chastain sing “Why Don’t You Do Right?” and she’s a shoo-in for her own Jessica Rabbit live-action solo movie (if a studio ever chooses to greenlight one).

Of course, Jessica Chastain isn't the first person to ever channel the beloved cartoon character. This past Halloween, 90 Day Fiancé’s Kara Leona had a perfect Jessica Rabbit costume, with her dark red hair matching her red dress perfectly. Also, in 2015, Heidi Klum’s Jessica Rabbit costume looked just like the cartoon (and it was kinda scary). Chloe Bailey, dressed as Roger Rabbit’s wife for Halloween in 2024, was also very eye-popping with her sequined red dress, long purple gloves and cigarette holder.

While I think Chastain's shoot would've been well-timed for Halloween, I think it's refreshing to see her as the “Drawn That Way” icon after the fact. Her vintage, glamorous appearance is like looking at a red-headed Marilyn Monroe. It’s hard to look away.

Of course, there's also a good reason the character is so beloved, as she's not only her own woman but she also stands by her man (or rabbit). While some may say Rabbit is too attractive for Roger, she said in Who Framed Roger Rabbit that it didn’t take much for her husband to win her over. The show-stopping cartoon simply said, “He makes me laugh.” In that way, she's not a vain character, and it's not hard to see why she's so respected.

Needless to say, Jessica Chastain was born to wear this costume, and she once again proves that she's a truly fabulous star. Here's hoping this won't be the last time she decides to channel a beloved character of any kind.

You can see why Jessica Rabbit is such a popular Halloween costume by streaming Who Framed Roger Rabbit with a Disney+ subscription. You can also watch Chastain’s new streaming release, Heartland, which is available with an active Netflix subscription.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3554. Martin McDonagh Calls Sam Rockwell “One of the Best Actors of His Generation, If Not the Best”

Director Martin McDonagh has become as well-known for making memorable films as he is for writing the complex male friendships within them.

"I like mining down into the sensitivity that I think a lot of male relationships do have, but aren't as – especially in American films – explored sensitively," he said about the subject during a panel conversation at the inaugural Vanity Fair Screening Room at LACMA on Friday. "It's not just a buddy film, and it's not a romance, and it's not just about cool CIA guys," McDonagh continued. “It's sort of the opposite in other ways. And that I think is interesting to explore because I think my male relationships are that way. They can be sensitive and sad and happy and all the things that a female relationship can be. So I think that's why I keep coming back to it.”

The conversation, which featured McDonagh and the film’s stars John Malkovich and Mariana di Girolamo, was moderated by VF's Senior Hollywood Correspondent Rebecca Ford following an exclusive screening of their new film, Wild Horse Nine. The acclaimed dark comedy follows two CIA agents (Malkovich and Sam Rockwell) who are not only behind the plan to overthrow the Chilean government in 1973, but have also had a hand in several other significant historical moments in the US and abroad.

Maria di Girolamo, John Malkovich and Martin McDonagh, in conversation with Rebecca Ford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on Friday, November 13, 2026.

Malkovich and Rockwell's characters engage in pithy, often hilarious banter throughout the film, and their onscreen chemistry is a highlight.

John Malkovich at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

"I love Sam," said Malkovich. “I knew him a bit socially before this, but I'd worked with him once before, which was a great pleasure on a film called A Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. He's like a kind of expert trainer at SeaWorld who can get the whales and the sharks and the dolphins to show things in exchange for a fish. And Sam is a great student of acting. He is a great student of film and of theater, and he's great fun, very hardworking, and just an ideal colleague. I couldn't imagine a better colleague than Sam and I've had some excellent colleagues.”

"He's one of the best actors of his generation, if not the best," adds McDonagh of Rockwell. "He's always surprising, always dangerous, always sensitive, always smart, always coming up with new stuff. And I think there's a danger to him that's lovely to write for. We always hope the characters will always be surprising, and with Sam's voice in the head, that really helps."

Mariana di Girolamo at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

For rising star Mariana di Girolamo, a Chilean actress making her English language movie debut with Wild Horse Nine, she was excited and only slightly intimidated to be a part of the cast.

"It was quite a challenge to perform for the first time in English," she said. "I prepared myself with a coach and we rehearsed with John, Sam and Parker [Posey] and Ailin [Salas] in a public theater in New York where I heard the script for the first time. That was amazing for me, for us." di Girolamo, who is very familiar with the fraught period of Chilean history depicted in the film, said she appreciated how McDonagh put it all in context. "It was my first time approaching that period of time in this way with this very beautiful dark humor. I was laughing about these things and feeling empathy with these CIA agents that committed a lot of horrific, horrific things. I've never read something like that, and the arc of my character is so beautiful, unique, I really wanted to be part of this."

Martin McDonagh at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair's Screening Room pairs this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that includes post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. The invitation-only events are welcoming an audience from the worlds of film, fashion, culture, politics, media, and tech, much like the magazine itself. VF editor Daniel Kile introduced the first screening, welcoming the audience to the Steve Tisch Theater at LACMA, which is not yet open to the public.

Maria di Girolamo, John Malkovich and Martin McDonagh, in conversation with Rebecca Ford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on Friday, November 13, 2026.

Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

#3553. Andrew Scott On What Makes Elsinore “So Moving”

Although the emotional core of Elsinore is centered around beloved actor Ian Charleston dealing with terminal illness, its star Andrew Scott says the film has as much heart as it does humor.

“The most singular thing about our film I think is the humor in it,” he said during a panel conversation at the inaugural Vanity Fair Screening Room at LACMA on Friday. “The tragedy in some ways is a little bit like Hamlet itself, but you can't make a film about Ian Charleston without having gags in it. He was incredibly funny. Every person [who knew him] said he was just wickedly funny, and flirtatious, and he was always looking towards the light, and he had a certain degree of courage. So that is something I think that we all share as a sense of humor.”

Andrew Scott, Billie Piper, Stephen Beresford and Rebecca Ford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

Elsinore tells the story of Scottish actor Ian Charleson (Scott) who attempts to perform Hamlet at the National Theatre while secretly living with AIDS. Scott has received early acclaim for his powerful portrayal of Charleson. Before the film began Vanity Fair’s West Coast Editor John Ross warned the audience that "first you're going to laugh, then you're going to cry," while watching Scott’s performance.

“I think … why the film is so moving is because [Charleson’s] not wallowing at any point. He was insanely courageous,” continued Scott. “So that to me was the thing that we were the most

insistent on in some ways. And that's really all down to finding actors who in this extraordinary ensemble have a really terrific sense of humor. And we kind of knew that we could, with the screenplay, get the best actors in the country. And I feel we did.”

The panel conversation featured Scott, costar Billie Piper, and writer Stephen Beresford, moderated by VF's Senior Hollywood Correspondent Rebecca Ford, following an exclusive screening of the film.

Billie Piper at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

For Piper, who plays Charleston's close friend Patsy, she relied heavily on Beresford's script for her prep, as well as information she gleaned from those who actually knew Patsy, and Charleston.

“I've spoken to a few members of the family, their friends, and then I sort of cherry-picked things from people I'd known in the beginning of my career, the louder figures in our industry,” she said. “And then I did my own interpretation and just had a good time. It's a very moving story, but I had a lot of fun playing that part. She's a really joyful character to play, I enjoyed the comedy. And I understand that a lot of her jokes are coming from a place of despair.”

Beresford, who has known Scott for 25 years, said he didn't initially think of his longtime friend for the role, but should have.

“The story of Ian, and Ian's Hamlet [performance] is legendary in the British theater,” he said. “So many people said it was the greatest Hamlet they'd ever seen, and that it had this incredible quality. So I knew about the story, and then it was brought to me actually as an idea by a producer who said, ‘What about writing about Ian Charleston, and what about Andrew playing Ian Charleston?’ And then I just thought, ‘Well, why didn't I have that idea myself five years ago?’ So yeah, that's really how it happened, and I started to research it, the details of the story were so incredible, and so moving.”

Stephen Beresford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026.

Scott, who famously played Hamlet onstage 150 times beginning in 2017, prior to filming Elsinore, closed out the panel conversation by reciting his favorite line from the classic tragedy.

“When Hamlet says the line about the war that was going on—and this was written 400 years ago—it just seems so relevant to what he might have been experiencing at the time, which is: ‘I see the imminent death of 20,000 men who for a fantasy, a trick of fame, go to their graves like beds.’ The idea that that was written 400 years ago, and that he was watching 50 percent of his friends die for no reason and be neglected by governments, and derided by the public. And it was just happening, and happening time and time again.”

Scott continued: “The reason that I love it so much is that when I was doing Hamlet myself, of course I wasn't thinking about the AIDS crisis, but the enduring nature of art, something that was written 400 years ago by Shakespeare, could actually be of use to somebody in 1989 and then be reproduced again in 2026 and be of use. And that idea of art being useful down the lines is so moving to me.”

Vanity Fair's Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci, Elsinore stars Andrew Scott and Billie Piper and writer Stephen Beresford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026.

#3552. Dustin Hoffman Tried To 'Fire Himself' From Rain Man, But A Tom Cruise Scene Changed His Mind

An Oscar-winning role that almost didn’t happen

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There is no question that Raymond Babbitt in Rain Man is one of Dustin Hoffman’s most celebrated roles. Hoffman won his second career Oscar for the role in the Barry Levinson-directed hit co-starring Tom Cruise as Ray’s brother, Charlie. The movie, which can be seen with an HBO Max subscription, received widespread acclaim, winning Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Original Screenplay at the 1989 Oscars. Cruise, however, wasn’t nominated (he has still never won an Oscar), which is a shame, because not only is he great in Rain Man, but he also played a key role in Hoffman staying with the movie, even though he “fired himself” on the first day of filming.

The legendary Hoffman recently sat down with GQ to do a career retrospective, and when talking about Rain Man, he told the story of how he really hated the way things were going on the first day of production. He thought his own performance of the autistic Ray was so poor that he told Levinson he would be happy to pay for the time, but he wanted to bail out early. Hoffman said of that first day:

It was a scene where we're standing around a car, Tom Cruise and I, and I said I'm quitting. I can't do this. It's awful.  And I knew it was awful, and it was. And I went up to the director, Barry Levinson, and I said, ‘I'm firing myself. I don't know what I'm doing. What I say sounds like…like five different parts I played in films. I'm putting them all [together] because I don't know what I'm doing.’

Levinson, to his credit, didn’t want to hear that from Hoffman and convinced him to stick with it for a couple of weeks, because he trusted that Hoffman would find the character. So Hoffman stayed on, but still had serious doubts. They went on for a few days, and Hoffman was still frustrated, unable to really find Raymond’s core.

While praising Cruise for his work ethic (and presumably his patience), Hoffman talks about another scene between the two actors as they drive across the country later in the movie. Shot after shot, Cruise was ad-libbing, and Hoffman, in his own words, explains that he just hated what he (Hoffman) was doing across from Cruise:

We had to do a scene where we're both in the car. He's driving, and I'm sitting in the passenger seat. It's about 10 minutes of film in each camera.  So, you know, do the 10 minutes that's in each [reel] and then just improvise. We do it two or three times, and I can't do it. And so when we were doing the scene, and he was brilliantly improvising.

This goes on for reel after reel, and Hoffman still isn’t feeling it. He went one:

We do it, we do it for hours. And I say to Barry, I can't, I really can't do it. He says, come here, I think, I think I found something. And on the two-shot, on both of us, Tom is asking me questions, and all I'm saying is, ‘Yeah,’ because I don't know what the fuck else to say.  I don't have an idea of this guy.

What Levinson had found in those scenes was that Hoffman had Ray. Hoffman realized that Levinson was right. He had found the character, and the rest is history. Rain Man and Dustin Hoffman would go on to win all those awards, and the movie remains, almost 4 decades later, one of the most beloved movies of the era. It really is too bad Cruise didn’t get the recognition he clearly deserved for one of his best roles.

The microphones are used in almost all of its features, like ANC, Adaptive Sound Control, and the headphones' Ambient Sound mode. They hear your surroundings to adapt their features accordingly.
