#3514. I Ain't Got No Body: The Various Non-Corporeal Aliens In Star Trek Explained

Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.

One of the primary features of "Star Trek" is theoretical biology. Given the wide panoply of alien species on display throughout the franchise, audiences have been invited to ponder alternate evolutionary paths besides the one that happened to bring us into being on Earth. What kind of planetary conditions would be required to form, say, a hyper-intelligent crystalline being? How did a horta evolve? What will we evolve into in the future? Will our brains adapt to become psychic over time? According to the "Star Trek: Voyager" episode "Threshold" (one of the show's most outraging to fans), it was revealed that humans will eventually evolve into giant salamanders.

This leads to a few logical evolutionary extremes, like the fact that some species on "Star Trek" have evolved into beings of pure energy. "Star Trek" has many examples of non-corporeal aliens who can only be perceived as light, as a psychic presence, as a sound, or as a vision beamed directly into our inferior, corporeal brains. To cite a notable example: In the original series episode "Is There In Truth No Beauty?," audiences were introduced to the Medusans, a highly intelligent, telepathic, and empathic species whose light-constructed bodies are so wildly complex that any human looking at them would instantly go mad. Only a mentally disciplined species like the Vulcans could look at a Medusan, and even then required a special filtered visor (pictured above).

These kinds of aliens expand the audience's mind as to what can be considered life.

In looking at fictional non-corporeal species, "Star Trek" expands our horizons. We're invited to ponder new perspectives about basic concepts like evolution, time, the nature of consciousness, and, perhaps, our own relationship to the cosmos. Non-corporeal entities are one of the coolest ideas "Star Trek" has to offer, and their recurring nature is a constant reminder that life is more complex, and the cosmos more ineffable, than we could ever hope to imagine.

On "Star Trek," non-corporeal aliens tend to appear as lights or clouds or glowing mists of energy. One might recall the smoke-like alien that made Kirk nervous in the episode "Obsession," one of the more underrated episodes of the show. Others might immediately think of Zefram Cochrane's glowing, cloud-like "companion" in the episode "Metamorphosis." That entity had the ability to sort of intuitively communicate with Cochrane (Glenn Corbett), and could also heal diseases and sustain human life beyond its usual biological barriers. A common theme of non-corporeal entities on "Star Trek" is that they are godlike and powerful, able to tap into the powers of the universe in ways we don't understand.

The Medusans may be one of the most popular non-corporeal entities on "Star Trek," but fans of "Deep Space Nine" would surely want me to acknowledge the wormhole aliens, a.k.a. The Prophets. In that show's pilot episode, "Emissary," Benjamin Sisko (Avery Brooks) travels into a stable wormhole and encounters bodiless creatures who can only communicate with him by appearing as people from his memories.

The wormhole aliens from "Deep Space Nine" are so, well, alien, they don't understand concepts like linguistic communication or linear time. They don't see cause leading to effect, but rather a widespread series of events that happen all at once. Sisko has to do the impossible, and explain the human habit of seeing time as a straight line.

And, of course, there are many species of godlike beings on "Star Trek" who often take the form of humans, despite not having physical bodies. Q (John de Lancie) from "Star Trek: The Next Generation" is one of these beings, as is Trelane (William Campbell) from the original series. Those two beings tend to see corporeal humans as lesser species and amuse themselves by taunting and playing with them. Less whimsical is Kevin Uxbridge (John Anderson), a member of a powerful energy species called the Douwd. Kevin took the form of a human, married, and witnessed his wife killed, leading him to, in a moment of ill-temper, commit instant galaxy-wide genocide of a single species. He's the deadliest character in all of "Star Trek."

The list goes on. Q tormented the Calamarain, which exist as ionized gas. There are the Organians, the Lights of Zetar, and the godlike Metrons, the latter of whom oversaw the fight between Kirk (William Shatner) and the Gorn in the episode "Arena," and plenty of other examples. In most cases, non-corporeal entities are so far beyond human experience, it's difficult to communicate with them, much less come to some kind of diplomatic understanding.

But sometimes non-corporeal entities do become our friends. On "Star Trek: Prodigy," the character of Zero (Angus Imrie) is a Medusan who managed to construct a robot-like vehicle for themselves, allowing them to interact with us flesh-beings without exposing themselves. Sometimes the ineffability of the cosmos works in our favor.

#3513. Anne Hathaway's 2024 Romance Movie Is A Must-Watch For Colleen Hoover Fans

We're in a golden age of romance movies based on popular books, over which presides queen Colleen Hoover. There have been four movies based on Colleen Hoover novels and they've thus far ranged from sort of okay to entirely forgettable. But there's no denying it can be fun to settle down with a film you know is going to be absolute nonsense and just turn off your brain while two hot people fall in love and do it and stuff. Unfortunately, once you've watched the four Hoover films, you're stuck with the books until the author decides which of her stories to adapt next. In the meantime, may I direct your attention to a romance starring Anne Hathaway and Nicholas Galitzine, which at least tries to be more than an excuse for more hot people doing it scenes.

"The Idea of You" sees Hathaway falling for He-Man in a romantic comedy that, wouldn't you know it, is based on a book — because Hollywood will seemingly only green-light love stories if they've been pre-approved by BookTok. This one adapts actress turned author Robinne Lee's 2017 novel of the same name, in which she tackled the notion of women losing their desirability post-40. The movie similarly explores this idea via Hathaway and Galitzine's age gap relationship, and did so successfully for the most part.

Hathaway, of course, starred in the latest Hoover adaptation, the dead-on-arrival "Verity," which was helmed by "The Idea of You" director Michael Showalter. Sadly, for those expecting a fairly straightforward romance, the "Devil Wears Prada" star spent a good chunk of the movie sitting motionless and glaring at Dakota Johnson while she stole her husband. "The Idea of You," however, was a much better Showalter x Hathaway collab, and it's available to stream right now on Prime Video.

With its older-woman-falls-for-boy-band-singer narrative, you'd be forgiven for thinking "The Idea of You" is a movie that started as fanfiction. But in a 2024 TIME article, Robinne Lee pushed back against interpretations of her book being Harry Styles fanfiction and explained the real impetus for her story. "I was learning the hard way that in Hollywood, after 40, women are much less desirable," she wrote. "The assumption was that we ceased to be sexual beings and were thus less valuable. I was eager to prove the industry—and our culture at large—wrong, in my own little way." Lee, who criticized those who dubbed her book "fluff" or "fanfiction," saw her story as being about "a woman's midlife sexual awakening," and strove to ensure it was both "tantalizing and complex."

Much of that is preserved in the 2024 film adaptation, which Michael Showalter co-wrote with Jennifer Westfeldt. Anne Hathaway plays single mother and art gallery owner Solène Marchand, who accompanies her teenage daughter to Coachella. There, she meets Hayes Campbell (Nicholas Galitzine), the lead singer of boy band August Moon and all round handsome English gent. Despite there being several years between the two, Solène and Hayes share an instant connection and embark on a passionate love affair. But the latter's popstar status invites scrutiny, and as you might expect given Lee's explanation of her novel, most of it is an excuse to attack the 40-year-old Solène for being with a younger man and generally hurl misogynistic abuse.

Can the pair's relationship survive? You'll have to watch "The Idea of You" on Prime Video to find out — which, if you're reeling from the absolute nonsense that was "Verity," is well worth doing.

"The Idea of You" premiered at the 2024 South by Southwest film festival before going straight to Amazon Prime Video in May of that year. While that direct-to-streaming trajectory might typically indicate a less than stellar romantic comedy, "The Idea of You" actually earned some impressive reviews — a testament to Robinne Lee's efforts to go beyond your typical romantic fiction fare as well as Michael Showalter and Jennifer Westfeldt's ability to preserve that effort in their adaptation.

On Rotten Tomatoes, the film holds a very respectable 81% "certified fresh" critic score — a damn sight better than the 32% "Verity" managed to eke out. /Film's Ryan Scott was certainly impressed, writing in his "The Idea of You" review, "this is the genre at its best." Otherwise, reviewers were won over by Anne Hathaway and Nicholas Galitzine's chemistry and performances. That's to be expected in Hathaway's case. The actor is usually the best thing about any movie she's in, and while there are arguably more compelling modern Hathaway performances — her chilling 2023 thriller that flew completely under the radar, "Eileen," being one example — she does a fine job in "The Idea of You," conveying all the vulnerability and strength of the Solène Marchand in Lee's original novel.

Galitzine, meanwhile, is also perfectly charming if a bit too impressed with himself. The man is no stranger to romance stories, either, having starred alongside Netflix's romance queen Sofia Carson in 2022's "Purple Hearts" (watch that if you want a more straightforward romantic drama). Otherwise, "The Idea of You" is a great palette cleanser for recovering "Verity" viewers but should also go down well with Colleen Hoover fans craving a bit more romance from their Hathaway-led entertainment.

Mormon Wives: Orange County doesn’t exactly live up to its name.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’ve ever watched The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives, you know there’s no shortage of drama. Just look at Taylor Frankie Paul, who’s had a swingers scandal, the cancellation of her season of The Bachelorette, custody issues with her children, and chaos surrounding production. But the Hulu reality series was popular and created a lot of buzz, so I was not surprised when they announced the spinoff, The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, currently on the 2026 TV schedule. However, the fact that it feels like the majority of the women in the new show are not Mormon and that some aren’t even wives is a bit weird and an interesting choice, considering the title, and viewers (including myself) have taken notice.

To catch you up in case you haven’t seen the original series, Jen Affleck, a 20-something Mormon wife and mother, joined MomTok in Utah to fight against the typical social norms and stereotypes that are common within the religion. After appearing in Season 34 of Dancing with the Stars as a celebrity contestant alongside fellow Mormon Wives star Whitney Leavitt, the mother of three with a fourth on the way decided to stay in Southern California, citing the fracturing of MomTok and the need for therapy to recover from everything that happened.

Seeming to instead have decided to jump right into another reality series, which again is an interesting choice, Jen has brought together a new group of friends, all of whom are mothers with their own drama and secrets, but who are not all Mormon, despite the show’s name. One has even admitted to signing on for the heightened visibility reality TV brings.

It’s hard not to notice that The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County is a cast divided into two groups, with the women who are Mormons being outnumbered by the women who are not. In the season premiere, cast member Aspyn Ovard (who's got a memorable storyline about being part of a throuple) says, “We’ve all been shaped by Mormonism in one way or another,” which is a bit of a vague statement when we don’t know all the details of the backgrounds of many of these women, and even she makes it clear that she’s very closed off to the church and its teachings.

I'm not the only one who has noticed this either, as this conversation has popped up all over social media, including places like Reddit, where fans have asked why non-Mormons are "even on the show." I get it's weird to call out someone's religious preferences, but when your show is called Secret Lives of Mormon Wives, I do think that leads to a certain expectation.

When you’re in the business of entertainment, building a franchise off of something successful and popular makes sense. But it’s hard to escape the weirdness of not really delivering on what your show’s title promises. All of this is not to say that the women who make up the OC spinoff cast don’t have compelling lives of their own, because they do, but the religious branding doesn’t entirely fit and feels like more of a subplot than a main focus, like it is in the original series.

And it all makes me wonder if the title should have just been something more reflective of Jen Affleck specifically? Just spitballing here.

For a reality show that’s supposed to be centered around Mormons, The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County actually positions them to be the villains of the season. McCall DaPron, the older sister of the OG series’ Mayci Neeley, exhibits confrontational behavior. She gets into frequent clashes with other cast members, often leaving them to wonder whether it’s possible to keep this friend group together.

Her strong commitment to her faith and her efforts to share it with others, including best friend and co-star Jordan McClanahan (whom she successfully converted), rubs anyone not as devoted the wrong way. This is especially true when her need to influence others’ opinions and actions creates conflict.

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives has had a seemingly endless amount of drama and scandals over four seasons, which are streaming with a Hulu subscription, but Mayci always came across like the most supportive one of the group on that show, where McCall seems less inclined to stay neutral. It’s hard to know how much of the drama is manipulated with editing, but it’s another interesting choice on a series that already seems to be trying to break its own formula.

All of this said, if there ends up being a second season of the OC spinoff, I will still definitely be tuning in!

Between Jen being pregnant with her fourth child at the same time she decides she wants a divorce, Aspyn trying to get her ex-husband to spend time with her current throuple, and Salomé Andrea figuring out if she can reconcile with a man she began dating in ninth grade and couldn’t marry in the Mormon church before she ultimately walked away from both, it is all definitely weird, but just weird enough to make me want to see what happens next.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe are down to $199 from $359 ahead of Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. #3510. Leonard Nimoy Loved This Star Trek Episode That Allowed Him To Show Off A Different Side Of Spock

What was Leonard Nimoy's favorite "Star Trek" episode? It's almost a trick question. Human beings are constantly changing and fickle creatures; the answer to our favorite anything can change depending on our moods. Nimoy, who played Spock for almost 50 years, couldn't be expected to give one consistent answer for that long.

But there are a few episodes that Nimoy consistently named among his favorites, including in his 1975 autobiography "I Am Not Spock." One of them was "This Side of Paradise," co-written by D. C. Fontana and Nathan Butler and one of the best Spock episodes of "Star Trek." The Enterprise visits colony world Omicron Ceti III, home to a plant species that secretes spores that take root in humanoid hosts. Once they do, the hosts remain in a state of perfect bliss, but they also lose all their ambition. (The story is a likely reference to the Lotus-Eaters in "The Odyssey.")

Spock is one of the infected. His stone face cracks into rubble as he becomes joyful, happily expressive, and even rekindles a romance with local botanist Leila Kalomi (Jill Ireland). Nimoy wrote in "I Am Not Spock" that he enjoyed the episode for showing Spock in a mood we almost never saw him — not coldly logical, sarcastic, or struggling to control his emotions, but genuinely carefree.

"This is a very special episode for me for obvious reasons and particularly because, where Spock was so totally adult in most of his attitudes and reactions throughout the series, this episode provided a chance to expose the complete child within. We saw him loving, picnicking, romping, and literally swinging playfully in the trees. It was a total exposure of internal Spock that so many people have always suspected was there."

Watching "This Side of Paradise" now, it might remind you of the Apple TV series "Pluribus," where all of humanity is turned into a blissful hive mind (collectively "The Others"). In "This Side of Paradise," strong negative emotions literally destroy the spores, which is also a weakness of the Others in "Pluribus."

In "This Side of Paradise," though, there's no identity theft. The spores let Spock be his innermost self. Compare other times we see Spock's emotions come out, like in "The Naked Time" where he cries over having never told his mother he loved her, or "Journey to Babel" where said mother, Amanda (Jane Wyatt), recounts how Spock used to cry because other Vulcan children bullied him. As only a half-Vulcan, Spock is especially self-conscious about living up to his people's teachings about logic.

When the spores hit him, those anxieties melt away. Note how Leila says to him he has "no need to hide [his] inner face anymore" and Spock says "I can love you," as if finally allowing himself something he'd previously denied.

Nimoy described other "Star Trek" episodes as favorites such as "Devil in the Dark," where the Enterprise crew visit a mining colony to find a creature killing the inhabitants. The culprit, a Horta (resembling a pile of living molten lava), is sentient and Spock telepathically communicates with it, discovering it was only acting to protect its offspring. Nimoy praised that one as a "wonderful episode about the fear of the unknown," and "Devil in the Dark" is known to be a favorite of William Shatner's, too.

"Devil in the Dark" and "This Side of Paradise" are very different episodes, but both ones anchored by Spock. Little surprise that Leonard Nimoy loved them.

#3509. 6 Horror Series Better Than American Horror Story

From TV powerhouse Ryan Murphy, American Horror Story's first season, Murder House, drew immediate attention with its all-star cast that included Connie Britton, Dylan McDermott, Jennifer Lange, Sarah Paulson, and Frances Conroy. Even more importantly, Murder House was genuinely compelling, balancing horror, drama, and emotional depth in one self-contained season.

At the time, a horror anthology felt both unique and timeless, evoking nostalgia for series like The Twilight Zone while still delivering something modern and fresh. For the next several years, American Horror Story continued to successfully reinvent itself, attracting stars like Lady Gaga, Kathy Bates, and Angela Bassett, and making new ones out of the likes of Evan Peters and Emma Roberts.

In its prime, the anthology format seemed to promise that American Horror Story could live forever. Eventually, though, the show began to feel like a caricature of itself, relying on the allure of fan-favorite actors and buzzy pieces of stunt casting. The show's horror became more campy and less genuinely scary, and new stories increasingly connected to previous ones in attempts to recapture the original magic.

This reached an unprecedented level in the show's most recent season, 13, which was a massive crossover of American Horror Story's first five seasons, as well as Cult and Apocalypse​​​. The thinnest of storylines connected the ambitious mashup, and even as fan-favorite actors reprised their most iconic roles, 13 felt like it forgot the show's own plot, making it a shell of what American Horror Story once was.

Though American Horror Story was once a pillar of the horror television landscape, these six shows have far surpassed the example it set.

Today, Mike Flanagan is the king of horror television. With hits ranging from the original Midnight Mass to the latest adaptation of Stephen King's Carrie, the writer and showrunner has proven that he is far from a one-hit wonder when it comes to telling scary stories on TV. His very first TV projects, though, felt truly like an elevated American Horror Story.

The Haunting of Hill House, inspired by Shirley Jackson's novel of the same name, was an immediate hit that put Netflix on the map for its horror limited series. Both terrifying and emotionally poignant, Hill House took extensive creative liberties from its source material to tell a story that felt simultaneously gothic and contemporary.

The same could be said of Flanagan's next limited series, The Haunting of Bly Manor. While Bly Manor was technically its own, separate show, it shared a title format, theme music, and tagline ("You're expected") with Hill House, setting the stage for a Haunting of... anthology of modernized adaptations of gothic horror literature.

Like Hill House, Bly Manor took a character-first approach without losing the genuine chills of a ghost story. In the end, Bly Manor proved to be truly haunting in every sense of the word, making the two projects the gold standard of contemporary self-contained horror.

Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen was Netflix's first major horror limited series made in the wake of Mike Flanagan's migration to Prime Video. The limited series, produced by the Duffer Brothers, proved that the streamer was capable of maintaining the high expectations of quality set by Flanagan's works.

The creepy story of Jerry Poole and Coldies Frozen Custard plays a more important role in Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen than you may think.

At first, Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen relied primarily on its unsettling tone as Rachel (Camila Morrone) prepared for her wedding with a gut feeling that something wasn't right. As it went on, though, the show became a rich, intertwined story of love, family dysfunction, and tall tales coming to life.

Morrone's down-to-earth and utterly likable performance set the groundwork for her character's intuition to be taken seriously, while Jennifer Jason Leigh and Adam DiMarco rounded out the cast with similarly compelling performances. In the end, Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen delivered on the promise of its title in a way that felt earned and full of equal doses of heartache and horror.

Netflix's latest record-breaking acquired series deserves its place in the streamer's Top 10. Set in a quaint yet terrifying, inescapable town, From is among the most memorable folk horror series made in recent years. Complete with flesh-eating nocturnal monsters, time travel, and an ancient, shapeshifting trickster seemingly behind it all, From utilizes classic horror imagery in a completely new way.

While its strange premise and laundry list of unsolved mysteries have led to frequent comparisons to Lost, From is definitively scarier, giving just as much attention to the genuine terror that faces the townspeople as the overarching mystery of why they've been brought there in the first place.

While the vampire-adjacent monsters offer ample nightmare fuel in and of themselves, From also taps into a more psychological horror with the promise that if the townspeople were to fail to solve the show's mystery, their demise would be at their own hands. Throughout the series, the Township has worked to drain its residents of hope and instead sow the seeds of division and violence among them.

Bates Motel served as a prequel to Alfred Hitchcock's Psycho, yet it was set in the present day. The temporal disconnect gave the show an odd, off-kilter feel from the very start, and Bates Motel continued to keep viewers on their toes despite the conclusion promised by the 1960 movie.

Vera Farmiga, Nestor Carbonell, and Olivia Cooke all delivered memorable performances that greatly expanded the world created in Psycho, but the true standout was Freddie Highmore's work as Norman Bates. Highmore's Norman was complex, multifaceted, and equal parts endearing and dangerous.

His descent to the state the character is seen in Psycho was a slow burn of impressive proportions, and the subtlety of his mannerisms and behavior created a believable confusion around Norman's state of mind. Though it ran for five successful seasons, Bates Motel deserves a lasting legacy within the horror genre.

Its vampire-centric premise makes True Blood immediately brings American Horror Story's Coven​​​​​​ to mind, but comparing the two actually cements how much more gritty, grounding, and emotionally resonant HBO's 2007 series really was.

With a plot involving vampires, werewolves, shapeshifters, fairies, and witches, True Blood's premise was high fantasy to the extreme, yet in execution, the show was actually a powerful character study and cultural exploration of the American South. Even while dating vampires and werewolves, Anna Paquin's Sookie Stackhouse was, first and foremost, a resilient, likable, and completely believable Louisiana girl.

Paquin's performance gave True Blood its down-to-earth tone, but the show also broadened its scope as it explored themes of religious prejudice, queerness in the South, and female independence. True Blood was often silly, but it also created a serious and genuine world that felt like it could, somehow, exist within our own.

Arguably the biggest breakout series of 2026, Widow's Bay has offered an entirely new take on the horror-comedy genre mashup. Rather than watering down its scares with jokes, Widow's Bay​​​​​'s first season was both laugh-out-loud funny and genuinely eerie.

The cursed town of Widow's Bay poses a very real threat to its residents, yet the depiction of how those residents respond to that threat takes a tone akin to a workplace comedy. Matthew Rhys' self-proclaimed first major foray into comedy is a phenomenal acting feat as he imbues the bumbling Mayor Tom Loftis with pitch-perfect line delivery and a heartfelt, if not misguided, passion for bettering the town.

Widow's Bay's season 1 finale raised the stakes on both a plot and character level, setting the stage for the show's sophomore season to be just as much of an event as its first. All in all, Widow's Bay is a testament to the limitless potential the horror genre holds today.

#3508. This Christian Bale Western Drama Flopped In Theaters But Is Worth Revisiting

For a long time it seemed as though audiences might see Clint Eastwood and John Wayne team up in what could have been the greatest Western ever made. That long-gestating, never-realized project was set to be called "Hostiles" and was supposed to be based on a script by Larry Cohen. Alas, the Duke remained entirely against collaborating with a spiritual successor so opposed to his traditionalist roots, and the film was never made. In 2017, however, we did get a movie called "Hostiles" which had similarly languished as a semi-finished script for years. This film had nothing to do with the planned Eastwood/Wayne vehicle, but it did focus on two seemingly opposed parties who find common ground as their harrowing story plays out on the plains of the Old West.

"Hostiles" stars Christian Bale as a United States Army cavalry officer forced to escort a Cheyenne war chief across the dangerous terrain of 1892 America. It's written and directed by Scott Cooper who most recently oversaw Jeremy Allen White's haunted performance in "Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere." Prior to that, Cooper worked with Bale on the 2013 crime drama "Out of the Furnace" and in 2015 he directed "Black Mass," the Johnny Depp-led crime drama based on real life mobster Whitey Bulger.

"Hostiles" came directly after "Black Mass" in Cooper's filmography, and saw him re-team with Bale for a film that was well received by critics despite being a box office disappointment. Today, the film barely gets a mention. But it should, as Cooper and Bale managed to deliver a taut Western drama that was worthy of far more attention than it got from mass audiences.

In 2017, Christian Bale led the weary and grim "Hostiles," a film that very nearly made our best dark Westerns list. Set in 1892, it follows Bale's Army Captain Joseph Blocker, who's nearing retirement and looking forward to leaving his military years behind him. But President Benjamin Harrison has one more job for Blocker. Before he's allowed to retire, he must escort a cancer-stricken Cheyenne war chief named Yellow Hawk (Wes Studi) and his family from Fort Berringer, New Mexico to his tribal lands in Montana. Bale's Army Captain initially refuses on the grounds that he and Yellow Hawk are old enemies. But he's coerced into accepting the job and sets out on the perilous journey.

Along the way he meets widow Rosalee Quaid (Rosamund Pike), who joins the group on a trek that becomes increasingly dangerous. As such, despite their differences, Blocker, Yellow Hawk, and their cohorts must come together to survive a harsh and unforgiving landscape.

As Deadline noted in 2018, "Hostiles" is based on an old manuscript from Donald E. Stewart. The screenwriter, who passed away in 1999, penned the Oscar-Winning 1982 biographical thriller "Missing" and the 1990s Jack Ryan films: "The Hunt for Red October," "Patriot Games," and "Clear and Present Danger." During the '80s, Stewart also wrote a version of what became "Hostiles," which came to Cooper by way of Stewart's widow. It seems she came across the manuscript while packing to move house, and having been impressed by "Out of the Furnace," sent it to Scott Cooper in the hope he could finally realize her late husband's vision.

Upon reading Donald E. Stewart's "Hostiles" manuscript, Scott Cooper decided to expand upon what he called the "kernel of an idea about a man who, in Christian Bale's character, has been indoctrinated by the United States government from a very young age essentially to fight and to kill." Thus began the process of finally bringing "Hostiles" to the big screen. Sadly, when it finally did hit theaters, the movie grossed just $35.7 million on what Deadline claims was a $39 million budget (The Hollywood Reporter put the budget at $50 million).

On the plus side, "Hostiles" did earn a respectable 71% Rotten Tomatoes score. It isn't the finest score, but not only did the film make /Film's best Westerns of the 21st Century list, RT isn't the most nuanced indicator of how critics actually feel about the movies they review. In other words, whether "Hostiles" is, in fact, one of the best Westerns of this century depends on who you ask. Richard Whittaker of the Austin Chronicle, for instance, found "Hostiles" to be "timeless yet contemporary," and praised the film for "diving headlong into the ongoing and often horrific impact of the United States' policies and attitudes to indigenous culture." Dan Jolin of Empire, meanwhile, called Christian Bale's performance "astounding." On the other hand, the San Francisco Chronicle's Mick LaSalle was unimpressed with the film's "dull characters," an "almost-endless tedium" and its "nihilistic violence."

The only way to know for sure where you stand on this mostly overlooked Bale-led Western is to check it out for yourself. Unfortunately, the film isn't streaming anywhere at the time of writing, but can be rented for a reasonable price from the usual digital platforms.

Some minor spoilers from the new NCIS season follow.

NCIS Season 24 is off to a hot start, and it's been giving a lot of screen time to Michael Weatherly's Tony DiNozzo, who is currently the new NCIS director. With that storyline dominating, there's been little time to follow other fan-favorite plotlines. This has really gotten me to thinking about how the show cooled off on a potential Jessica Knight and Nicholas Torres romance. CinemaBlend recently had the chance to speak to Knight actress Katrina Law, and I had to ask her about what's going on.

I recently had a chance to speak to Law, and after talking about the recent episode marking the first time she worked with her daughter, I had to know what's going on with Torres. I wondered if fans should just give up on Knight and Wilmer Valderrama's character having a relationship. Here's what she said:

Well, as we know in the show, especially one that's gone on to season 24, nothing's ever dead. And there's always a chance for anything to come back. that being said, I feel like there's such a fun dynamic between night and tours that kind of verges on the, the, the side of brother and sister. And with mixed with a little bit of tension in there, which just makes it kind of awkward and fun and like a little sizzly underneath

Law can't just outright spoil anything she's already filmed for the 2026 TV schedule, but it's good to hear this perspective. It seems she's fine with the current situation as it stands, which has remained professional (and only somewhat spicy) so far. As a fan, it always feels like there's a chance it could escalate into something, but both characters seem to wonder if it's worth the trouble.

I actually personally think, based on her first comment, that Law might not want Knight to have a relationship with Torres. Is it because of what she said after, and the guilt she'd feel for Brian Dietzen's Jimmy Palmer? She continued:

If we do lean into that, I feel so bad for Jimmy, because, you know, Knight in Shining Palmer, and I just feel like that's just so brutal. But you know, television, we got to get the viewers in, so who knows where we're going.

I can appreciate Katrina Law's empathy when it comes to Jimmy Palmer. Jimmy and Jessica's relationship was fun while it lasted, but it feels like the door is closed on them ever reconciling and getting back together. Hear me out: Is she just supposed to ignore Torres and the obvious chemistry just because it might hurt her ex's feelings?

Personally, I think fans would say no, and I have a feeling Jimmy would say the same. He's a mature adult, and he's gone through the ups and downs of romance. Provided Nick doesn't start some feud with him sometime ahead of time, I don't see him putting his foot down and not giving this relationship his blessing. It may make work just a little awkward, but I think he'd be able to move past it.

If not, maybe we could see Brian Dietzen's character put in for a transfer, and Jimmy would join another NCIS spinoff. He was a recent guest star on the New York spinoff, so maybe that opens the door to him joining their team at a later date? I'm sure Sam would love to have a vet like him on board, and fans would love to see Jimmy get a new place to spread his wings.

All that aside, though, we'll have to keep watching NCIS on CBS on Tuesdays at 8:00 p.m. ET to see if there's any momentum between Knight and Torres. In the meantime, there's never a shortage of crimes for the team to solve, and it's been fun to see them navigate that with Tony as their boss.

#3506. D&D’s World of Warcraft Book Fixes the RPG’s Biggest Endgame Issue

WoW understands what big, scary monsters need in D&D

WoW understands what big, scary monsters need in D&D

It’s no secret that, in Dungeons & Dragons, the job of a Dungeon Master gets increasingly harder as the player characters rise in level. Building challenging encounters for a high-level party can be daunting. In the past, I wrote about how high challenge rating (CR) monsters often feel inadequate to perform the task of “end-game bosses,” unless a DM puts measures in place (such as the use of minions) that, however, can have a negative impact on the game.

Let’s imagine that the big bad of a D&D campaign is a powerful devil, such as a Pit Fiend. The monster has a CR of 20, but that doesn’t mean it will prove a good challenge for a level-20 party — quite the opposite: the poor devil doesn’t stand a chance. A good DM can make the encounter harder by adding more creatures to act as backup, but that means having to run a dozen monsters instead of one, which can slow down combat significantly. Also, grinding through endless cannon fodder may not be fun for players who have waited months (or years) to kick the villain’s butt.

Complex problems like these require creative solutions. That’s where the latest D&D book, World of Warcraft, comes in. The new book presents several high-CR monsters that can provide a solid challenge on their own for high-level parties. The solution is deceptively simple: Just hit them all at once.

The discrepancy between player characters and monsters in D&D’s 5th edition (and in its 5.5e expansion) can be summed up in three main issues: numbers, scaling, and resources.

By their most common cultural understanding, monsters are solitary creatures. It’s part of the mystique of the “monster” concept: an aberrant entity that doesn’t fit within the laws of society or nature. Of course, D&D players are all familiar with goblin armies or swarms of carrion crawlers (yuck!), but these monsters are usually low-level: strength in numbers and all that. Once you move up the ladder, monsters often keep to themselves.

D&D, however, is not a solo game. Adventuring parties are usually composed of a minimum of four characters, and that number can go up, depending on how deranged the DM is (personally, anything more than five would quickly lead me to a nervous breakdown). For a fight between adventurers and a monster to be “fair,” the latter should be at least four times as powerful as a single player character. But that’s never the case.

This very French werewolf is no longer one of the scariest monsters in Ravenloft

The problem with the challenge rating system (and the encounter-building guidelines provided in the Dungeon Master’s Guide) is that player characters do not scale up in power in a linear way, but monsters do. A CR 6 monster will usually be twice as “strong” as a CR 3 one, whereas a level 6 character is many times more powerful than a level 3 one. This is because characters acquire increasingly complex abilities, spells, and magic items. Their progress is not linear, and almost exponential.

Finally, the whole 5th edition of D&D is designed not to be fair to monsters because of its grindy nature. Character classes are built on resource management. A D&D party is expected to have two or three combat encounters in each adventuring day, before needing a long rest to refresh their resources. This means that, if the only encounter a level 5 party faces in a day is a CR 5 or 6 monster, the poor critter will quickly get annihilated. Instead, the DM is supposed to feed the party a couple of lower-level encounters beforehand. But what if that doesn’t fit the story, or the party is just good at avoiding unnecessary combat?

The World of Warcraft book has 15 monsters of CR 20 or higher, only six fewer than the entire Monster Manual. In the MMORPG, there are many powerful “raid bosses” that require a great deal of teamwork to defeat, and the book succeeds in translating that mechanic to D&D. High-level monsters in World of Warcraft are designed to face multiple players, which immediately fixes the first issue with D&D monsters: numbers.

World of Warcraft monsters are all designed with area attacks or other crowd-control options. This means they can hit multiple player characters at once, or separate and isolate party members effectively, thus reducing the need to add extra bodies to a fight just to keep some players busy.

You can look at any high-level monster in the World of Warcraft book, and it will invariably have at least one AoE (area of effect) attack. But two comparisons are particularly meaningful, because they involve WoW monsters that have almost exact duplicates in the Monster Manual.

The Red Dragonflight Dragon is, unsurprisingly, World of Warcraft’s version of an Ancient Red Dragon. While the Dragonflight has a slightly lower CR of 21 compared to the Ancient’s 24 (and, accordingly, fewer hit points), the WoW version does a much better job at keeping a whole party occupied.

Both dragons have a breath attack and a one-use-per-day AoE spell (Fireball for the Ancient and Flame Strike for the Dragonflight). Both can cast Command at level 2 at will. The Ancient also has a level 3 Scorching Ray available at will, but it substitutes one of its Rend attacks. The Dragonflight, instead, has a legendary action called Bellowing Roar, which hits every creature in a 30-foot cube, dealing thunder damage and pushing the targets away. It can only be used once per turn, but it truly makes the difference, giving the dragon a free AoE attack that also moves its enemies around, as a great alternative to the breath attack (which recharges on a 5-6 for both dragons).

The book is experimenting with complex boss fights and transformative subclasses

The other example is World of Warcraft’s Pit Lord, a demon that is almost an exact copy of the Pit Fiend from the Monster Manual. They have the same CR of 20 and most of the same traits and abilities, including the excellent Fear Aura. However, the Pit Lord gets another AoE option in the form of the Rain of Felfire action, which hits every creature in a 30-foot radius with both fire and psychic damage. It also gets Trampling Charge as a bonus action, which lets the Pit Lord move up to its speed, hitting every creature in its path for bludgeoning damage and a chance to knock them prone.

The Pit Fiend, on the other hand, only gets a Hellfire Spellcasting action, which lets it cast Fireball twice, or one Fireball plus a Hold Monster or Wall of Fire. It’s very powerful, but it recharges on a roll of 4-6, so on average it only works once every two turns. It’s also weak against characters who have resistance to fire damage (which can be expected if the party is prepared to face a devil).

Overall, it’s clear how these World of Warcraft monsters are built with Area of Effect and crowd control effects in mind, which makes them better endgame bosses for a party of high-level characters. This exposes some big design flaws in D&D 5th edition, at least when it comes to monsters. Nowhere is this clearer than when you look at some of the most powerful monsters that appeared in the core D&D books.

The second-highest CR monster in the Monster Manual is the CR 25 Colossus (beaten only by the Tarrasque). The Colossus has exactly one area attack: its Divine Beam action, which is massive, but it recharges on a 5-6 and replaces its other actions. This looks particularly ridiculous because this is a gargantuan size construct that towers over buildings, and yet its Stomp attack only hits one creature.

If we look at Monsters of the Multiverse instead (a book that introduced many of the 5.5e updates early), we can find one of the most iconic endgame monsters in D&D: Demogorgon, Prince of Demons, the Sibilant Beast, and a massive wimp. Despite its CR of 26, Demogorgon is not the deadly challenge that player characters of that level would expect. It has only two attacks, which can be a combination of Tentacle and Gaze. The latter is powerful and can mess up a party with confusion, charm, and stun effects, but it still has a single target. Demogorgon’s only AoE attack is its 3-per-day use of the spell Fear – which replaces its other attacks.

As a side note, Demogorgon also has less HP than Lich King Arthas.

This doesn’t mean that you should try to jam WoW characters and creatures into all your high-level D&D campaigns. But there are important lessons that can be learned from the World of Warcraft book.

High-level monsters should have multiple AoE attacks and crowd control effects. This balances the numbers game, which is usually in favor of the adventurers, without needing to add mobs to the encounter (and thus making the DM’s job easier!). If the party attacks a monster four or five times in a combat round, then it’s only fair for the monster to hit multiple party members in the same round.

It’s not hard to design an AoE attack for your homebrewed monsters, or add one to the creatures presented in the Monster Manual. Reskinning and customizing monsters may look complicated, but it’s a great skill for a DM to have. Adding or subtracting traits and actions or tinkering with a monster’s damage, attacks, and HP can turn a boring encounter into a challenging one on the fly.

If you’re looking for guidance on how to improve combat encounters, I suggest checking out Keith Ammann’s books, Mike Shea’s Lazy Dungeon Master series, or checking the Sly Flourish website for free resources.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3505. This TP-Link Wi-Fi 7 Travel Router Is 27% Off for This Early Black Friday Deal

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $87.99 from $119.99 in an early Black Friday deal—marking its lowest price to date. This is not a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas so it slips easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

#3504. 10 Best Western Movie Gunfights Of All Time, Ranked

While Westerns boast breathtakingly rustic vistas and memorably rugged main characters, chances are, we're there to see some sharpshooting gunplay. Many Western movies that everyone should watch at least once are anchored by a riveting action set piece between frontier gunfighters. These sequences range from drawn-out battles throughout harsh landscapes and dusty towns to quick-draw showdowns over in a single burst of gunfire. We're looking back at personal favorite gunfights in the history of Western movies, each earning a spot in cinematic history.

Silver screen legends like John Wayne and Clint Eastwood immortalized themselves through the gunfight scenes in Westerns they starred in. In many cases, the single most iconic scene in a given Western is its gunslinging action sequence. After all, the Wild West archetype is one revolving around its laconic gunfighters, not its bucolic communities on the fringes of civilization.

With those qualities in mind, these are the best Western movie gunfights of all time ranked, epitomizing the genre's gunslinging appeal.

So much of the classic 1953 Western "Shane" is the build-up to its titular protagonist finally showing everyone what he's got. Played by Alan Ladd, the character is a drifter with a mysterious past who comes to work on a farm on the frontier. When these homesteads are targeted by an unscrupulous land baron, Shane's lethal skills quickly come in handy. This comes to a quick-draw climax as Shane kills the murderous crook along with his sadistic hired gun Jack Wilson (Jack Palance), though Shane himself is wounded.

Ladd's Shane is the ultimate gunslinger archetype, though he really only gets one gunfight in the entire movie. Fortunately, "Shane" makes this sequence count, with this violent inevitability expertly staged and crafted. To heighten the mood, much of this climax is filmed in a shadowy saloon as Shane overcomes the obvious trap that he knowingly walks into. Fans still debate over 70 years later if Shane survived this gunfight, which is a testament to how memorable the sequence and its ambiguous aftermath are.

Even though it became a Western that flopped at the box office, the 2007 remake of "3:10 to Yuma" does its 1957 predecessor proud. That said, the difference between the two movies are most acutely felt in how they each end. The 2007 remake features farmer Dan Evans (Christian Bale) escorting outlaw Ben Wade (Russell Crowe) to a train station, with Ben begrudgingly going along for the last run. What follows is a running gunfight against those trying to stop Dan, who still finds the time to convince Ben to cooperate.

The last few minutes of the "3:10 to Yuma" remake are its most exciting, while filmmaker James Mangold still delivers on its main character arcs. Any sense of triumph is quickly undercut by the movie's tragic conclusion, differentiating it from both its short story source material and the 1957 film. The movie handles that fake-out marvelously while not mitigating the excitement that came before during this desperate run. Easily one of the greatest Western movies of the 2000s, "3:10 to Yuma" saves its best for last.

For as breezy as the overall movie is, the most well-known scenes in "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" are its most relentlessly intense. Though the duo being pursued by a posse across the Wild West for their train robberies stands out, the movie's ending is arguably its most famous sequence. Having relocated to Bolivia to resume their criminal activities, Butch (Paul Newman) and the Sundance Kid (Robert Redford) are ambushed by the authorities and take shelter in a nearby building. Charging outside, Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid go out in a blaze of glory, with the movie ending on a freeze-frame as the pair are gunned down.

The alternate ending of "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" thankfully wasn't used, which would've actually shown its likable duo gruesomely killed. Instead, the scene leaves the carnage to the audience's imagination, rather than treading the same territory as the ending of "Bonnie & Clyde." That freeze-frame approach works well for the overall movie, giving the story its inevitable ending but without dwelling on the violence, staying in line with its general tone. The only gunfight on this list which doesn't show its decisive salvo on-screen, "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" focuses on its title characters' legend rather than its tragedy.

John Wayne led a lot of different Western movie gunfights, from classic quick-draws in "The War Wagon" to shadowy shootings in "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance." But the Wayne-starring gunfight that stands out from the rest of his work is his climactic confrontation in "True Grit." Wayne plays U.S. Marshal Rooster Cogburn in the 1969 movie, finally catching up with a crew of outlaws he had been pursuing for the entire film. After being insulted by the gang's leader Ned Pepper (Robert Duvall), an incensed Cogburn charges them alone with a gun in each hand and his horse's reins in his teeth.

John Wayne considered "True Grit" to be his first decent role in 20 years, and his one-man charge cements his character's place in his legacy. The action sequence isn't just the movie at its most rousing, and it shows a more ornery side to Wayne's usual frontier archetype. Expertly twirling his rifle in one hand to chamber a new round, just as he did in "Stagecoach" three decades prior, Wayne hasn't lost a step. Putting a furiously gun-toting Wayne back in the saddle, "True Grit" proved this old dog still had some new tricks.

Over a decade later, "Django Unchained" is still Quentin Tarantino's biggest movie, at least from a commercial standpoint. The final act of the 2012 movie takes place in Candyland, a notoriously brutal plantation run by the cruel slave owner Calvin Candie (Leonardo DiCaprio). Subjected by Calvin's nightmarish hospitality in an effort to rescue Brunhilda (Kerry Washington), the enslaved wife of Django (Jamie Foxx), King Schultz (Christoph Waltz) kills Calvin. This kickstarts a particularly blood-soaked gunfight, as Schultz is killed and Django battles gunmen around the plantation, until he is eventually forced to surrender.

The sanguine shootout may not be the final showdown in "Django Unchained," but it's a scene that we wish would never end. After the smug cruelty that Django and Schultz endure in Candyland, the action sequence feels like a cathartic release as Django exacts comeuppance on his hosts. To heighten the effusive enjoyment of the scene, Tarantino uses "Unchained (The Payback/Untouchable)" by James Brown and Tupac, while making every bullet hit like an artillery shell. The best gunfight that Tarantino has filmed to date, "Django Unchained" has its titular hero bring bloody retribution to its main villain's antebellum lair.

For much of "Unforgiven," the violent backstory of outlaw Will Munny (Clint Eastwood) was only hinted at, with Munny himself focused on being a farmer and single father. After learning that his old friend Ned Logan (Morgan Freeman) was murdered by the sadistic sheriff Little Bill Daggett (Gene Hackman), with his body mockingly displayed, Munny's lethal demeanor resurfaces. Storming into Little Bill's saloon, Munny shoots him and several of his associates, maintaining a clear-eyed, if furious, focus. After finishing off Little Bill, Munny threatens everyone to properly bury Logan or experience his wrath again before departing from the rainy frontier town for good.

The "Unforgiven" ending reveals that some legends are better left to fade away, and Munny is every inch the killer that he was reputed to be. Moreover, Munny inadvertently demonstrates Little Bill's own insight against him, staying calm and collected during the chaos of the gunfight, allowing him to take down all his enemies. Keeping in tone with the rest of the revisionist Western nature of the movie, this burst of violence isn't particularly flashy or stylized. But that makes the carnage all the more grounded and with understated menace as Eastwood delivers his definitive word on the genre that made him a star.

The most famous shootout in real Wild West history was the gunfight at the O.K. Corral in 1881 between the Cowboy outlaw gang and lawmen led by Wyatt Earp. Though this fateful showdown has been dramatized plenty of times in Western movies, the most entertaining depiction is in "Tombstone." Roughly serving as the centerpiece of the movie, the scene only lasts less than a minute, like the historical event. Several of the outlaws are killed in the exchange, while both of Wyatt's brothers are wounded before inciting the wrath of the other gang members.

"Tombstone" presents its historical figures in a stylized and colorful light, helping make it one of the best Western movies of the 1990s. Comparatively, the gunfight at the O.K. Corral is played relatively straight, which helps it stand out from the rest of the movie. The action is quick, brutal, and consequential, setting in motion the back half of the movie's stakes. Certainly one of the best gunfights in a relatively modern Western movie, "Tombstone" knows a lot is riding on its marquee confrontation and delivers accordingly.

The single most recognizable shot in Sergio Leone's "Once Upon a Time in the West" is the sight of three gunmen confronting Harmonica (Charles Bronson) at a train station. The scene opens the film, playing out largely with diegetic noise as the three gunfighters await the incoming train with their target. This sets the stage for Harmonica's arrival, earning his nickname from his first appearance with a screeching melody played from his mouth organ. Unfazed that he's outnumbered three-to-one, Harmonica takes his position against his three enemies and guns them all down singlehandedly though wounded in the skirmish.

"Once Upon a Time in the West" is bookended with genre-defining gunfights, but the opening sequence is the superior of the two. Leone's masterful positioning his actors in frame and suspense building until the inevitable draw finally punctuates that crescendo with a single exchange of gunfire. With Leone, it was all about finding ways to fuel that tension before letting it finally go off like a pressure cooker, a lesson that has visibly influenced Quentin Tarantino. "Once Upon a Time in the West" is among Charles Bronson's best movies and seeing him anchor the movie's opening gunfight sets the mood for Leone's requiem to the genre.

If "Once Upon a Time in the West" is best known for its opening, the following year's "The Wild Bunch" is best known for its ending. The movie follows a group of aging American outlaws in the early 20th century, led by Pike Bishop (William Holden), who flee to Mexico after a botched bank heist. The ensemble get caught up in the revolution south of the border, culminating in the quartet making their last stand against the full might of the Mexican army. Gathering around a machine gun emplacement, the group are eventually overwhelmed and killed but not before massacring scores of soldiers.

The gruesome to "The Wild Bunch" was reportedly as brutal to film as it was to watch, heightening the verisimilitude of the sequence. In a matter of seconds, this situation escalates out of control, full of fire and fury as Pike and his associates stand in the face of oblivion. There's no mistaking that these four men are marching quietly to their deaths, but as the scene reveals, they're going out on their own terms and they're not going alone. More than just the tale of four old outlaws, "The Wild Bunch" signals that the Wild West era didn't die out peacefully but with a violent fire in its guts.

Of course a Clint Eastwood Western was going to top this list, and of course it was going to be "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly." Virtually every Sergio Leone Western, like "Once Upon a Time in the West," has a standout shootout sequence, but the greatest is in his 1966 epic. The movie reaches its crescendo when it brings its titular trio together in a sprawling cemetery as they search for a hidden stash of loot. With the three gunslingers at odds, the characters have a tense staredown before Blondie (Eastwood) guns down Angel Eyes (Lee Van Cleef).

Powered by a stirring score by Ennio Morricone, the climax is one of the most effectively staged sequences Leone has ever directed. The intercutting of close-ups between the three main characters before being punctuated by a single burst of gunfire with mounting suspense all the while is masterfully done. The moment also provides Blondie with another opportunity to pull a fast one on Tuco (Eli Wallach), secretly unloading his pistol for the duel. The quick-draw gunfight that epitomizes Leone's meticulous style, "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" ends on a truly iconic note.

#3503. The Office's Downfall Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

In 2005, two TV shows premiered as mid-season replacements, which isn't usually a great sign for said series' potential longevity. One was "Grey's Anatomy" on ABC, which became one of the longest-running TV shows in history. The other? "The Office," an adaptation of Ricky Gervais' British series of the same name that became one of the biggest hits in the entire history of NBC.

With Steve Carell leading the way as the well-meaning but unbelievably buffoonish Michael Scott (the regional manager of the Scranton branch of paper company Dunder-Mifflin), the American version of "The Office" made it past a somewhat rocky first season and became a small-screen staple, launching the careers of Carell and co-stars like John Krasinski, B.J. Novak, and Mindy Kaling. (It also, arguably, led to an uptick in small-screen mockumentaries like its successors "Modern Family," "Parks and Recreation," and "Abbott Elementary.") After running for nine massively successful seasons, "The Office" wrapped up its run in 2013 with a finale that actually stuck the landing ... but the road to the finish was rough.

You can argue all you want about how to pinpoint the downfall of "The Office," but I won't entertain any debate. The answer is that "The Office" hit a major point of no return in Season 7 when Carell left the show, which led to Michael Scott moving away from Scranton and decamping to Colorado. Despite its best efforts to continue relatively uninterrupted, the series just didn't functionally work without Michael Scott.

It's perfectly understandable that Steve Carell wanted to leave "The Office" behind after spending so long playing one character. (He's a pretty talented guy, after all.) Still, the show should have just ... ended. Even the lead-up to Michael's exit was, all things considered, sort of bleak. This is conjecture on my part, but it really felt like, in Season 6 episodes like "Scott's Tots" and "Koi Pond," the show was leaning into Michael's worst impulses and making him straight-up unlikable instead of silly but well-meaning.

The reason for Michael's departure, however, is undeniably sweet. After human resources representative Holly Flax (Amy Ryan) makes her debut appearance in the Season 4 finale "Goodbye Toby," she and Michael ultimately fall in love before she gets moved back to her original Dunder-Mifflin branch in Nashua due to higher-ups fretting about the pair's relationship. Then, in Season 7, she returns to Scranton, and while Holly and Michael have been broken up for some time when she finds herself back in northeastern Pennsylvania, they get back together ... but their happy ending is threatened when family troubles mean that Holly needs to move back to Colorado.

Thankfully, by this point in the series, Michael is back to being essentially likable again, so he does the right thing: He proposes to Holly and tells his colleagues he's moving with her. His final episode, "Goodbye Michael," is incredibly moving, especially the moment where Pam Beesly-Halpert (Jenna Fischer) says goodbye to Michael in the airport. Yet, the show loses its footing forever as he departs, and it never recovers. Why? Well, the string of potential replacements for Michael is lackluster at best and egregiously unfunny at worst.

One of the many crimes committed in the final two seasons of "The Office" is that the show managed to make English treasure and comedy legend Catherine Tate actively exhausting, but I'm getting ahead of myself. First, "The Office" pulls out the stops by bringing in Steve Carell's "Anchorman" cohort Will Ferrell (the proverbial comedic big gun) as Deangelo Vickers, a deeply confusing and unfunny new manager who's written off after getting a brain injury during a pickup basketball game. From there, Creed Bratton's erratic "Creed Bratton" briefly becomes the manager (and it goes just as well as any "Office" fan would expect), and while James Spader's unfathomably bizarre Robert California has his moments as one of Creed's successors, he doesn't work, either.

Ultimately, Tate's Nellie Bertram and Ed Helms' Andy Bernard are the people who run the Scranton branch most consistently in Michael's absence, and not only are they both terrible at the job, neither of them recreates the magic that only Carell could bring to the series. Instead, Tate's Nellie is, at varying times, exceedingly ridiculous or shrewd (it depends on the episode you're watching), whereas Andy is so expendable that "The Office" briefly writes him off. (This was done to free up Helms to go film "The Hangover Part III" at the time.) Moreover, everyone eventually gets simplified to the point of parody (i.e. Flanderized, to use a popular "Simpsons"-inspired term), so much so that Andy, himself an Ivy League graduate, becomes borderline illiterate. Put simply, it's a mess.

Yes, "The Office" has a great series finale, but the journey to getting there was rough without Michael Scott. Decide for yourself: The show is currently streaming on Peacock.

It's an exciting time to be a Marvel fans, given the release of VisionQuest's finale for those with a Disney+ subscription, as well as the upcoming Marvel movie Avengers: Doomsday being a month and change away from its release. Just last week, Anthony Mackie went viral for seemingly spoiling Paul Bettany's role in Doomsday, but now he's defending those comments. The question is: do we actually believe him?

What we know about Avengers: Doomsday is super limited, so there are countless theories and rumors surrounding the project. The Doomsday cast list includes tons of heroes, but Kevin Feige also confirmed that more surprise heroes would be included. So when Mackie spoke about hanging with Bettany on set, fans thought he might have accidentally revealed a twist. In a clip from The Tonight Show's Instagram, the Hurt Locker actor defended himself to Jimmy Fallon, saying:

So Paul Bettany's my man. That's my homie, right? We hang out all the time. He was shooting VisionQuest next door to where we were shooting Avengers. So, me being me, you know, I steal a golf cart and I pull up. I am a pull up-er. If I hear you're there I'm pulling up.

This potentially offers some much-needed context about Mackie's viral comments about hanging out with Paul Bettany while shooting Doomsday. If the actor is to be believed, he knew that VisionQuest was also shooting at Pinewood Studios in the U.K. at the same time as principal photography for the next Avengers flick. That's how he was able to see his frequent co-star, instead of shooting the crossover event together.

Tom Holland has a reputation for Marvel spoilers, but Mackie's comments about Bettany quickly went viral, especially since VisionQuest featured the return of Elizabeth Olsen's Wanda Maximoff. If The Scarlet Witch will appear in in Doomsday, why not Vision? In the same interview Anthony Mackie went on to say:

I didn't say he was in Doomsday. I said he was next door shooting his show. Just like Tom Holland was next door shooting Spider-Man. He was next door! He wasn't in the movie... I guess.

The "I guess" certainly doesn't inspire confidence. Given Marvel's tight security, actors sometimes have to tell white lies in order to guard the shared universe's spoilers. Case in point: Andrew Garifeld lied about returning as Spider-Man for years ahead of No Way Home's release. As such, we're going to have to wait until the next Avengers movie hits theaters to find out whether or not Mackie was telling the truth about Bettany (and Holland).

All will be revealed when Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list. Anticipation for The Russo Brothers' blockbuster is at a fever pitch, luckily the wait is nearly over for its debut on the big screen.

#3501. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

#3500. Robert Downey Jr.'s 90s Supernatural Fantasy Flop Is Worth Revisiting

It's no exaggeration to say that Ron Underwood's 1993 fantasy comedy film "Heart and Souls" boasts one of Robert Downey Jr.'s best performances. He wasn't nominated for an Oscar (although he surely deserved to be), but at least he won a Saturn Award for Best Actor for his work on it. Yet, because it flopped at the box office, it's rarely ranked among Downey's best movies of all time.

Downey stars in "Heart and Souls" as Thomas Reilly, an arrogant yuppie who is possessed by a pack of friendly ghosts that have been following him since birth. Thus, over the course of the movie, Downey takes on the speech patterns and affectations of his ghostly co-stars (Kyra Sedgwick, Tom Sizemore, Alfre Woodard, and Charles Grodin), and he does so with utter aplomb. The result is a film that's funny, profound, and sentimental in equal measure. It has the mood and structure of a high-concept Hollywood comedy, but with a toe rooted in the warmth of something like "It's a Wonderful Life." Plus, its view of the afterlife is pretty light and fun and makes sense in a secular way.

The world of ghosts plays by its own rules in "Heart and Souls," but it's not oblique or difficult. Here, the living and the dead are cosmically bound, like sometimes-invisible family members contracted to make wrongs right and assuage regrets. It's a positive and touching movie with its messages tucked in between hilarious bouts of Downey zaniness. Ultimately, Thomas learns to be less selfish and far more understanding to his girlfriend, Anne, played by Elisabeth Shue. See what I mean about the amazing cast?

"Heart and Souls" opens in 1959 and introduces us to our ghost characters while they're still alive, each of them boarding the same ill-fated bus. Julia (Kyra Sedgwick) is hoping to find her boyfriend, whose marriage proposal she regrets rejecting. Penny (Alfre Woodard) has to work a late shift away from her sons. Milo (Tom Sizemore) is a small-time crook who conned some valuable stamps from a local kid and regrets it. And Harrison (Charles Grodin) is a singer who just fled an audition due to overwhelming stage fright.

Sadly, their bus driver, Hal (David Paymer), gets distracted and crashes the vehicle, killing everyone on board in front of a car carrying a woman in labor. The four passengers, now ghosts, then witness a young Thomas being born. Over time, the ghosts realize they're physically bound to Thomas (meaning, they get dragged along if he walks away) and grow up with him. However, because they're invisible to everyone but him, Thomas' parents assume he's mentally unwell. So, the ghosts eventually decide to become invisible to Thomas to protect his mental health.

Fast-forward to the present, and the ghosts are unexpectedly visited by the now-deceased Hal. He tells them that Thomas is their "earthly vessel" and they should've been spending their time using him to right the wrongs in their lives so they can finally enter the afterlife. Now, they have to solve their biggest regrets in the next few days or risk oblivion.

Thomas, meanwhile, has become a heartless foreclosure banker who believes he had schizophrenia as a child, causing him to see his childhood "friends." But after the ghosts reappear to him, he eventually accepts that, yes, they are real, and he agrees to help them solve their earthly problems and ascend.

I maintain that "Heart and Souls" is one of the best films of its year. And, to reiterate, Robert Downey Jr. gives an Oscar-worthy performance in it. However, he wouldn't win his Oscar until "Oppenheimer" decades later, having only just been nominated for an Academy Award for the first time right before "Heart and Souls" came out for his turn as Charlie Chaplin in Richard Attenborough's biopic "Chaplin."

Overall, critics were mixed on "Heart and Souls." Most reviews tended to praise the performances from the movie's gaggle of stars, as seen in Michael Wilmington's review for the Los Angeles Times. He noted that "Heart and Souls" was about the spiritual crisis of modern humanity, "buried under several tons of Hollywood slick." But, he added, you should trust the film's actors. To quote him directly:

"There's one great opportunity for virtuoso fun here: the chance handed Downey to impersonate the mannerisms of his co-stars whenever one takes over his body. With [...] delicate, precise mimicry [...] he slips delightfully into [Alfre] Woodard's feline assurance, [Tom] Sizemore's swagger, [Kyra] Sedgwick's sexiness or [Charles] Grodin's repressions. The character he's playing — the same kind of languid, self-obsessed, inwardly anxious hedonist he played throughout the '80s — isn't deep, but Downey digs something comic out of his superficiality."

If that sounds fun or intriguing, it can serve as your "in" to "Heart and Souls." You may discover a new gem.

The Governors Awards kick off awards season these days, which means some of Hollywood’s best and brightest trekked across Los Angeles in a bunch of finery to walk the red carpet – or in this case, blue carpet. Some big names from Zendaya to Florence Pugh to Timothèe Chalamet and Glenn Close debuted some memorable celebrity fashion, and I just want to talk about some of the bold looks.

Florence Pugh has been on a very romantic kick lately promoting East of Eden. She’s worn Victorian blouses with big ruffles, and there’s been a lot of puff in her sleeves lately. She did the opposite for the 17th annual Governors Awards. Her satin dress was form-fitting and very different than what we’ve seen her in promoting her Netflix show. But we’re getting close to Dunesday season, baby.

The dress was yet another winner from Valentino, who also made Pugh's infamous sheer dress. I'm still thinking about its ethereal nature.

Charlize Theron also opted for a memorable color. She paired a red curve-hugging dress from Tom Ford with a red lip, and I just can’t stop looking at it. Plus there’s nothing like posing with your dog next to a bathtub to give a little extra allure.

A post shared by Charlize Theron (@charlizeafrica)

Both looks were well-recieved, and lots of fans commented to Charlize with something along the lines of, “Red is definitely your color!” I mean, I can’t disagree with that.

Some did call Zendaya’s brown dress with hip pads “flawless,” while other comments mentioned it’s “giving sophistication and allure." A subset of people also said Zendaya understood the assignment, as she’s doubtless wearing earth tones to kick off the Dune: Part 3 press tour, but some fans just could not get over the way the dress moved and hung, and the color also seemed to be an issue for some.

Some of the comments about the dress itself noted it was a rare miss in her longstanding collaboration with Law Roach.

Zendaya takes so many fashion risks. She’s done the whole tennis method dressing thing. She once wore a C-3PO armored look and that was seemingly less divisive than this brown dress. Despite it being vintage, I’ve certainly not seen much like it on the red carpet, and if this is her kicking off the Dune press tour, it’s certainly a memorable way to begin.

But did it smolder as much as Pugh and Theron? OK probably not.
