#3498. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

#3497. Why Walter Koenig Held His Tongue To Keep His Star Trek II: The Wrath Of Khan Role

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

"Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan" gives Pavel Chekov (the late Walter Koenig) one of his meatier arcs in any of the "Star Trek" films. In his new assignment as first officer of the USS Reliant, Chekov and his captain, Terrell (Paul Winfield), scout planets as a testing site for the Genesis device. But what they think is planet Ceti Alpha VI is actually the barren Ceti Alpha V, where the Enterprise left Khan Noonien Singh (Ricardo Montalbán), the 20th century's most infamous genetically engineered warlord, and his followers at the end of the episode "Space Seed."

Chekov and Terrell are captured and brainwashed via Ceti eels implanted in their ears. Khan and his people thus seize the Reliant, and boom, we have our movie. The sequence on Ceti Alpha V is predicated on Khan and Chekov recognizing each other. When Chekov and Terrell come across Khan and co.'s makeshift home, Chekov recognizes the name "Botany Bay" (the name of the sleeper ship where the Enterprise found Khan in "Space Seed"). Once the pair are captured, Khan recognizes Chekov and proclaims "I never forget a face."

Chekov also speaks to and of Khan as if he witnessed the events of "Space Seed." Except, technically, he didn't. "Space Seed" was made in "Star Trek" Season 1, and Koenig/Chekov only joined the cast in Season 2. Ergo, he obviously never appeared in "Space Seed" and shared no screentime with Khan. Oops!

Over 40 years later, Trekkies still note the inconsistency and rationalize it. Koenig, for his part, has said he recognized the error when he read the script, but chose to stay silent to preserve Chekov's role. Considering how often "Star Trek" overlooked Chekov, it's hard to blame him.

"Wrath of Khan" writer Harve Bennett wasn't a "Star Trek" fan when he took the job. That worked for the best. "Wrath of Khan" is widely credited for revitalizing "Star Trek" and part of that is because Bennett and director Nicholas Meyer brought fresh eyes. To that end, they couldn't expect everyone who would go see "Wrath of Khan" had previously seen "Space Seed." So, the movie doesn't rely on the episode outside of its big picture story details, which are easily explained via some dialogue in Khan's first scene. (I saw "Wrath of Khan" before "Space Seed" as a kid, and I followed the former just fine.)

But Chekov knowing Khan is the kind of detail that evidently slipped by Bennett. Koenig, who was asked to read the script and give it a "Trekkie read," had a vested interest in not pointing out the mistake. As Koenig put it when interviewed in "The Fifty-Year Mission: The First 25 Years" by Edward Gross and Mark A. Altman: "I was faced with the ethical dilemma of mentioning it to Bennett or letting it go. I chose survival as opposed to ethics."

Chekov is the only member of the "Star Trek" main cast who shares physical screentime with Khan in the movie. (Khan and Kirk only ever talk via viewscreens and communicators.) It's also Khan's first appearance in the movie, as well as the scene from "Wrath of Khan" that I rewatch the most in isolation. Montalbán's performance, savoring every line, is just spectacular. I can see why Koenig would, as an actor, want the chance to be in a scene as strong as that one, and he holds his own balancing Chekov's courage and fear.

For Koenig's part, his cheeky theory to explain away this inconsistency was that Chekov once made Khan wait an uncomfortable amount of time to use the Enterprise's restroom. "Chekov was on the Enterprise, just offscreen" has become the go-to fanon answer. The novel "To Reign in Hell: The Exile of Khan Noonien Singh" by Greg Cox legitimizes that; Chekov is said to have led a failed effort to retake the Enterprise from Khan, and is part of the detachment that helps Khan and his people get settled on Ceti Alpha V.

Despite the continuity gap with "Space Seed," Chekov was the best pick among the main characters as the one captured by Khan. Amusingly, this is precisely because he's the most ancillary one. The Enterprise can function without him in a way it wouldn't without Spock (Leonard Nimoy) or Dr. McCoy (DeForest Kelley).

While Koenig evidently feared that they would swap Chekov's part out in the script, the only other main character who could work would be Uhura (Nichelle Nichols), which would add some icky subtext to Khan violating her body with the Ceti eels, or Sulu (George Takei). With Sulu, you run into the same problem because he wasn't in "Space Seed" either! While Sulu/Takei was part of the show in Season 1, he was absent for that particular episode. If it had been Sulu who landed on Ceti Alpha V with Terrell and met Khan, you might be getting forum posts highlighting that inconsistency today.

Walter Koenig may have created a small problem in "Wrath of Khan" by staying silent here, but he helped fix a much bigger one, too, by suggesting moving Spock's death to the end of the film.

#3496. Scarlett Johansson’s New Crime Thriller Sets First Box Office Record Ahead Of Wide Release

Paper Tiger is already a winner at the box office.

2026's Paper Tiger is a crime drama written and directed by James Gray that opened in theaters on November 13 following its world premiere at the 79th annual Cannes Film Festival. The movie is set in 1986 and follows two brothers played by two-time Oscar nominee Adam Driver (Star Wars: The Force Awakens) and Emmy nominee Miles Teller (Whiplash) getting involved with the Russian mob. Driver's fellow two-time Oscar nominee and Marriage Story co-star Scarlett Johansson (Avengers: Endgame) also stars as Hester Pearl, the wife of Teller's character, Irwin.

Per Box Office Mojo, Paper Tiger earned a 3-day gross of $215,009 at the domestic box office in its opening weekend, during which it was playing in just six theaters. This gives the movie a debut per-screen average of $35,834, which breaks James Gray's record by a wide margin. The writer-director's previous highest debut per-screen average at the domestic box office was his 2016 movie The Lost City of Z, which debuted with a per-screen average of $27,543.

The Lost City of Z was previously the only James Grey movie to have a per-screen average of more than $15,000 during its debut. Below, see a breakdown of the performance of every movie helmed by the filmmaker so far (except 1994's Little Odessa, which doesn't have reported domestic release data) and how his new Scarlett Johansson movie compares:

Because the scale of the releases of James Gray movies has been widely variable, this record is not necessarily a strong predictor of how Paper Tiger will perform in the long term. For instance, while The Lost City of Z is the previous record-holder, its overall worldwide haul is limited because it never played in more than 900 theaters at the domestic box office in a single weekend. Meanwhile, Ad Astra, which is the director's highest-grossing overall, opened in wide release on more than 3,000 screens.

However, this early record could indicate that Paper Tiger may be James Gray's second movie since We Own the Night to pass the $50 million milestone worldwide. Should that be the case, it will be a solid return on investment, as the movie's reported budget is just $15 million, which most likely places its estimated break-even point somewhere around $37.5 million.

It could potentially perform even better than We Own the Night. Both titles are star-studded crime dramas (the 2007 title starred Joaquin Phoenix, Mark Wahlberg, and Eva Mendes), but We Own the Night had mixed-to-negative reviews, earning a Rotten Tomatoes splat thanks to a 57% score. Meanwhile, Paper Tiger reviews have been glowing, earning the new movie a Certified Fresh score of 85%.

#3495. Stephen King Named This Alfred Hitchcock Thriller As One Of His Favorite Scary Movies

Back in 2017, IndieWire amassed a list of Stephen King's favorite scary movies based on the titles he had either previously recommended on social media or written about in his 1981 non-fiction book "Danse Macabre." Among the many, many films included were Ridley Scott's "Alien," Mario Bava's "Black Sunday," Brian De Palma's "Carrie" (itself based on King's own litany of feminine rage), and George A. Romero's "Dawn of the Dead."

Somewhat surprisingly, Alfred Hitchcock's 1972 serial killer "Frenzy" made the cut as well. "Frenzy" was Hitchcock's penultimate film and is famously the only one of Hitchcock's movies to receive an R rating in the United States. Indeed, one might be startled to see actual on-screen nudity in a film from The Master of Suspense. The murders in "Frenzy" are notably brutal, too, and the movie, quite shockingly, contains scenes of sexual assault. This was clearly an attempt by Hitchcock to push the envelope, and one can only speculate if he was drawn to the film's twisted serial killer mentality, the sweatiness of the overall picture, or its sheer amount of on-screen violence.

"Frenzy" tells the story of Richard Blaney (John Finch), a sad-sack and impoverished London-based former military man who is accused of sexually assaulting his ex-wife, Brenda (Barbara Leigh-Hunt), and using a necktie to strangle her to death. However, the necktie is connected to a string of other murders that have been committed all over the city, as the real killer is Richard's creepy friend Bob Rusk (Barry Foster).

As with so many other Alfred Hitchcock movies, the main character in "Frenzy" becomes a falsely accused man on the run (see also: "The Wrong Man," "Stage Fright," "The 39 Steps," "Young and Innocent," "North By Northwest," "Saboteur," "I Confess"), and he has to elude capture to clear his name. Along the way, Richard ends up finding an ally and lover in his former co-worker Babs (Anna Massey) ... although, with Rusk still engaged in his murderous shenanigans, that doesn't bode well for her.

Hitchcock films excel at making audiences unwittingly root for the bad guy (see "Dial M for Murder" and "Psycho" for two better-known examples), and "Frenzy" includes a sequence where Rusk has to retrieve a personal item of his from a victim whose body he has already disposed of. Because of this, viewers are forced to watch as he struggles with the tension of having to retrieve the incriminating evidence, and while we might not feel sympathy for Rusk, we do become involved in his plight. (It's one of the most noteworthy scenes in Hitchcock's filmography.) You can see, then, why Richard turns to Rusk for help at one point, not knowing that his friend is the murderer.

The final act of "Frenzy" gets a little involved and maybe spins a little too far off with its trials and prison sentences, but know that the ultimate conclusion is very satisfying. It's a tonally unique movie as well, feeling very loose and 1970s-y. And where many of Hitchcock's previous films felt mannered and polite despite involving murder and fetishes, "Frenzy" is comparatively casual, focusing more on Rusk's overcooked murderous mindset and the sexual element of his killing spree.

What many cineastes saw as the sexual subtext of Alfred Hitchcock's previous movies becomes text in "Frenzy." By the 1970s, the filmmaker could afford to be a little more frank. The murder scenes, more so than in any other Hitchcock movie, "Psycho" included, are brutal and unsettling. There's even one particularly memorable shot in "Frenzy" of one of Rusk's victims, freshly dead, with her eyes wide and her tongue lolling out, that will remain in your nightmares for quite some time. This is not the balletic, aesthetic, obfuscated violence of Hitchcock's earlier movies. This is disturbing.

Many critics responded very positively to "Frenzy" at the time. Roger Ebert gave the film four stars (out of four), writing that it was both a departure for Hitchcock and a return to form. As he put it:

"This is the kind of thriller Hitchcock was making in the 1940s, filled with macabre details, incongruous humor, and the desperation of a man convicted of a crime he didn't commit. The only 1970s details are the violence and the nudity (both approached with a certain grisly abandon that has us imagining 'Psycho' without the shower curtain). It's almost as if Hitchcock, at seventy-three, was consciously attempting to do once again what he did better than anyone else."

Ebert added that "Frenzy" possesses a nice macabre sense of humor, another feature Hitchcock's fans appreciate from the Master. Vincent Canby, writing for the New York Times, listed "Frenzy" as one of the 10 best films of its year, and it was a hit at the box office to boot. (There's a reason we here at /Film once listed it as one of Hitchcock's 20 best movies.) Clearly, Hitchcock hadn't lost his talent for snagging audiences.

Bowen Yang made a surprise cameo on Saturday Night Live this past weekend. The beloved former cast member appeared in multiple sketches, first as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during the cold open and later as Mary Todd Lincoln Tunnel in John Mulaney’s wild musical number about New York City. Yang seemed comfortable and back in his element, but it turns out the behind the scenes wasn’t exactly smooth sailing. Sarah Sherman actually had to fill in for him during dress rehearsal, leading to a hilarious visual that’s making the rounds.

Yang is currently crushing it as Mary Todd Lincoln in the Broadway production of Oh, Mary! His schedule on the show, however, isn’t exactly SNL friendly. The Lyceum Theatre offers two performances every Saturday: one at 5 PM and one at 8:30 PM. Since SNL’s dress rehearsal starts at 8 PM, there was no way for the actor to appear in both; so, during the cold open, Sarah Sherman appeared in Yang’s part, hilariously wearing a sign that said Bowen Yang. According to Late Nighter, Marcello Hernández warned the crowd ahead of time, though I can’t imagine they expected this visual, which Yang later posted to his Instagram account…

A post shared by Bowen Yang (@fayedunaway)

It’s unclear exactly when the details of Yang’s appearance came together, but he reportedly did head to Studio 8H after his Broadway show on Friday to do a rehearsal for his two scenes. I can’t imagine longtime showrunner Lorne Michaels would be okay with a random celebrity doing a cameo without the standard rehearsing schedule, but he obviously knows Bowen well enough to know he didn’t need the full runthrough.

He clearly didn’t either, as he was a standout during the live show in both the cold open and as Mary Todd Lincoln Tunnel in the musical number. Saidah Belo-Osagie reportedly played the second part very capably during the dress rehearsal, but that was never going to work for the live show. She had another role in the sketch, and also, Mary Todd Lincoln Tunnel was clearly written for Yang, as he’s currently playing Mary Todd Lincoln in the aforementioned show. He probably would have been personally offended if he wasn’t asked and tuned into SNL to see someone else doing an outrageous take on the part he’s currently playing on Broadway.

We’ve gotten two consecutive weeks with cameos from former cast members, as Bobby Moynihan appeared in the Davis S Pumpkins anniversary sketch and in a segment on Weekend Update as Drunk Uncle. Personally, I’d love to see SNL try and do double appearances more often. It’s always fun to see old favorites surprise fans by appearing in a sketch, but it’s even more fun to see those familiar faces show up twice during the same episode so they have a little more to do.

SNL is currently on hiatus for a few weeks, but it’ll return in early December with a new episode hosted by Amanda Seyfried. I cannot wait, as she should bring something new and exciting to 30 Rock and will hopefully continue the momentum as the show has recently dropped its strongest episodes of the season, including this past weekend's heater where John Mulaney brought some of the sharpest social commentary we've gotten in a long time.

#3493. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

#3492. Slow Horses officially moves beyond the books with 2 more seasons

Seems like Jack Lowden isn’t going to be James Bond

In an interview with The Times ahead of the UK release of Anton Corbijn’s thriller A Talent for Murder, star Olivia Cooke spoke about her role on Apple TV’s hit spy show Slow Horses. Cooke said that shooting had begun for the series’ eighth season, which would be its last, and that she was so depressed by the news she was crying in her makeup chair. “We’re all melancholy, distracted,” she said. It turns out there’s no reason for tears.

Apple announced today that Slow Horses has been renewed for two more seasons. Season 6 ended in October, and production has already been completed for season 7, which is expected to be released in fall 2027. The series keeps to an exceptionally tight production schedule – the writers’ room for season 7 opened while season 6 was still being filmed. That’s allowed Apple to be extremely consistent with the release schedule, dropping at least one six-episode season annually since the show premiered in 2022.

Cooke’s report seemed believable because Slow Horses is running out of material. The series is a faithful adaptation of Mick Herron’s bestselling Slough House series, with each season typically corresponding to a single novel. Season 6 compressed Herron’s sixth and seventh books, Joe Country and Slough House. Season 7 will adapt Herron’s 2022 book, Bad Actors, and season 8 will adapt his 2025 book, Clown Town. Herron hasn’t said that he’s finished with the series, but given how far ahead Apple works, it is going to run out of material unless the author delivers a new book soon.

Without Herron’s tightly written John le Carré-style spy stories to provide the plot, further seasons of Slow Horses could decline in quality. The risk seems especially high given that series creator and showrunner Will Smith left Slow Horses after season 5. Slow Horses is one of the best shows on TV, so hopefully there’s a good plan in place for further adventures of the misanthropic spymaster Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman) and his squad of failed MI5 agents. I would hate to see the series fall apart like Game of Thrones did when showrunners David Benioff and D. B. Weiss moved past what George R.R. Martin had written.

Cooke revealing that she’s on set for season 8 is a bit of a spoiler given how season 6 ended with her character Sid Baker fleeing MI5 custody. River Cartwright (Jack Lowden) went to find Sid, and was seemingly poisoned. Assuming the show continues to closely follow the plot of the books, neither River nor Sid will be part of the main cast of season 7, but they will return for season 8. That means Slow Horses’ renewal probably came with a bit of professional bad news for Lowden.

River thinks he’s James Bond even though he’s just as much a screw-up as the rest of his colleagues. Ironically, Lowden is considered a frontrunner for the upcoming Bond movie directed by Denis Villeneuve. Other lead contenders include Josh O’Connor, Callum Turner, Nicholas Hoult, and Robert Pattinson. While it’s possible that Slow Horses will actually kill River off and leave Lowden free to join the Bond franchise, it seems more likely that Villeneuve is going with another actor and River will just keep irritating Lamb for years to come.

#3491. If You Liked Colleen Hoover's Verity, Watch Dakota Johnson's Acclaimed 2025 Movie Next

If you liked seeing Dakota Johnson starring in a twisted psychosexual drama like "Verity," which is based on the novel by Colleen Hoover, you might want to check out the more adult romantic drama "Materialists," Celine Song's acidic essay on modern dating from 2025. /Film's Bill Bria said in his review of "Materialists" that it was structured like a typical rom-com, but more heartfelt, full of yearning and depth.

More than anything, though, "Materialists" deals with a deeply cynical approach to romance, just as the title would lead you to believe. It's about how modern matchmaking has become a painfully specialized industry because modern adults have become all too fixated on the superficial qualities — and the earning power — of their potential mates. Johnson plays a cold-hearted matchmaker-for-the-rich named Lucy who has trouble weaning her male clients off of the idea of dating younger women exclusively. The movie itself seems to wince whenever one of Lucy's clients says they desire a woman who is "fit"; those characters might as well be yelling "no fat chicks."

Over the course of the film, Lucy finds herself torn between two potential boyfriends who have both appeared — or reappeared — in her life. On the one hand, she can pursue Harry (Pedro Pascal), an unbearably handsome, unfathomably rich, and suitably tall man who ticks all the boxes on the average dating profile requirement list. On the other hand, she has reconnected with her ex-boyfriend John (Chris Evans), a struggling actor who was always disorganized and never wealthy, but who loved her deeply. Does Lucy choose a life of poverty undergirded by true love, or does she follow her more cutthroat, materialistic instincts, and pursue the wealthy man who can give her a life of luxury?

For long portions of "Materialists," Lucy's choice seems obvious. Harry may not have the same kind of passion as John, but he is definitely interested in Lucy, and he is happy to share his wealth. There is a coldness, however, to his well-moneyed lifestyle, and something vaguely transactional about his love affair. She also becomes startled when she learns a secret about Harry that we won't spoil here. She begins to question if her attraction to him is genuine, or if it just checks the right boxes on a typical dating profile.

As "Materialists" unspools, however, it begins to skew away from the acidic nature of its opening act and begins strolling toward a drama about romantic truthfulness. Lucy is also thrown for a loop when she unwittingly matches one of her long-single clients Sophie (Zoë Winters) with a man who sexually assaults Sophie. Lucy subsequently doubts her every romantic instinct, and a portion of "Materialists" becomes about Lucy trying to reach out to Sophie to make amends. Perhaps she can mitigate her bad romantic instincts by being a genuine friend to this woman.

The ultimate answer is perhaps a little treacly, but Lucy finds herself drawn back to John. The pair had previously broken up over his incapacity for amassing wealth and her frustrations with the boring everyday financial struggles they went through. Now, however, she is beginning to appreciate the nature of human connection, and John looks more and more romantically alluring.

Of course, one could argue that Dakota Johnson, in being torn between Chris Evans and Pedro Pascal, is hardly in an unenviable place. We should all be so lucky to have two devastatingly handsome movie stars equally eager to court us.

"Materialists" was a pretty big hit, making almost $108 million worldwide on a relatively small budget of only $20 million. When the movie hit streaming, "Materialists" became a hit for HBO Max. The film isn't terribly deep in its commentary on the foibles of modern romance and the shallowness therein, but it's at least about something, and it features multiple beautiful people alternately romancing one another. It also, according to our exclusive interview with writer/director Celine Song, was modeled on a film noir, giving the film an alluring, mysterious quality. All those elements put together seemingly were what drew people out in such numbers.

Critics largely liked "Materialists," as evidenced by its 77% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 307 reviews. Angelica Jade Bastién, writing for Vulture, felt that the movie didn't delve deeply enough into its own thesis that modern romance is directly tied to capitalism. Indeed, she wrote that, in its last act, the film "pivots to a more conventional romantic narrative of the kind it had promised to upend, if not outright critique."

Stephanie Zacharek, writing for Time Magazine, was more generous, writing that Celine Song is speaking very much to the moment, analyzing what romance means in an ego-driven and money-driven world of Instagram and an easily reduced sense of personal value. "That's the world 'Materialists' takes place in," Zacharek writes, "and Song sees what's funny and what's terrible about it at once—even as she acknowledges that it's human to yearn for beautiful things, and for comfort. She's chosen the perfect actors for this enterprise."

If you want a romance that mixes acid with some thoughtfulness, check out "Materialists."

Sing Sing was one of my favorite movies of 2024 and one of the best movies of that year. Colman Domingo shines. He once again proves that he’s one of the best actors of his generation. Domingo’s brilliant scene partners, many not professionally trained actors, magnify his performance.

Using former Sing Sing Prison inmates, and some of those the story was based on, was a revolutionary idea. When I saw Union County, I became more convinced that films should enlist locals or real-life inspirations so those stories appear as characters in more films.

Will Poulter plays Cody, a man in a court-ordered recovery program in Union County. He’s doing fairly well in it until he reunites with his foster brother Jack (Noah Centineo). The film depicts both of their struggles to stay sober, while also highlighting these recovery programs and the people who use them. I first saw Union County at the Davis Theater in Chicago at a special screening with Poulter in attendance.

He explained his experiences with making the movie and having real people from Union County in it. You feel that community throughout. It, in a way, makes Union County feel more grounded in reality than other films with similar topics.

Addiction and recovery are popular subjects in art. Union County may be among the best films about addiction because it feels intimate and quiet while honestly and organically tackling addiction and recovery. Director Adam Meeks puts respect and care into the film’s authenticity and highlights the community without judgment.

I love hearing filmmakers, actors, and creatives speak about their work. You get a better understanding of the process and intentions behind things. You also get a firsthand look at the passion for the project. Therefore, I enjoyed hearing Poulter speak about the importance Meeks and he put into their work with the community. Someone in the audience at the Davis Theater showing knew a person who appeared in the film. She therefore further highlighted how the community bonded even more while making Union County.

Many actors carry the prejudgment that they don’t like working or associating with those outside the acting and filmmaking world. Therefore, it is refreshing to see and hear about those who care about working with all scene partners, whether they’re an extra or an Oscar-winning actor, with the same courtesy, respect, and compassion.

Union County digs into the many aspects of addiction, including mental health. It’s another very honest movie about the mental struggles of addiction. Effectively showcasing things like the mental health struggles of addiction likely comes from consulting those with addiction while creating this film.

Besides Poulter and Centineo’s brilliant performances, Union County gets a lot of its power and authenticity from the people in the community playing extras or small roles. They don’t feel like people playing a part but those putting their real life on the screen in one way or another. It’s these types of lived experiences that make movies such as Sing Sing and Union County unique but also profound.

Many movies are all about escapism, while others remind you of the tragedy and hope of everyday life. The latter films often stay with you longer. It’s more transformative when those who understand the experience of the characters personally participate in the making of movies.

#3489. Ms. Marvel Star Iman Vellani Believes This Is The Perfect X-Men Story (And She's Right)

Whatever role Kamala Khan has to play in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Marvel Studios needs to keep actress Iman Vellani on its payroll. A genuine comic book expert and enthusiast, Vellani is currently flexing her knowledge as co-host of Marvel's "Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday" podcast, running through all 15 films on the official "Doomsday" prep list. On the "X-Men" episode covering the original 2000s "X-Men" film trilogy, Vellani got into her love for the source material of "X2" — Chris Claremont and Brent Anderson's 1982 graphic novel, "X-Men: God Loves, Man Kills."

"If I had to recommend a single 'X-Men' comic that kind of encapsulates, like, it's the purest distillation of what these characters represent, it's 'God Loves, Man Kills,'" Vellani said, echoing common consensus among "X-Men" fans. The book's villain is Reverend William Stryker, a televangelist who believes mutants are demonic. When Stryker's "Purifiers" abduct Professor X in a plot for mutant genocide, the X-Men ally with Magneto against their common foe.

"Stryker's speaking for God, but he's preaching hatred and murder. It's so dark and explores how a lot of people's beliefs are often more dangerous than the people themselves," said Vellani. ("X2" left out the comic's religious themes and is a lesser story.)

Claremont wrote "X-Men" for 16 years and almost 200 issues. It's a soap opera, and it's so hard to pick a single story that stands out as ideal for new readers. Except for "God Loves, Man Kills," which, as Claremont told Vox in 2017, was the entire idea: "If you never read an issue of ['X-Men'] but wanted to know what the series, the concepts, the characters, the reality was all about — and to do so in a way that had, and sadly still has, relevance to the 'real world' — this was the story."

To this day, "God Loves, Man Kills" is one of the few books in Marvel's library that reaches true literary prestige, and which can compare to the great works of their rival publisher DC, like Frank Miller's "The Dark Knight Returns" or Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons' "Watchmen." It runs over 60 pages, three times as long as a typical "X-Men" issue. The art is also moodier and more down to earth than other Chris Claremont-written "X-Men" comics; heavier shadows and no flat coloring reflects the less fantastical tone.

The comic also adds more texture to how humans hate and fear mutants. The opening scene is Stryker's Purifiers gunning down two mutant children and stringing their bodies up. (Adding to the lynching imagery, both children are Black.) There's no robotic Sentinels hunting mutants here, only hateful human beings. "Genocide in the name of God. A story as old as the race," Magneto bitterly observes of the Purifiers.

The rest of the comic remains bracingly political. Claremont wrote "God Loves, Man Kills" in response to "the rise of the evangelical movement across the United States and their insertion into the political process" during the 1980s. Reverend Stryker would fit right in with the Moral Majority. (It's worth noting that one of the evangelical movement's casus belli in those days was opposition to school desegregation.) While "God Loves, Man Kills" remains a clear product of the 1980s, its themes are timeless; you would only have to change the allegory's specifics to set it today. Perhaps in 2026, Stryker would propagate mutant hatred with social media and podcasts instead of television.

But while "God Loves, Man Kills" remains Claremont's masterpiece to most, it's not without controversy — for one scene in particular.

Kitty Pryde gets in a brawl with a boy who calls her a "mutie lover" (unaware she is a mutant). Her Black friend Stevie Hunter tries to calm her, so an enraged Kitty asks Stevie if she'd be preaching tolerance if the slur had been the N-word instead of "mutie." In the original printing, the slur was written in full, though modern printings censor it.

I've never forgotten reading that when I was about 13-years-old: a Marvel comic was allowed to print something like that? The shock value has a point to make; it's easier to say "stick and stones" about bigotry if you're not its target. It makes the racism against mutants feel real and harmful, yet it tests allegory's limits: Mutants aren't real, but anti-Black racism is.

Chris Claremont more elegantly tied mutants' oppression to reality a year earlier in 1981 when, in "X-Men" #150, he revealed Magneto as a Holocaust survivor. (Claremont is Jewish himself.) "God Loves, Man Kills" comes off of that then-fresh reinvention and was pivotal in cementing Magneto as no longer a megalomaniac. Throughout the story, Magneto urges the X-Men to make their alliance permanent, but on his terms. When Kitty instead asks Magneto to join them, he refuses: "For all our sakes — mutant and human — I hope you [succeed]. But should you fail, it will be my turn."

Magneto and the X-Men both believe Stryker's hatred will endure even with his defeat. Stryker's claim that mutants are made in the Devil's image also hits especially hard for Nightcrawler, who does look demonic despite being a practicing Catholic. Later works, including "X-Men: The Animated Series," would explore that religious conflict inside Nightcrawler, pushing on the boundaries that "God Loves, Man Kills" tested first.

#3488. No, We Aren’t All Eating 'Too Much' Protein

If you’ll permit me a rant—I promise to make it fact-filled and interesting—I am sick of the articles that seem to pop up every few months claiming that we are all eating “too much” protein. They convey an inaccurate picture of how the body uses protein, and they demonize perfectly healthy meals that happen to be high in protein. It’s time to set the record straight.

It is true that most of us eat more than the RDA (recommended daily allowance) of protein, but that's a good thing—the RDA is meant as a minimum. It's true that protein-boosted foods are trendy, and that they're not necessarily great dietary choices in the big picture. It's also true that you can eat a healthy diet with little to no meat, but meat is not synonymous with protein. Let's look at what we actually know about the role of protein in a healthy diet, and how to tell if you're eating too much or too little.

As a refresher, protein is one of the three calorie-containing macronutrients (fats, carbs, protein) that make up most of the food we eat. Proteins are made of amino acids, and these amino acids are required for the growth, repair, and functioning of our bodies.

We can get protein from a variety of sources. Meats are particularly protein-dense; a chicken breast contains about 35 grams of protein. Other animal products, like milk and eggs, are also rich in protein. Plant-based foods tend to have less protein than animal products, but it’s not hard to meet or exceed protein requirements even on a vegan diet. Beans, grains, and soy products like tofu contain significant amounts of protein, for example.

If you’d like a cheat sheet on how much protein you’re supposed to eat based on your activity level, you can find one here. And that’s a good place to start dissecting this “too much protein” myth, because before we can declare an amount of protein to be “too much,” we need to understand how much is “enough.”

The government communicates targets for different nutrients to encourage us all to eat a healthy, balanced diet. These targets are the basis for the “% daily value” labels on the back of packaged foods, and for the nutrient makeup of school lunches. The RDA, or recommended daily allowance, is defined as “the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirement of nearly all (97 to 98 percent) healthy individuals in a group.”

In other words, if 100% of us were to eat the RDA of protein, at least 97% of us would be getting enough protein—we'd be meeting the minimum to be healthy. That's right, this number is a minimum to avoid malnutrition, not a maximum, and not a recommendation for optimal health.

By the way, if you're wondering how that number is determined? For protein, it is based on nitrogen balance. Humans break down proteins, as part of our body’s daily function, and we excrete nitrogen as a result. If you eat enough protein (which contains nitrogen), the amount of nitrogen you excrete will be the same as, or more than, the amount you eat. In other words, if you aren’t breaking your own body proteins down (in excess of what you eat), then whatever you’re eating must be, in some sense, enough.

In this way of thinking, the RDA is the minimum to stay healthy. More is fine; less would mean that you may not be getting enough. For some nutrients, there is also an UL, or upper limit, telling you that more than a certain amount is too much. Upper limits are calculated for vitamins and minerals; there is no upper limit defined for protein.

Therefore, there is no official definition for “too much” protein. If somebody eats more than the RDA, they’re not eating too much; they’re just eating more than the minimum. You’re supposed to eat more than the minimum.

The RDA for protein is set at 46 grams per day for a 125-pound woman, and at 56 grams per day for a 154-pound man. (The USDA chose those as their examples.) That’s based on an RDA of 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram bodyweight, which works out to 0.36 grams per pound. So a 200-pound person would need 72 grams of protein per day.

This USDA report found that most adult men average roughly 90 to 100 grams of protein per day, although men aged 70 and up only get about 80 grams of protein per day. Women tend to average around 70 grams per day, with those aged 70 and up averaging 62 grams.

Above the RDA? Yes. Too much? I don’t see any way of arguing that. And before you say that we’re getting almost double the recommendation, let's check the math. Those RDA numbers are for 125- and 154-pound people. On the other hand, the averages for what we eat are based on actual people, not ideals. The average American man is 200 pounds, and the average American woman is 171 pounds. So, to compare the numbers:

The average woman is 171 pounds, so her RDA would be 62 grams per day. (Women, on average, eat 70 grams of protein per day.)

The average man is 200 pounds, so his RDA would be 72 grams per day. (Men, on average, eat 90 to 100 grams of protein per day.)

Again, there’s no need to stick to the minimum; going 8 grams over, or even 28 grams over, is fine. It’s probably better to go over than to just scrape by, and many of us arguably don’t get enough. Let me explain.

Let’s start with older adults. Not only does protein intake tend to decrease with age, older adults are vulnerable to issues that stem from a loss of muscle mass. People tend to lose 3-5% of their muscle mass per decade starting at age 30, but strength training and protein intake can support maintaining our muscle, and thus likely prevent or reduce that decline.

The Dietary Guidelines include a note that “About 50 percent of women and 30 percent of men 71 and older fall short of protein foods recommendations.” Meanwhile, a study found that older adults who don’t meet the recommendations are “more likely to be limited when stooping, crouching, or kneeling, standing or sitting for long periods, walking up 10 steps, preparing meals, and walking for a quarter mile.”

So even if it’s true that the average adult gets more protein than recommended, there are clearly a lot of elderly folks who don’t. These are the same people who have more issues functioning in everyday life. This may be a chicken-and-egg situation—was the functional decline a cause or an effect of the change in their diet?—but this sure does not seem to be a group of people who should be eating less protein.

There’s another large group of people who benefit from more, not less, protein: people who are pregnant or lactating. Instead of 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight (62 grams for a 171-pound person), the RDA for people who are pregnant or lactating is 0.5 grams/pound (so, 86 grams of protein per day).

When you’re pregnant, you also have higher caloric needs, so the increased total amount of food makes it easier to get the higher protein amount. Still, it makes more sense to spend your energy on making sure you’re getting enough protein, rather than worrying about getting too much.

You knew we were heading in this direction (I say between reps of barbell squats, wiping protein shake off my lips): People who exercise should get more protein than just the RDA.

While the fear-mongering “too much protein” articles sometimes mention that bodybuilders or elite athletes need their protein, they tend to hand-wave this away as a special concern that doesn’t apply to normal people. But I think it’s worth a closer look—and honestly, this situation applies to a lot more people than just a few athletes.

Officially, there isn’t an RDA for athletes; people who exercise can stave off malnutrition with the same 0.36 grams per pound as everyone else. But that doesn’t mean that the RDA is the best target to aim for.

The International Association of Athletics Federations, which governs track and field competitions, recommends that most athletes who are maintaining or gaining weight eat 0.59 to 0.77 grams of protein per pound of bodyweight per day. That’s 101 to 131 grams for the average 171-pound woman, and 118 to 154 grams for a 200-pound man.

A group of organizations, including the American College of Sports Medicine, largely agrees, recommending a range from 0.54 to 0.9 grams per pound for all athletes whose weight is stable or gaining. That includes people who do endurance training like distance running, as well as strength athletes whose exercise involves mainly lifting weights. Those ranges would go as high as 153 grams for our 171-pound woman, and 180 grams for our 200-pound man.

You don’t need to be an Olympian to consider yourself an “athlete” in this sense. If you’re training for a half marathon, you’re doing plenty of distance running, and should fuel accordingly. And if you’re “just” lifting weights in the gym, but taking it seriously enough that you’re training regularly and working hard, you should consider eating in these ranges as well.

Dieting to lose weight is not only a popular American pastime, it’s also arguably good for at least some people's health. If you’ve been on a diet recently, or if you’re planning to go on one, you aren’t a person who should settle for the RDA either.

Research shows that protein intake (and strength training—they go together!) is important to maintain muscle mass when we’re losing weight. After all, you’re aiming for fat loss, not trying to get your muscles to waste away. Muscle loss is especially a concern with weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, but any dieter should be aware of this issue.

For example, this study found that diets ranging from 0.48 to 0.72 grams of protein per kg of body weight (that’s 82 to 123 grams for our 171-pound woman, 96 to 144 for our 200-pound man) resulted in less weight regain after the diet, and helped people to maintain muscle mass and feel more full while they were dieting.

And if you’re losing weight and exercising? The IAAF recommends that athletes who are “undertaking high-quality weight loss” need at least 0.72 grams per pound of bodyweight, and possibly as much as 1.09 grams per pound. That would be 186 grams for a 171-pound athlete, or 218 grams for a 200-pound athlete. Most people won’t need to go that high, and it’s unclear whether athletes need to go that high. But I’m including these numbers so you see how high the ranges actually go.

Ultimately, weight loss is widely understood to be more effective and have healthier results with higher protein intakes rather than lower ones. When people focus on just eating less, without thinking about what their diet actually consists of, it’s easy to forget about protein. But the evidence suggests that you should increase protein when you’re decreasing overall calories.

The idea that protein causes weight gain is a common talking point in those articles about “too much” protein, and it’s sort of true—but it also doesn’t mean what you think it means.

When you eat more food than your body needs, your body can store it as fat. That’s true no matter what the excess is made of—protein, carbs, fat, or even alcohol. The protein you eat gets used for many different things in your body. You can build it into muscle tissue, use it for growth and repair of different kinds of cells, and so on. You can also use it for energy—basically, burning it for the calories.

So if you were eating a perfectly balanced diet, and then decided to add an extra 100 grams of protein per day, then sure, a lot of that protein would be used for energy, and since we’d have excess energy, it would get stored as fat.

But if you ate more protein, but that protein replaced other foods in your diet, then there would be no excess calories to store. Nobody is saying you should chug a couple of protein shakes on top of your regular diet. They’re saying (I’m saying) that you should plan your meals and snacks to include more protein.

For example, if your regular lunch is a turkey-and-cheese sandwich with a side of chips, you could improve the protein content of your diet by adding more turkey to the sandwich and replacing the chips with an apple. Same total calories, but more protein. As long as your total calories for the day aren’t in excess of your needs, the “extra” protein won’t get stored as fat.

In general, high protein diets don’t have any serious health consequences. There’s a major exception, though: in some medical conditions, you may be told to limit your protein intake to protect your health.

For example, people with chronic kidney disease are often advised to use the RDA (0.36 grams per pound of body weight) as a maximum rather than a minimum. Your kidneys play a role in processing protein for excretion, so a lowered protein intake reduces the amount of work that a damaged kidney has to do. That said, once a person with chronic kidney disease begins dialysis, they may be advised to increase their protein intake for better health now that their body has help to handle the higher levels.

People with certain other disorders, like phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, may also be advised to eat a low-protein diet. Obviously, if you have one of these conditions, you should be getting your dietary advice from your medical team (ask for a referral to a dietitian!) rather than from general articles on the internet.

Besides those known medical issues, the occasional findings about eating “too much” protein tend to fit into the “X is good for you/X is bad for you” ricochet news cycle. They’re not holistic assessments of protein in general on health in general, but rather specific research questions that are still being figured out.

For example, this 2017 study found that a high-protein (and high-fiber) diet seemed to slightly worsen one measure of insulin resistance, but it also improved metabolic health and body composition. The researchers concluded that the subjects’ body chemistry was probably just responding appropriately to the changed nutrient content of their diet. A few years later, a study of high-BMI women with insulin resistance saw improvements to their insulin resistance on a high-protein diet.

Or to take another example, a study in 2024 found a link between high-protein diets and atherosclerosis. But if you look at what the researchers were actually studying, they were looking at how leucine (one amino acid found in protein) affects the mTOR biochemical pathway in certain types of white blood cells. By the way, that mTOR pathway is involved in a lot more body processes than atherosclerosis, and does a lot of good things too.

So are these results interesting, and worth further study? Definitely. Worth changing protein recommendations? Only if this effect turns out (1) to actually lead to worse health outcomes, and (2) to outweigh the known benefits of higher protein. The body of evidence doesn’t yet support lowering protein recommendations, nor adding an upper limit.

So if protein is good for us, and most of us can’t really get “too much,” why are so many people arguing that we’re overdoing it? I think part of the reason is just misunderstanding (the writers don’t tend to have a background in nutrition and especially not in sports nutrition), but more often, I think they’re talking about a different issue entirely.

Often the “too much protein” stuff is just a way of talking about the environmental effects of meat consumption or dairy farming. People making this argument are trying to pry the double cheeseburgers out of our hands and reassure us that we’ll be okay. I don’t think an attack on protein is an appropriate way to make that point, since plant-based proteins exist and are a fine alternative. But I understand where they’re coming from.

Ultimately, if you’re trying to make the argument that we’re eating “too much” protein for our health, you really can’t do that without some evidence that we’re eating so much protein that it’s harming our health on a widespread level. And that evidence just doesn’t exist.

#3487. How Starship Troopers Author Robert A. Heinlein Really Felt About His Hollywood Experiences

Robert A. Heinlein wasn't fond of working as a screenwriter in Hollywood, and he definitely hated working in TV.

The famed sci-fi author loved the movies, but was always more comfortable sticking to his preferred medium of the printed page. Heinlein was quoted in a 1994 issue of Cinefantastique Magazine saying that working on a Hollywood screenplay meant a great deal of stress, but also that seeing a completed movie he had worked on was a rewarding experience. Heinlein, however, was pretty negative about his experience working on 1960s TV. That, he recalls, was totally miserable.

Movie fans may know Robert A. Heinlein's name best for writing the 1959 novel that provided the source material for Paul Verhoeven's 1997 sci-fi war satire "Starship Troopers," a movie full of disturbing details. He was also behind the short story " '—All You Zombies—' ," which was adapted into the wibby-wobbly time travel movie "Predestination." Sci-fi fans, however, know him as a giant of the genre, having written books like 1951's "The Puppet Masters," 1961's "Stranger in a Strange Land," and many others besides.

In the '50s, Heinlein was also tapped by Hollywood to write a few screenplays, and the famed author is a credited screenwriter on movies like Irving Pichel's 1950 film "Destination Moon" (which adapted elements of Heinlein's 1947 teen novel "Rocket Ship Galileo") and Richard Talmidge's 1953 film "Project Moonbase." About "Destination Moon," Heinlein noted that he was actually pleased with the results.

It was when he was approached in the 1960s to write the pilot for an unmade TV series called "XXII Century," however, that Heinlein's experience in Hollywood turned sour. That show, it seems, was a huge headache.

To give you an idea of how well "Project Moonbase" was received by the public, it was featured on an episode of the bad-movie showcase program "Mystery Science Theater 3000." Robert A. Heinlein didn't comment on that movie directly. But "Destination Moon" has been recognized by Steven Spileberg as the movie that taught him about cinematic suspense, and Cinefantastique quoted Heinlein about his rewarding experiences working on it:

"[I]t had cost me eighteen months work, my peace of mind, and almost all of my remaining hair. Nevertheless, when I saw the 'rough cut' of the picture, it seems to have been worth it."

Heinlein wrote his masterpiece, "Stranger in a Strange Land," several years after his experiences working on "Moonbase" and "Moon," so Hollywood started looking at him again. A producer named Howie Horowitz called Heinlein about making a TV pilot, and the result was a script called "XXII Century" (also called "Century XXII" various places online). The script can be purchased on the Heinlein archive website, and that edition contains pages and pages of notes, seemingly requiring that Heinlein repeatedly alter his work.

"[I]f the series is never produced, I hope I have sense enough to stay home and write books in the future, and leave the movie never-never land to those who enjoy the rat race."

It seems those pages of notes didn't leave Heinlein in a good mood. It was the last time he would be directly involved in any major Hollywood production.

The basics behind the pilot of "XXII Century" can be found on the Libertarian Futurist Society website. "XXII Century" was to take place in the year 2163, and followed the plight of a secret society of powerful superhumans who had the ability to think rationally at all times, even if it pained them. They had cordoned themselves off from the rest of society, and developed a benevolent dictatorship.

The LFS website notes that this premise was culled from Robert A. Heinlein's 1949 novella "Gulf." In the pilot episode, called "The Man Who Wasn't There," it was explained that the United States, Russia, and China engaged in a devastating war in the year 1984. Thereafter, the former two affected authoritarian governments founded moon colonies, and eventually began sending criminals and undesirables there. Fast forward a few centuries, and "XXII Century" can begin. The moon colonies were matriarchal in nature, as there were far fewer women than men, and were also meant to reflect a post-racism future, where prejudice was left behind. And all of this was written before "Star Trek" ever made it to the air in 1966.

Why did the show fall apart? The Space Review has some commentary on "XXII Century" from noted Heinlein scholar Bill Patterson, and he said that the script was way too daring for its own good, and that there was no way it could have ever made its way to the small screen. The project was abandoned, Heinlein lost interest in television, and he went back to writing hit novels. The TV show sounds great, but Heinlein was likely better off in his preferred medium.

YES! There are spoilers below for You Can See Everything, which you can still catch in theaters as part of the 2026 movie schedule.

Now that the cat is officially out of the bag regarding Amanda Seyfried’s surprise role in the hit A24 release You Can See Everything, I’ve been waiting to hear from Christopher Abbott. The East of Eden star plays Elizabeth Holmes’ partner, Billy Evans, in the recreations that Seyfried is also a part of. Like so many spoilers in the movie, the cast and crew have been pretty mum about the production. Finally, we’ve heard from Abbott.

Abbott has been very busy over the last couple of years with projects like Wolf Man and The Testament of Ann Lee, plus his Tony-nominated performance in Death of a Salesman on Broadway this year. He's been a little overshadowed in the hype around You Can See Everything, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. Seyfried’s appearance is such a WTF moment that, speaking as an audience member, it’s almost like we were all still processing that to even register Abbott’s cameo as Evans. It took a couple of minutes before I put it together, honestly. Abbott himself admitted to the process being rushed for him, as well, telling The Hollywood Reporter:

Nathan and Lance, not that long before I went to go work on [it], had just called me and asked me to come mess around. I got to see some of the footage that they had shot before.  I did it, so you know, it was a very kind of quick run-and-gun thing for me, at least.

Abbott also revealed that because it was so quick, he didn’t have a lot of time to prepare or study the character and relied on the footage that Fielder and Oppenheim shot while they were embedded with Holmes and Evans before the former Theranos fraudster reported to prison in 2023. Of the prep, Abbott says:

I've been a fan of both of them for a long time, so I kind of said yes before they even told me what they wanted to do. For me, it was just sort of fun to not to make it so basic. I didn't really know of him until they showed me the footage from the thing. So I just thought it was a very interesting character. I didn't dive deep. I sort of had just enough time to maybe try to do some version of mimicry or find little nuances.  He's an interesting subject.

I think part of what makes it work so well in the box office hit is that we, as an audience, like Abbott, weren’t really familiar with Evans. By the time Abbott appears, we know as much about Evans as he did when he took the role. He’s playing the same villainous character we’ve seen over the previous two hours of the movie, and it works really well.

Abbott probably won’t get any Oscar buzz like Seyfried is getting, but that’s not a slight on him in the least. He provides another bonkers moment in a movie full of them. I really can’t wait for this movie to hit streaming so I can really dive back into it and his performance.

One couple in The Big Bang Theory universe is more tragic than Georgie and Mandy, despite their divorce being set up by Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage’s own name. Before First Marriage even began, The Big Bang Theory revealed Georgie’s multiple divorces through Sheldon’s stories, making Mandy’s appearance in Young Sheldon feel particularly bittersweet as a result. Young Sheldon ending with season 7 forced the Coopers’ story to continue in Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage, putting the story’s focus on the titular couple.

Now in season 3, First Marriage has yet to show obvious signs of Georgie and Mandy’s incompatibility. If anything, their problems in Young Sheldon before they even got together seemed more insurmountable. However, knowing their marriage as seen in both Young Sheldon and Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage will end makes the titular couple particularly tragic, even as they are still going strong in First Marriage season 3. There nonetheless is another couple briefly shown in Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage whose fate in The Big Bang Theory makes them more tragic.

First Marriage season 3 only gave us a glimpse of what Mary and Fred Fagenbacher’s relationship could be, as it was mostly tackled in relation to how it bothered Georgie and how it provoked his and Mary’s conflict. It’s unclear whether Mary and Fred will be the focus of Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage season 3 again, or whether their relationship will become more serious. Georgie & Mandy's First Marriage season 3's premiere overturned a way it always characterized Georgie in a manner that can better the sitcom.

In contrast, even already knowing about Georgie and Mandy’s divorce, it’s possible that they rekindle their relationship in the future. After all, the clue is in Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage’s very name, implying that there could be more. This gives them some hope, unlike Mary and Fred, whose future apart we know about through The Big Bang Theory.

Fred Fagenbacher’s introduction to Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage as Georgie’s antagonist first and Mary’s romantic interest second makes his and Mary’s relationship extremely controversial. Mary and Georgie’s conflict in First Marriage season 3 was already proof of that. However, that doesn’t make Mary and Fred’s relationship a bad one.

#3484. This '90s Crime Thriller Has One Of Samuel L. Jackson's Most Underrated Performances

Samuel L. Jackson stars in F. Gary Gray's 1998 police thriller "The Negotiator" as Danny Roman, a Chicago police negotiator said to be the finest in his district. He's clearly very good at his job, and right from the jump, audiences get to see Danny's charisma and confidence at work as he talks down a desperate situation. Indeed, Jackson is such a forceful and badass actor that it's quite easy to believe that he'd be a good police negotiator.

The plot of "The Negotiator" involves a twisty scheme perpetrated by a hidden cadre of dirty cops to frame Danny for embezzling money from a police disability fund. As a result, Danny comes under the scrutiny of a potentially shifty Internal Affairs officer named Niebaum, played by the great J.T. Walsh. When Danny begins to discover that he is being set up, he storms into Niebaum's office and takes him, along with three other people, hostage. He wants justice.

Of course, being a police negotiator, Danny knows exactly how hostage situations work, and he insists on talking to another crackerjack negotiator named Chris Sabian, played by Kevin Spacey. (I know, I know.) At the time, seeing Spacey and Jackson play opposite one another was very exciting, and the best scenes in "The Negotiator" are when Danny and Sabian interact. The two of them have to somehow find the truth about the embezzlement scheme while under the scrutiny of the Chicago PD. There are many moments of characters being put in imminent danger.

"The Negotiator" was a modest hit in 1998, and I, alive at the time, recall it having many fans, as several of my peers ended up buying the film on home media. These days, though, it tends to be overlooked.

1998 was a good time for both lead actors in "The Negotiator." Samuel L. Jackson had caught everyone's attention in the early 1990s in films like "Jurassic Park" and, more importantly, was widely lauded for his performance in "Pulp Fiction," which netted him an Oscar nomination. This was in addition to piles of credits that he merrily racked up with expedience. Meanwhile, Kevin Spacey, many years before being ousted for a pattern of sexual assault, had gotten a lot of attention in 1995 for his performance in "Seven" and won an Oscar for Best Supporting Actor for his turn in Bryan Singer's "The Usual Suspects." By 1998, when "The Negotiator" came along, they were both riding high.

On paper, "The Negotiator" sounds like a pretty rote police thriller. There's corruption in the Chicago PD, run by a network of unscrupulous cops, and only honest cops can find out the truth through extreme measures and rid the world of injustice. The screenplay, credited to Kevin Fox and James DeMonaco (the guy who would go on to create "The Purge"), is tight and efficient, but it's not Oscar-worthy or super-original. The film sings because it features some great performances from some notable actors. Jackson is great, as he always is, but one should also give credit to the ever-reliable J.T. Walsh for playing tightwads with such aplomb. (Walsh tragically died several months before "The Negotiator" was released.)

In addition, the movie's cast includes great character actors like David Morse, the reliable Ron Rifkin, a pre-"CSI" Paul Guilfoyle, John Spencer (who's better known for having played Leo McGarry, one of the best characters on "The West Wing"), and a just-then-kind-of-becoming-famous Paul Giamatti. That's a lot of character for a standard police thriller.

As noted, "The Negotiator" was a modest success, and it was liked well-enough by critics. Director F. Gary Gray, who had previously made "Friday" and "Set It Off," proved to be capable with the more "Hollywood" material and would go on to helm giant blockbusters like 2017's "The Fate of the Furious," which was most certainly a big-ol' "Hollywood" picture.

Roger Ebert gave the film three-and-a-half stars out of four, declaring it a triumph of style over story and of acting over characters. He admitted that it wasn't until he sat to write his review that he realized how clichéd the movie actually was. That's how swept up he had become in the drama. Ebert added that he liked how the movie managed to be talky while skipping to the next plot point without being too obvious, writing:

"Yes, there are clichés all through the movie, including the obligatory role of Roman's new wife (Regina Taylor), who wants him to stop taking the dangerous assignments. Yes, the TV news crews supply the usual breathless bulletins and obnoxious questions. Yes, the action scenes are unlikely [...]. But 'The Negotiator' works because it takes its conventional story and jacks it up several levels with Gray's craft and style. And because [Samuel L.] Jackson and [Kevin] Spacey are very good."

"The Negotiator" is hardly a lost classic, and many might stay away from it because of Kevin Spacey's presence. Still, it should be reiterated that Samuel L. Jackson gives a very good performance in the film, which F. Gary Gray directed the heck out of.

#3483. Star Trek: Picard Started As A Pitch For An Underused Original Series Character

Over the course of its three-season run, "Star Trek: Picard" took viewers along for the final voyage of the legendary Starfleet captain played by the equally legendary Patrick Stewart. But while the series was heavily rooted in Picard's history, referenced storylines in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," and even spent its final season giving us the "TNG" crew getting back together for one last ride that viewers really wanted all along, the original idea for the show was apparently very different.

According to an interview with Trekcore, "Picard" co-creators Alex Kurtzman and Kristen Beyer started out with an idea that would've featured another character from the "Star Trek" universe that arguably deserved the spotlight even more than the famous captain: Nyota Uhura, the groundbreaking communications officer of the original "Enterprise," originally played by Nichelle Nichols.

Early in the development of what would eventually become "Picard," Beyer and Kurtzman started with the idea of bringing Nichols back to play her iconic role for the first time since 1991. Beyer recalled the initial idea:

"We were actually beginning with an Uhura story, and the idea was that we very much wanted to see we could bring Nichelle [Nichols] back in at this point in time, and then see what kind of stories [Uhura] might tie in to. And then Patrick's name came into the mix, and could we get him, would he be interested ... so the very first idea was a meeting between Uhura and Picard — a very, very young Picard."

Kurtzman gave a few more details about the idea, indicating that at one point, Uhura's role may have been more of a cameo than as the driving force of the show:

"The original idea was that a young Picard had been called to a hospital where Uhura had a mission for him, and it was related to the Borg."

It's an intriguing idea for a lot of reasons. From a real world perspective, it would've rectified a glaring oversight in how Nichols' legacy has been overlooked. Despite the fact that her portrayal of Uhura, which featured television's first interracial kiss between Nichols and costar William Shatner, was praised by no less than Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and inspired real-life astronaut Mae Jemison, among others, Uhura was extremely underused in the original series, even having her scenes rewritten to minimize her role. She's also the only member of the original series' bridge crew to never return for another appearance after "Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country." Nichols was offered and turned down a small cameo role on "Star Trek: Voyager," but sadly, since she passed away in 2022, her return will always be something fans never get to see.

There are also a lot of fascinating questions from the nerdier in-universe view as well. Considering that "Star Trek: The Next Generation" takes place nearly 100 years after the events of the original series, any meeting between Uhura and Picard might seem pretty unlikely. That said, "Star Trek" has always found a way to keep its classic characters in circulation, whether it was through the transporter trickery that allowed Scotty (James Doohan) to come back in the "TNG" episode "Relics," the extended Vulcan lifespan that saw Spock still traveling the universe well into his second century, or just the extended lifespan of the utopian future that gave us a 137-year-old Dr. McCoy wandering around the "Enterprise-D" in the pilot episode of "TNG."

The bigger question is about the Borg, who did wind up being a major element of "Picard." They were a completely unknown species when the "Enterprise" first encountered them in the second season of "TNG," so Uhura knowing about them well before Picard took command of the Federation flagship, and telling him about them, is certainly a surprising development. Then again, the Borg are no strangers to time travel. It's entirely possible that Uhura's long career in Starfleet could've seen her encounter them, even if she probably should've given everyone else a heads up before all that stuff where they captured Picard and then blew up half the fleet. The Borg may have given us some of the best moments in "Trek," but a warning could've saved the Federation a lot of trouble

We're also left wondering whether this meeting between Uhura and a young Picard would've been a prelude to Patrick Stewart's return, or if we'd have seen another actor taking over the role, much like Celia Rose Gooding did with the role of Uhura herself on "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds." There are a couple of obvious choices for the role, of course, but it seems unlikely that they could've gotten Tom Hardy (who played Picard's younger clone Shinzon in "Star Trek: Nemesis"), and that kid who played a young Picard in the "TNG" episode "Rascals" has to be pushing 50 by now. Sadly, we'll never know.
