#3482. Five Race-Day Smartwatch Hacks Every Marathon Runner Should Know

I love my Garmin Forerunner 970, but the fact is, most runners don't need all the features it has to offer. In fact, for most road races, you can get by with whatever smartwatch you already own—as long as you know how to use it. If you've got a marathon or half-marathon coming up, these five tricks will only take a few minutes to set up, and they can save you from one of many of the small-but-avoidable disasters that can derail a good race.

Nothing spikes pre-race anxiety like standing in a corral of hundreds of people watching your watch fail to latch onto a signal. Tall buildings, crowded starts, and a sea of other devices make the first minute of GPS unreliable, which can leave your opening mileage pace wildly off.

The fix is simple: start the GPS search early. Step outside, into the open, as soon as you've dropped your bag, and select your run activity at least 10 to 15 minutes before the starting gun. If your watch supports multi-band or dual-frequency GPS, turn it on in the activity settings, since it's noticeably better in dense downtown starts. Then, don't press start until the gun goes off (or you cross the line, if you want chip-accurate pacing).

Bonus tip: If you're in a start corral with a long wait, you can lock the signal and then pause the activity screen. Just remember to hit start when you actually take off.

Multiple data screens are great for training, but overwhelming during a race. Too many numbers invite overthinking, and seeing the "wrong" number at mile two can lead you into a very stressful mile ten.

My recommendation is to build a dedicated race screen with three to four fields at most:

Lap pace or average lap pace (not instant pace, which jumps around constantly with GPS)

Distance or lap distance, so you know where you are relative to the mile markers

Heart rate, especially in the early miles when adrenaline tempts you to go out too fast

Elapsed time, for splits against your goal

Keep it clean and stripped down, and avoid the temptation to add cadence, power, vertical oscillation, and everything else. You can always review those stats during your cool-down.

A text from your boss at mile 14 is nobody's idea of a good time. Before race day, switch your watch to Do Not Disturb or Airplane mode, or turn on a dedicated activity mode that blocks notifications. This also saves battery, which matters if your marathon is going to take you four-plus hours.

After blocking the outside world, you can set race-specific alerts, like a high heart-rate alert to keep you honest in the first half. I also know runners who set a recurring time or distance alert for fueling—say, every 30 to 40 minutes, or every 5 miles—so remembering to down a gel or a sports drink doesn't depend on your fading brain.

Here's one thing I learn the hard way, every time: Your watch will almost always say you've run farther than the race course says you have. Race courses are measured along the shortest possible route, but along the way, you'll weave around people, take wide turns, and generally add extra distance. I've run marathons where my watch reads closer to 26.6 miles (nearly an extra half mile), so my "on pace" watch is actually behind my chip time.

The hack: Ignore the watch's auto-lap and press the lap button manually at each mile marker (or at every kilometer marker, if that's what the course uses). This gives you pace data aligned to the official course, not the satellite's best guess. It also gives you a quick mental check against your plan. If you've set up your watch for it, display average lap pace, then glance at it a few hundred meters after each marker to see how you're tracking. And don't panic if your watch beeps for a mile before you pass the marker—trust the course and your lap presses, and do your best to ignore the mismatched distance adding up.

Rain, sweat, high-fives, and a hasty cup grab at an aid station can all trigger accidental taps on a touchscreen watch. Few things are worse than discovering at mile 18 that you accidentally paused, ended, or switched screens on your activity. So before the race, turn on your watch's screen lock, so a stray touch doesn't do anything.

If your watch has a configurable wake gesture, consider turning it off to save battery, and set the backlight to a short timeout. While we're talking watch-wearing protocol, remember to wear it snugly, one finger-width above your wrist bone, for a better heart-rate reading as you sweat. Finally, if your watch has one, use the post-race auto-save reminder. (Otherwise, do your best to hit stop after you cross the finish line.)

Again, you don't need the most premium running-specific watch ahead of race day. If you have time, test these hacks on a long run, so that you're not wasting any precious mental energy during the big day.

#3481. New James Bond Actor Has Been Officially Announced: Robert Pattinson is 007

A yearslong search for the new 007 has finally come to an end

After years of speculation about who will succeed Daniel Craig as the new 007, the next James Bond has finally been cast. Amazon MGM Studios announced Monday that Robert Pattinson will officially take over the role of Bond in the franchise's next film, which is being helmed by director Denis Villeneuve.

Pattinson will be the seventh big-screen Bond, who has been portrayed previously by Sean Connery, David Niven, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan, and Daniel Craig.

Pattinson's confirmation as the new James Bond was something of a surprise, given that a half-dozen other actors were apparently in contention and screen-tested for the role. Pattinson beat out Jack Barton, Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Jacob Elordi, Paul Mescal, and Harris Dickinson, all of whom were heavily reported to be testing for Bond. Pattinson came in as a late contender, surprising many who had expected either Jack Lowden or Callum Turner to land the role.

Pattinson has had an incredibly big 2026 already, starring in The Drama, Primetime, and The Odyssey. He'll next appear in Dune: Part Three, which is also being directed by Denis Villeneuve. Pattinson is in the middle of filming The Batman: Part 2, the next stand-alone DC Studios film starring the Caped Crusader. The Batman's return is set for 2028.

Bond last graced the big screen in 2021's No Time To Die, which was Craig's fifth and final outing as the legendary super spy.

The next James Bond movie — currently known as simply Bond 26 — does not have an announced release date.

#3480. Bill Pullman Starred In This '90s Neo-Noir Drama That Tried Suing The Oscars

Before we discuss John Dahl's "The Last Seduction" starring Linda Fiorentino and Bill Pullman, let's set the table. In the indispensable documentary "A Personal Journey With Martin Scorsese Through American Movies," the legendary director discusses the concept of artistic smuggling. The idea is that clever filmmakers can slip subversive themes past unsophisticated producers who are more focused on making a tidy profit than crafting a movie that means and says something.

Back in the B-movie heyday of the 1950s, this practice was common, particularly in genre pictures. Film noir offered a particularly fertile ground for such felonious messing around. Tales of compromised characters doing the wrong thing to get over or simply survive resonated in the wake of the Great Depression and World War II. People knew hard times and found cruel catharsis in watching folks trying, and typically failing, to game the system.

Noir never went away. It mutated with the ever-troubled times, as any fraught moment in American history could serve as the backdrop for a sexy, politically charged thriller. Then third-wave feminism hit in the 1990s, and femmes fatales became protagonists. And we were rooting for them.

It's hard to top the great Sharon Stone as Catherine Tramell in Paul Verhoeven's "Basic Instinct," but I think the best third-wave femme fatale is Fiorentino's Bridget Gregory in "The Last Seduction." From the minute her dirtbag husband, Clay (Pullman), slaps her for insulting him, she begins spinning a complex web that will lead to his undoing. Fiorentino is magnificent every step of the way, and she would've waltzed into a Best Actress Oscar had the film been treated with the respect it deserved. Alas, despite a lawsuit to get her into contention, the Academy refused to budge. And this is a case where smuggling might've hurt a film noir.

In a 2015 interview with Creative Screenwriting, "The Last Seduction" screenwriter Steve Barancik explained the film's creatives pitched the movie to ITC Entertainment as standard-issue Skinemax sleaze. John Dahl, of course, aspired to make a high-quality neo-noir, and once the film's actors read Barancik's script, they knew the project had a chance to be something special. That's how the movie attracted respected names like Linda Fiorentino (who demanded Dahl cast her), Bill Pullman, Peter Berg, Bill Nunn, Dean Norris, and the dearly missed J.T. Walsh.

When an ITC executive panicked early on, the filmmakers got a tongue-lashing. "He shut down production and called the principals of the movie on the carpet, and they all had to pledge that they had no artistic pretensions," Barancik recalled. After the film was completed, ITC sold it off to HBO before it could get theatrical distribution. Unfortunately, if a movie doesn't get an Oscar qualifying run in theaters, it's ineligible for consideration. Again, the distributor October Films brought a suit against the Academy on Fiorentino's behalf, but the organization's rules were clear: no qualifying run, no nomination.

Fiorentino did earn Best Actress prizes from the Independent Spirit Awards and the New York Film Critics Circle, but she likely would've won the Best Actress Oscar if she'd been allowed to compete. (Instead, the prize went to a deserving Jessica Lange for making a meal out of her role in Tony Richardson's film "Blue Sky.") I don't blame Dahl and company for their smuggling gambit, but ticking off ITC was a costly mistake.

#3477. 36 Years Later, Home Alone's Best Line Is Still The Funniest Christmas Movie Quote Ever

"Home Alone," as directed by Chris Columbus (who later kicked off the "Harry Potter" movie franchise), is an undisputed Christmas comedy classic. But while there are definitely yuletide themes of appreciating your family, the film also has a mean streak several miles wide.

If you've somehow never seen it, "Home Alone" follows eight-year-old Kevin McCallister (Macaulay Culkin) after his large family accidentally leaves him at home in Chicago while running late for a Christmas vacation flight to Paris. Kevin, whose family either ignores or bullies him, at first relishes being alone before coming to miss his relatives. Meanwhile, two burglars, the "Wet Bandits" Harry (Joe Pesci) and Marv (Daniel Stern), plan to rob the McCallister house. Thus, in the third act, Kevin fills his home with comical but extremely painful booby traps. (The Wet Bandits' physical misfortune is the closest filmmaking has come to recreating "Looney Tunes" slapstick in purely live-action.)

"Home Alone" was the second highest grossing film of 1990 behind "Ghost," but it received only decent reviews overall. To this day, the movie has a positive but unimpressive rating of 66% positive on Rotten Tomatoes and a similar 63% on Metacritic. Roger Ebert gave the film 2.5/4 stars in his contemporary review, praising Culkin's charm but criticizing the Wet Bandits' subplot.

"[Because] all plausibility is gone, we sit back, detached, to watch stunt men and special effects guys take over a movie that promised to be the kind of story audiences could identify with," Ebert wrote. Yet, for most others, that implausibility is what makes "Home Alone" so funny.

As part of Kevin's new freedom, he watches grown-up movies like the fictional black and white gangster film "Angels with Filthy Souls." The movie shows one scene where a gangster named Johnny (Ralph Foody) refuses to pay another criminal, Snakes (Michael Guido), and then shoots Snakes with a Tommy gun.

"I'm gonna give you to the count of 10 to get your ugly, yella, no-good keister off my property, before I pump your guts full of lead!" Johnny declares, skipping straight from two to 10. "Keep the change, ya filthy animal," Johnny declares as Kevin covers his eyes and shuts off the movie.

Kevin later plays a cruel trick on an unsuspecting pizza boy (D. Danny Warhol) by carefully pausing and fast forwarding/rewinding the movie at the right moments from inside the house. ("What money?" Johnny asks Snakes. "Well, you have to pay for your pizza, sir," the delivery boy explains.) Later, when Marv comes snooping around the house, Kevin lets the scene play out in full to make him think he wandered into a gang deal that turned deadly. This time, Kevin uses firecrackers to simulate the sound of gunfire and also mouths Johnny's "Keep the change, ya filthy animal."

"Home Alone 2" repeated the gag with a sequel, "Angels with Even Filthier Souls," where Johnny guns down his girlfriend (Clare Hoak) for supposedly sleeping around behind his back. There, it's arguably even funnier because it's a Plaza Hotel concierge (the much-missed Tim Curry) reacting to the prank and ultimately concluding, "There's an insane guest with a gun!" Some would argue that "Home Alone 2" is even better than its predecessor, and "Angels with Even Filthier Souls" is definitely a case where going bigger proved better.

#3476. The 7 Greatest Flintlock Fantasy Books of All Time, Ranked

Fantasy doesn't always have to revolve around castles, kingdoms, and sword-wielding knights. Flintlock fantasy takes the genre into a more technologically advanced era, inspired by the 17th, 18th, and early 19th centuries, when firearms were transforming warfare and political revolutions were reshaping entire societies.

These novels combine gunpowder weapons and industrial innovation with traditional fantasy elements such as sorcery and mythical creatures. Their worldbuilding tends to draw on the Age of Exploration, the Enlightenment, the American and French Revolutions, or the Napoleonic Wars, and the plots tend to have a military and political focus. These are the best books in the Flintlock subgenre, proving that it's a subgenre full of endless possibility.

"True change has never been bloodless." In this one, the first of a trilogy, we're transported to a society where the blood of dragons possesses extraordinary properties, allowing certain individuals known as the Blood-blessed to perform supernatural feats. These abilities have become essential to commerce and warfare, with powerful trading companies competing to control the increasingly scarce dragon blood supply. The blood is kind of like the spice in Dune, the way it warps culture and politics.

Against that backdrop, petty thief Claydon Torcreek is recruited for a dangerous expedition into unexplored territory, while highly skilled corporate agent Lizanne Lethridge undertakes an undercover mission, and Corrick Hilemore, the second lieutenant of an ironship, pursues brigands. Together, these characters give us an expansive understanding of its fictional world. That said, the action sequences are probably the highlight, combining espionage and naval combat, guns and blood magic.

"Can you be haunted by someone who isn't dead?" Django Wexler has written many solid fantasy books, including some for Dungeons & Dragons and Magic: The Gathering. Ranking among the best of them, The Thousand Names is the opening entry in his Shadow Campaign series, which draws heavily from the Napoleonic era. It focuses on the soldiers of the Vordanai army stationed in a distant colonial territory. After a rebellion forces the surviving troops into retreat, the enigmatic Colonel Janus promises to transform their fortunes.

Among the soldiers serving under his command is Winter Ihernglass, a woman who has disguised herself as a man to escape her troubled past. Meanwhile, the ambitious officer Marcus d'Ivoire struggles to understand the increasingly unconventional strategies employed by his brilliant new commander. While the plot is juicy, the book ultimately stands out thanks to its unusually meticulous treatment of military organization and battle tactics.

"Doesn't matter how good your bullets are if you don't aim carefully." The Alloy of Law is set 300 years after author Brandon Sanderson's bestseller Mistborn, retaining that book's magic system (which involved "burning" certain metals for special powers) but surrounding it with a world inspired by the Wild West and the Industrial Revolution, all gun-slinging and train robberies. The main character is Waxillium Ladrian, a nobleman who has spent years working as a lawman in the frontier territories.

Following a personal tragedy, Wax returns to the bustling city of Elendel to assume responsibility for his family's declining fortunes, only to find himself up against a dangerous criminal organization. Fortunately, he's no pushover. Wax's unusual combination of powers allows him to manipulate metal and alter his weight. This means he can deflect incoming bullets, launch himself across rooftops, and alter the momentum of his own shots midair. Needless to say, his abilities make for some cool gunfights.

"The secret of gunpowder is that anyone—a man, a woman, a child, a cripple—can kill with it." Guns of the Dawn is a brutal standalone novel by author Adrian Tchaikovsky, perhaps best known for writing the masterful sci-fi novel Children of Time. It centers on Emily Marshwic, a young woman from a respectable family in the kingdom of Lascanne. When a devastating war against the neighboring nation of Denland breaks out, Emily is conscripted, forced to abandon her comfortable existence and confront the horrors of the frontline.

From here, the book nimbly fuses a Regency-era comedy of manners with gritty black-powder warfare, kind of like Jane Austen meets military fantasy. The tale takes us from drawing rooms and rolling estates to war-torn swamps ringing with the crack of muskets and the thud of artillery, the bite of a bayonet never far away.

"I am beginning to feel the need of a glass of wine to fortify myself against this conversation." This gem reinterprets the Napoleonic Wars by introducing dragons into the armies of Europe's competing empires. The plot follows William Laurence, a disciplined British naval captain whose life changes dramatically after his crew captures a French vessel carrying an extraordinarily valuable dragon egg. When the creature hatches, Laurence unexpectedly forms a bond with the young dragon, whom he names Temeraire.

This development forces him to abandon his promising naval career and join Britain's Aerial Corps, where dragons and their human crews play an essential role in defending the country against Napoleon. Adding dragons to any setting generally makes it more fun, but here author Naomi Novik's does so without sacrificing all that much historical authenticity. Indeed, the social conventions and military hierarchies of the era still feel real and well-researched.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

"Age is no guarantee of maturity." Promise of Blood is a combustible mix of adventure, revolution, elaborate magic systems, and hard-hitting gunpowder warfare. Kicking off the Powder Mage trilogy, it begins with Field Marshal Tamas orchestrating a bloody coup against the monarchy of Adro, overthrowing (and executing) the country's sorcerous elite. However, the revolution quickly creates new dangers, including political instability, foreign intervention, and even the possibility of divine retribution.

As Tamas attempts to consolidate his authority, his son Taniel, a talented powder mage, becomes involved in a deadly investigation, while retired investigator Adamat uncovers conspiracies threatening the fragile new government. The politics and intrigue are compelling, and the magic system is entertaining, too. Unlike traditional wizards, powder mages ingest or snort black powder to enter an addictive "powder trance" that grants superhuman strength and heightened senses, letting them extend rifle ranges far beyond normal limits and even curve bullets with their mind.

"Can a magician kill a man by magic?" Simply put, this is one of the greatest historical fantasy novels of all time, layering ancient supernatural traditions onto Regency-era England and the Napoleonic wars. Set in an alternative version of early 19th-century Britain, the story follows Gilbert Norrell, a reclusive scholar who astonishes English society by demonstrating that practical magic still exists. His accomplishments eventually attract the attention of Jonathan Strange, a younger and considerably more adventurous magician who becomes Norrell's pupil.

Eventually, their contrasting philosophies metastasize into a bitter rivalry, particularly concerning the dangerous and mysterious legacy of England's forgotten magical traditions. Writer Susanna Clarke grounds all these fantastical elements in an immersive world, richly recreating the period's social conventions. She even borrows from the prose style of the era's classic writers such as Jane Austen and Charles Dickens. Talk about ambitious.

The 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 ahead of Amazon’s Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date. The rest of the U6 Pro lineup is discounted as well, so you can pick up the same TV in sizes from 55 inches to a massive 100 inches, for anyone with the room for something closer to a home-theater-sized screen. Whichever size you choose, you’ll get free delivery to the room of choice—a service that normally costs $19.99. As for the TV itself, it’s a 2026 model that sits below the U7SG (also on sale for $1,297.99, from $1,999.99) in Hisense's lineup as the brand's entry point into Mini LED, pairing a 4K panel and local dimming with a matte, anti-reflective coating meant to cut down on glare, notes this PCMag review.

For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night. It also does a good job cleaning up lower-quality content, which is useful for older cable broadcasts or compressed YouTube videos—and its Fire TV interface makes it easy to jump between those kinds of content and the major streaming services without needing a separate streaming device.

The U6 Pro also brings plenty to the table for gaming, with HDMI 2.1, VRR, ALLM, and a 144Hz refresh rate that PC gamers can push to 240Hz at a lower 1080p resolution. That said, the panel’s slow response time and poor motion performance can reportedly make fast-moving scenes look noticeably blurry. Viewing angles are limited too, with the picture losing quality fairly quickly when you move off-center—and its built-in speakers aren’t particularly impressive either, so a soundbar could be worth budgeting for.

#3474. Star Trek's Leonard Nimoy Would Only Appear As Spock In Public Under One Condition

For many actors, playing an iconic role in a beloved series can be a bit of a mixed blessing. On the one hand, you've got the success, fame, and the knowledge that your performance has become part of the cultural zeitgeist and touched the lives of millions of fans across the world. On the other, though, there's the risk of being typecast or ignored for roles that could show your range, overzealous fans who confuse your personal thoughts and feelings with those of your character, and the occasional circus that wants to put you on display like a sideshow act. Those extremes are naturally going to be exacerbated when you're playing one of the most iconic characters in the history of television.

Such was the case for Leonard Nimoy, who found worldwide fame playing Mr. Spock on the original "Star Trek," and developed a somewhat complicated relationship with his overly logical alter-ego, going as far as titling his first autobiography "I Am Not Spock," before calling his second "I Am Spock" 20 years later. For him, though, it seems that the worst part wasn't the typecasting or the fans, but those famous pointy ears. As he revealed in an interview with the Philadelphia Inquirer (via MeTV) during the original run of "Star Trek," he was willing to appear as Spock in public, but only if he didn't have to wear his character's signature makeup.

While his time in the makeup chair certainly wasn't as arduous as later "Trek" actors like Michael Dorn, whose Worf costuming took a two and a half hours during the early seasons of "Star Trek: The Next Generation," Nimoy was not a fan of the pointed, alien ears that became a trademark of his character. He even struck a deal with "Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry to give Spock an in-universe ear surgery if Nimoy didn't get used to them by the end of the show's first 13 episodes. Even the network executives initially thought they were a bad idea, less for Nimoy's discomfort and more because of the fear that audiences would see Spock as a demonic figure — a worry they got over really quickly once they saw how popular the first officer of the "Enterprise" was with fans.

Nimoy, of course, eventually got used to wearing the ears on set, presumably due at least in part to an increase in salary after Spock was almost cut from the show's second season. Off the set, though, he flatly refused to wear them in other appearances, as he told the Inquirer in 1968:

"Spock and his makeup are okay within a dramatic environment, but not outside. [...] I turned down $50,000 last year, because I won't make personal appearances in makeup, except for my hair which I don't mind."

Keep in mind that this is $50,000 in 1967. While that might be a worthless sum in the post-scarcity utopian future of "Star Trek," it's the equivalent of over $512,000 in today's money. Sure, it's important to draw a line between actor and character, but for half a million bucks, you probably wouldn't have a hard time finding someone willing to have their ears pointed permanently.

Nimoy, however, apparently valued the roundness of his lobes more than the money, a dilemma that would've torn Ferengi society apart if it had happened within the "Star Trek" universe. If only he'd come up with the ear-hiding headband look that he rocked in "Star Trek IV" a few decades earlier (seen in the screenshot above), Nimoy could've had it all.

#3473. What Is The Covey In The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping?

Within the world of the two "Hunger Games" prequels — "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" and "Sunrise on the Reaping" — there's a group called the Covey, and two of their young women are major influences on the narratives. So, who are the Covey, exactly?

So, "covey" is a real word. According to Merriam-Webster, it refers to "a mature bird or pair of birds with a brood of young" (or "a small flock"). This is perfect, because the two major Covey characters in this franchise — Lucy Gray Baird, played by Rachel Zegler, and Lenore Dove Baird, played by Whitney Peak, in the film versions of "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" and "Sunrise on the Reaping," respectively — are often referred to by the men who love and despise them as birds of some sort. Again, though: what is the Covey?

In the "Sunrise on the Reaping" novel by Suzanne Collins, Lenore Dove's boyfriend and our protagonist Haymitch (played by Joseph Zada in the movie adaptation) informs the reader that, when Lenore Dove occasionally sings for him in their private refuge of a nearby meadow, it's particularly special because "she never does it in public." He adds, "None of the Covey do. Her uncles are really more musicians than singers, so they just play tunes and leave the singing to the audience if they're so inclined."

Those uncles — Clerk Carmine and Tam Amber, the former of whom appears in the film version and is played by Jeffrey Hallman — took Lenore Dove in, though Haymitch notes that her father was always "something of a mystery." (Note that shared last name of "Baird," though.) So, are the musically inclined folks in the Covey from District 12? That's complicated. (Also, they did sing before the events of "Sunrise on the Reaping.")

So, what's the deal with the Covey's origin? As Haymitch notes in "Sunrise on the Reaping," they have a dark backstory. "Her people were great travelers once, going from district to district to perform their music," he recalls. "Tam Amber remembers it, as he was about my age when the war ended and the Peacekeepers rounded up the Covey, killing all the adults and confining the kids to our district."

This is exactly what Lucy Gray Baird tells a young Coriolanus Snow (Tom Blyth in the film adaptation), the future president of the dystopian region of Panem, and a Capitol reporter during "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" as she prepares to fight as the District 12 tribute in the 10th Hunger Games. As she puts it in the book version of the story, "'It's Lucy Gray and I'm not really from [12]. My people are Covey. Musicians by trade. We just took a wrong turn one day and were obliged to stay.'"

When asked which district the Covey does come from, Lucy Gray provides an explanation: "'No district in particular. We move from place to place as the fancy takes us.' Lucy Gray caught herself. 'Well, we used to anyway. Before the Peacekeepers rounded us up a few years back.'" When the reporter tries to clarify that this makes her a District 12 denizen, she loses interest in the conversation. Also, remember how I mentioned singing? Lenore Dove's generation of the Covey might not love singing in public, but Lucy Gray famously does in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" ... and it helps her charm audiences and even win the Hunger Games at the time.

District 12 is the only district we've seen pretty comprehensively in the "Hunger Games" franchise as of this writing (it's possible that Suzanne Collins could write a prequel set in a different district), and the rules are a little looser there across all the books. Capitol Peacekeepers tend to allow sales of illicit materials like the white liquor to which Haymitch ultimately becomes addicted, and they also allow concerts from the Covey, which we see prominently featured in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes." In the book version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch shares that these privileges have continued years after Lucy Gray's live performances:

"[The Covey] worked out a deal with the mayor, whose house boasts the only real piano in District 12. Lenore Dove can practice on it if she plays during an occasional dinner or gathering. Her in a faded green dress, an ivory ribbon tying back her hair, lips tinted orange. When her family performs around District 12 for money, she makes do with the instrument she is playing now, which she calls her tune box."

Essentially, the Covey is a musical group who play instruments and sing — well, the latter depends on the timeframe — and were traveling artists before the districts of Panem fully formed. Between their preference for brightly colored clothes, their musical talents, and their yearning for freedom, the Covey stand out in Panem ... and two of its number, Lucy Gray and Lenore Dove, are extraordinarily important to the story.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" hits theaters on November 20, 2026.

This year's nominees group together some big hitters in the award conversation, and while the Grammys and the Game Awards may feel miles apart, they could still give us some insight into how awards season will shake out.

The Grammy Award for Best Score Soundtrack for Video Games and Other Interactive Media was announced in 2022 and first awarded during the event's 2023 show. The inaugural award went to Stephanie Economou for her work on Assassin's Creed Valhalla: Dawn of Ragnarök. The most recent winner, in 2026, was Austin Wintory for Sword of the Sea. Wintory had previously been nominated for a Grammy in 2013 prior to the video game category's creation for his work on Journey.

Here are the 2027 Grammy Award nominees for best video game score soundtrack:

Haab has previously been nominated twice, winning in 2024 alongside Stephen Barton for Star Wars Jedi: Survivor. Joe Henson has also previously been nominated for his work on Marvel's Spider-Man 2. Paesano, Smith, and Otowa are all first-time nominees in the category.

The presence of big AAA games like 007 First Light and Marvel's Wolverine reinforces their place in the awards conversation amongst the wider public, even if Wolverine was largely panned. But First Light seems to be a major contender this year across a number of categories, including Game of the Year. It is also possible that the Grammy nominees could look very similar to the Game Awards' own picks for the score category.

There are a few major omissions from the Grammys. As GTA 6 isn't out yet, that one makes sense. Indie games have had a small but strong presence in the Grammy nominees since the award's creation, and their complete absence from this year's list is very surprising. The real best score of the year, Ace Combat 8's score, also doesn't appear on the Grammy list, but that's because the game missed the eligibility period. It will be eligible at The Game Awards, though, so fingers crossed it'll get some recognition.

#3471. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.

#3470. Dunesday Will Blow Barbenheimer Out Of The Water At The Box Office

The biggest double bill in cinema history is just around the corner — so much so that it's going to blow Barbenheimer out of the water. The dual threat of Greta Gerwig's "Barbie" and Christopher Nolan's "Oppenheimer" was a force to be reckoned with in 2023. But Dunesday is going to be even bigger as both "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Dune: Part Three" are set to deliver blockbuster openings in December. It's going to be massive.

On the weekend of December 18, Marvel's "Avengers: Doomsday" will lead the pack with a whopping $340 million opening, per Box Office Theory. That number could easily go higher but it's automatically going to be one of the biggest openings for any movie ever. "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" ruled the box office back in July with a $360 million opening, setting a new all-time record. "Doomsday" is poised to be in that ballpark. But that doesn't mean that "Dune 3" is going to be left fighting for scraps.

Denis Villeneuve's third entry in the "Dune" franchise is expected to open with at least $91 million, though that number could easily eclipse $100 million. "Dune: Part Two" had a box office debut that was twice the size of the first movie's, opening to $82.5 million in March of 2024. So, even on the low end and despite the stiffest competition imaginable, it's poised to set a record for the franchise. In short? This double bill is going to deliver all the way around.

For context, Barbenheimer was a bombshell box office success, with "Barbie" opening to $344 million globally and "Oppenheimer" debuting to $175 million. Mind you, the numbers we're citing for "Doomsday" and "Dune" right now are only domestic. The global number will easily eclipse what Barbenheimer did.

Looking closer at "Avengers: Doomsday" specifically, this is going to continue what has been a much-needed fruitful stretch for Marvel Studios. Marvel's 2025 box office proved that the MCU has fallen from grace, with "Captain America: Brave New World" and "Thunderbolts" both falling well short of expectations. Even "The Fantastic Four: First Steps" only did modestly well.

However, "Brand New Day" ended up becoming one of the biggest movies of all time with $2.5 billion worldwide following its record-shattering opening in July. It trails only "Avatar" ($2.92 billion) and "Avengers: Endgame" ($2.94 billion). "Avengers: Endgame" passed "Avatar" to reclaim the title of the highest-grossing movie ever earlier this year thanks to the "Avengers Endgame: Encore" re-release. The "Doomsday" opening projections are right in line with "Endgame," which originally opened to $357 million domestically.

Speaking of that, "Avengers Endgame: Encore" also ruled the box office, taking in $143 million worldwide. Despite some of the cynicism and mixed results that have dominated the conversation around the Marvel Cinematic Universe in the 2020s, that re-release proved that audiences are amped to see "Doomsday," the first proper "Avengers" movie in seven years. It certainly doesn't hurt that directors Joe and Anthony Russo, who directed "Infinity War" and "Endgame," are back in the saddle.

The movie also features former "Iron Man" star Robert Downey Jr. as the villain Doctor Doom. That, coupled with a massive cast that encapsulates several different generations of Marvel stars, has made this a must-see event. Even many fans who opted out of many recent MCU entries are clearly on board to see Earth's Mightiest Heroes duke it out with Victor Von Doom.

Circling back to the saga of one Mr. Paul Atreides, "Dune: Part Three" opening to over/under $100 million even on a weekend with no competition would be insanely great. Warner Bros. also has the benefit of IMAX screens for "Dune," which will add a lot to the bottom line since IMAX has proved that it's more important to the box office than ever before, time and time again.

Disney launched an IMAX competitor called Infinity Vision (which raises some serious questions), but that move lets you know how valuable those premium format screens are. In any case, "Dune: Part Two" finished its global run with $715 million worldwide. In light of an even bigger opening in the cards, the third entry in the series should easily be able to eclipse that number. It also has the benefit of January being just around the corner.

January tends to be a pretty dead month, with studios typically not releasing their A game during that time. That's why Clint Eastwood's "American Sniper" became the biggest January movie ever at the box office, despite being released in late December. Movies released in December tend to have very long legs thanks to a lack of competition. "Dune" and "Avengers" are both going to benefit from that in a big way.

These numbers are undoubtedly going to shift in the coming weeks as release dates creep closer, but what's clear is we're in for a downright unprecedented weekend of moviegoing to help close out 2026. Instead of one of these movies being left out in the cold, the industry is in for a record-breaking weekend.

"Avengers: Doomsday" and "Dune: Part Three" both hit theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3469. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

#3466. The Boys Is Switching Genres & Main Characters For New Prime Video Series

While The Boys franchise will soon return to screens, its next incarnation will be almost unrecognizable thanks to a complete genre and cast change. It is always hard for beloved TV shows to return to the screen after a break, but it can be even harder for franchises to reboot with a new project. The announcement that Hulu is rebooting the iconic ‘90s sci-fi cop show The X-Files was met with equal parts excitement and trepidation since the new show will feature all-new stars and an all-new story.

Some viewers feel that this offers a fresh take on the material, while others might find it disappointing and feel that the new show can’t hope to live up to its predecessor. This is even trickier in the world of superhero shows, where it can sometimes seem like every imaginable take on the genre has already been explored. From DC’s True Detective replacement Lanterns to Prime Video’s period mystery Spider-Noir, there seems to be a superhero show for everyone out there.

Of course, this also leads viewers to wonder whether anyone needs another superhero show, and especially another one from a franchise as famous as The Boys. When The Boys debuted in 2019, the adaptation of comic book writer Garth Ennis’s infamously shocking superhero satire of the same name was a breath of fresh air. Raw, jaw-dropping, and hilarious, The Boys had a knack for seemingly predicting real-life events and a staggering cast. However, five seasons, two spinoffs, and countless knock-offs later, The Boys’ spinoff Vought Rising arrives in a very different cultural climate.

Starring Jensen Ackles and Aya Cash, Vought Rising will see the duo reprise their roles as Soldier Boy and Storefront. However, before viewers get too excited, The Boys cast reunions end there. Set in the 1950s, Vought Rising serves as a prequel to The Boys and its first spinoff, Gen V, charting the origins of the titular mega corporation while focusing on Soldier Boy’s story and Stormfront’s original villainy in the aftermath of World War II.

Where The Boys is a hyper-contemporary, bawdy political comedy, Vought Rising will be a period murder mystery heavily influenced by film noir movies of the era. Outside of Ackles and Cash, Vought Rising features little cast crossover with the original series, and its historical setting means Vought Rising will have none of the earlier show’s explicitly timely satire. Of course, this could arguably be a good thing.

Shows like Netflix’s costly Mark Millar adaptation Jupiter’s Legacy clearly attempted to replicate the approach of The Boys. Furthermore, its own spinoffs Gen V and The Boys Presents: Diabolical, as well as other R-rated superhero comedies like Doom Patrol, Peacemaker, I’m A Virgo, and Harley Quinn all made the show’s formula feel less innovative. As such, a change of pace could be surprisingly well-timed.

Admittedly, shows like Lanterns and 2019’s Watchmen reboot did already fuse the mature R-rated superhero show premise with a dark murder mystery storyline. However, Vought Rising is still better off taking this approach rather than simply replicating the formula of The Boys shortly after its series finale. That said, the new show won’t be without its own struggles.

Chief among these is Vought Rising’s cast change. Soldier Boy and Stormfront were fan favorite characters throughout The Boys, and finding out how both villains came to be will be fascinating. However, they were both unambiguously evil villains, so Vought Rising may have a hard time getting viewers invested in vile characters who viewers already know won’t get their just deserts for decades.

Furthermore, The Boys had one of the most impressive TV casts in decades, and many of its stars became A-list actors precisely because of their breakout roles on the show. Thus, Vought Rising may struggle to match The Boys when it comes to the new show’s star power.

#3465. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3464. Russell Brand Was Sentenced for Rape and Sexual Assault on Monday. By Friday, Netflix Had a Sleazy Doc Ready to Go

The term that comes to mind most is “ambulance-chasing.” Earlier this week, just one week after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault and two days after he was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for his crimes, word spread that Netflix was prepping a documentary on the comedian-turned-criminal.

Olivia Isaacs’ documentary has been in the works for a while. Deadline’s initial story on the project even noted that it “was referenced during the trial” and that while “giving evidence at London’s Southwark Crown Court, Mark Pinheiro, a former friend of Brand, said he had been approached by a producer about the Netflix show.” Related Stories Box Office: ‘Club Kid’ Scores Best Limited Expansion of the Year as Younger Audiences Embrace Jordan Firstman’s Oscar Hopeful Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price

But that the project — “Russell Brand: Open Secret,” a slim and unfocused documentary feature that clocks in at just under 90 minutes — was being dropped on the streamer to ride the wave of interest after Brand’s conviction and sentencing felt distasteful. How essential, after all, could this be? And what could it tell us about Brand’s actual trial, sentencing, and conviction?

Turns out, not much. Isaacs’ film doesn’t get into the trial until its final five minutes (counting its end credits to boot), when it uses title cards to share the conviction news, note that all of the allegations contained in the film itself “pre-date” those that led to the conviction, and make clear that Brand’s legal team was contacted after the Monday conviction and chose not to respond. That’s perhaps the most interesting part of the film’s literally tacked-on final moments: a desire to show its work when it comes to the journalism and attendant standards behind Brand’s long-simmering takedown.

Other elements are far less successful, as Isaacs’ film leans hard on tired tropes and cloying conventions. Captions frequently mention “[unsettling music playing]” or “[dramatic music playing]” during the most benign moments. Old footage of Brand, from home video to early stand-up gigs, is played slowly, all the better to maximize the sense that something is wrong with this man. Far more effective are interviews with those who were allegedly victimized by Brand, but those are often drowned out by played-out techniques.

The film opens with a typical “rise and fall” style montage, charting Brand’s humble beginnings, meteoric rise to fame, profound injection into the cultural consciousness (he met the queen! and also Tom Cruise!), stumble into right-wing ideology, and eventual criminal convictions for horrific acts the film posits everyone knew about forever.

It is, after all, called “Russell Brand: Open Secret.”

Isaacs’ film lacks a thesis beyond the general idea that everyone knew Brand was a creep from the jump. She assembles a hodgepodge of talking heads to hammer that home, including fellow comedians, some genuinely freaked out ex-girlfriends, a handful of accusers (including one who, reticent to appear on camera, is replaced with an actress, one of the film’s most thoughtful choices), and some bizarrely starry-eyed commentators (journalist George Monbiot comes across particularly badly here, zipping from talking about his early delight in Brand and his now-held belief that Brand’s far-right switch is the most horrifying aspect of all of this, oof).

Most compelling are Times journalists Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace, who worked tirelessly to investigate myriad accusations against Brand for years (Urwin first began to look into Brand in January of 2019). Even smushed up against a herky-jerky timeline and a loose sense of purpose, the way that Urwin and Wace talk about the precise nature of their work, what they can and cannot report, the women they spoke to, and the ways in which they were nearly shut down (and, in fact, many other investigations of its ilk were allegedly turned off) is both gripping and necessary.

With more time and better access, the film could have focused more on the police and legal minds that helped build the case against Brand, but in the rush to get this out in the world, that was surely not a major aim.

By its midpoint, Isaacs’ film turns its lens on the culture that helped give rise to Brand, the wild “noughties” when “ladette culture” ruled and being overtly sexy and crude was de rigueur. Women were into Brand! Being ruthlessly unfunny and breathlessly boorish was hot! Also, his dad was mean to him! Diddy and David Walliams jump scares! These are some of the insights on offer in “Open Secret,” and the only thing truly revealing about them is how huge of a mistake it was to let someone as outwardly disgusting and deeply unwitty as Brand get into a place where he could pick and choose his “damsels” or his “whores,” depending on who is talking about them.

The film speed-runs through the last few years of Brand’s life and career, as he pivots into far-right shock politics and Christianity just as the walls are starting to close in on him. Brand may have alleged that his former cadre of famous friends and stalwarts won’t “touch him with a barge pole” these days, but the film’s distinct lack of bigger talking heads stands out. That could stand some further interrogation, too, but there’s simply no time for that. (Well, there is, but not if you want to be a part of this news cycle.)

The four-day gap between Brand’s conviction and the film’s release is zippy, even for Netflix, which has gotten progressively speedier with its true crime joints. In July of 2024, it was announced that Netflix would release a multi-part Karen Read documentary, just days after her first murder trial ended in a mistrial due to a hung jury on July 1, 2024. Three episodes dropped earlier this month.

In January of 2026, the streamer announced a Lucy Letby project with “unprecedented access” after the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) announced it would bring no further criminal charges against the former nurse, who was sentenced to life imprisonment for a slew of charges of murder and attempted murder of infants in her care following a review of additional allegations. “The Truth and Tragedy of Moriah Wilson” was first publicly announced in February of 2026, almost three years after Kaitlin Armstrong was convicted of first-degree murder of the cyclist in November of 2023.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” will surely capture lots of eyeballs as this part of the news cycle winds down, but what the film trades for immediacy, it more than loses in actual insight. Part two can’t be far behind. Let’s just hope it takes far more time to make and far more consideration to craft.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” is now streaming on Netflix.

#3463. These Early Black Friday Ring Camera Deals Start at $24.99

If you’re browsing home security options, Ring has one of the best early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar. Right now, you can add an indoor camera and another one at your front door for less than $65. The Ring Indoor Cam 2K is 58% off at $24.99 (originally $59.99), while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is 60% off at $39.99 (originally $99.99)—both at their lowest-ever price.

Both offer features like 2K video and two-way talk, but the indoor cam is the simpler purchase if you mainly want to check on a pet or kids and see what’s happening near an entrance. It plugs into an outlet, so there’s no battery to recharge, and its low-light color video helps preserve detail when lights are off or dimmed. However, since it’s a fixed-view camera, keep in mind that you’ll need to position it carefully.

The Battery Doorbell is the better pick if alerting you to visitors, deliveries, and potential intruders is your priority. You can install it without wiring, though you’ll need to recharge its built-in battery. It also requires a 2.4GHz wifi network.

The main catch with both devices is the ongoing subscription cost: Live viewing, two-way talk, and basic real-time notifications all work without a subscription, but reviewing saved footage requires a paid plan, starting at $4.99 per month or $49.99 annually for one device; coverage for multiple devices at one location starts at $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually.

At these prices, the Ring Indoor Cam 2K is perfect for occasional live check-ins, while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is better suited to monitoring your front entrance. Buying both makes sense if you already have a Ring plan that covers extra devices.

#3462. Will ‘Dune’ and ‘Avengers’ Drown Out Everything Else at the Box Office This Christmas?

Look, it’s only November, but we know we’re not the only people getting excited about Christmas already. In fact, we know that some studio executives have been thinking about the holiday season a lot for a while now. That’s because they know as well as anyone that they have two juggernauts to contend with: “Dune: Part Three” and “Avengers: Doomsday,” which open on Dec. 18 in true clash of the titans fashion.

There’s a question that if those movies take up so much oxygen, will there be room for anything else? The last “Dune” movie surpassed $700 million globally at the box office, and “Avengers: Doomsday” has already sold over $60 million in pre-sales. Those top two titles create enormous competition for everything opening on Christmas weekend itself. Those include the Dwayne Johnson threequel “Jumanji: Open World” from Sony, the football biopic “Mr. Irrelevant” from Paramount, Robert Eggers’ horror film “Werwulf” from Focus, and Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” from Neon. Paramount’s “The Angry Birds Movie 3” is also opening on December 23 just ahead of the rest. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Club Kid’ Scores Best Limited Expansion of the Year as Younger Audiences Embrace Jordan Firstman’s Oscar Hopeful Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price

Anyone will tell you the Christmas holiday is always crowded at the movies. And there’s usually room for multiple blockbusters to draw crowds. Despite the onslaught of new titles, U.S, distributors are confident they’ll be able to secure the screens they need to be successful. For instance, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” this year opened at the end of July to $360 million domestic, and “The Odyssey” in its third week in theaters still made $50 million. Even during the “Barbenheimer” weekend, “Sound of Freedom” in its third week managed to bring in another $19.8 million. There’s always opportunity if the demand is there.

Recent Christmases have been similarly crowded. Last year had “Avatar: Fire and Ash,” “The Housemaid,” a new “Spongebob,” and “Marty Supreme” open the weekend before Christmas, then “Anaconda” and “Song Sung Blue” over the holiday itself. 2024 had “Mufasa: The Lion King,” “Nosferatu,” “Sonic the Hedgehog 3,” “A Complete Unknown,” “Babygirl,” and “The Fire Inside” all in a short span just before Xmas.

But this Christmas does bring some unique challenges that studios are preemptively working around for their titles that are not “Dune” or “Avengers.” Both of those films have had tickets on sale for months, and both are locked in a fight for premium large format screens that distributors would be lying to say they didn’t want, even if it’s for a family film that doesn’t need it. Warner Bros. and Legendary’s “Dune: Part Three” specifically will exclusively be on IMAX screens, which has famously left “Doomsday” without them, leaving Disney to create its Infinity Vision certification to drum up excitement.

To compete, “Angry Birds 3” is still opening in 3D if on otherwise standard format screens. “Werwulf” won’t have IMAX as Focus did for “Nosferatu,” but it has pre-sold select 35mm screenings of the film that have already done quite well (they went on sale on the full moon last month). The hope, too, is that titles like “Jumanji” and “Mr. Irrelevant” appeal to crowds that are distinctive from the male, fanboy-heavy audiences for “Dunesday.”

One source IndieWire spoke with argued that even though this Christmas is top heavy, it’s arguably lighter in sheer quantity than we’ve seen in recent years. What we’re not seeing is a movie like “Marty Supreme” or “Uncut Gems” getting a run in a more mid-size or limited number of screens. Universal doesn’t have a movie opening in that window, nor does Amazon MGM. Other awards titles like “The Debut” from A24 are going earlier in the month and aren’t doing the limited, Christmas day, qualifying run before going wide in January (GKIDS’ “Look Back” may be an exception, opening December 30).

There are some potential holdovers that could generate money well into Christmas. Rival studio execs are keeping an eye on movies like Disney’s animated “Hexed” or Universal’s “Focker-in-Law,” and Focus’ “Elsinore” will also be going wider shortly before the holidays.

The hope now is that all of these films get their flowers and collectively put an exclamation point on a stellar 2026, with the box office now projected to finish far above $10 billion domestic, a number that might’ve been a pipe dream this time in 2025. That’s reason for holiday cheer, indeed.
