#3435. The Brits Are (Finally) Subverting the Cozy Crime Craze

“I get it, because I love invoking that nostalgia, but I think that term also implies a certain ease,” Mark Gatiss recently explained to Variety his apprehension at the “cozy crime” label being applied to his latest labor of love. “And doesn’t have to be just wallpaper; it can have teeth.”

As much a meditation on navigating sexuality in the immediate aftermath of World War II as a period procedural, Gatiss’ PBS series “Bookish” certainly has plenty to chew on. In fact, alongside “Ludwig” and “Death Valley,” it’s leading the British charge to subvert a sub-genre widely dismissed as undemanding background fodder.

Indeed, once the domain of Hallmark Channel, whose twee franchises (“Curious Caterer,” “Crossword Mysteries”) are as formulaic as their tradwife propaganda romances, the cozy crime drama is undergoing something of a commercial and creative renaissance of late. According to a recent study, 75 percent of 18-29 year-olds, a generation embracing everything ASMR to knitting to drown out the noise, consider themselves fans. Related Stories ’12 12 12′ Review: Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s Ticking-Clock Heist Thriller Runs on Broken Time ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne Sizzles in Peacock’s Brutal Trauma-Drama About Crime-Solving Sisters

“Bookish” centers on Gatiss’ Gabriel Book, a secondhand bookseller in post-war London who — thanks to a mysterious letter signed by Winston Churchill — is entrusted to apply his encyclopedic knowledge with the Met Police. Yet while its 1940s setting, killing methods (poisoned bonbons) and great British fondness for the cuppa (“Without tea, I am merely reconstructed dust,” Book declares) may be the stuff of Agatha Christie, its themes are unusually progressive.

For Book is also in a lavender marriage with Polly Walker’s strong independent woman Trottie, explaining why beyond his remarkable sleuthing abilities, he remains something of a buttoned-up enigma. Laced with an air of melancholy, the series quietly but effectively delves into the hardships of staying in the closet at a time when homosexuality was still 20 years away from decriminalization, while also exploring the concept of platonic love, the disillusionment of women forced to retreat from the workplace, and the PTSD suffered by returning soldiers. A Lacey Chabert vehicle this is not.

As its Best Comedy win at the International Emmys would suggest, fellow two-season wonder “Ludwig” is slightly more jovial. In fact, it compels far more as a tragic-comic character study than a murder-mystery, its tendency to withhold vital information until the last-minute ensuring it’s practically impossible for armchair detectives to play along.

As the corduroy-clad, socially-awkward puzzle maker, David Mitchell essentially plays David Mitchell; no bad thing, of course, as his hilarious victory on “LOL UK” proved. Much of the BritBox show’s joys derive from watching a bumbling introvert, who poses as his detective twin brother to investigate his disappearance only to become the force’s secret weapon, struggling to adapt to center stage and the complexities of modern life. From his inability to make small talk to his near-pathological dislike of all mod-cons, Ludwig is a reluctant hero and, at times, an impenetrable one, too. (“Whichever one didn’t do it knows that the other one did and is protecting her. While the one that did do it knows we can’t prove that the one who didn’t do it, didn’t do it”)

However, as with “Bookish,” creator Mark Brotherhood balances Ludwig’s quips and idiosyncrasies with a genuine sense of longing, not only for his missing sibling, but for the dad who abandoned them as youngsters as well as the sister-in-law he obviously holds a torch for. Come for the cryptic capers, stay for the complex family dynamics and post-millennial tensions.

Also returning to BritBox for its second season this month (out November 17), “Death Valley” is undeniably the most meta of the three, fully leaning into all the tropes — amateur sleuths unfathomably allowed to permeate crime scenes carte blanche, picture-perfect visuals which double up as tourist board ads (in this instance, the scenic Vale of Glamorgan), a distinct lack of blood, cursing or anything that shatters the illusion of a stiff-upper-lip utopia — while simultaneously skewering them in a blatant case of “have your cake and eat it.”

Here, BAFTA nominee Timothy Spall plays John Chapel, a curmudgeonly reclusive “thespian with a capital T” best known for starring in a long-running cozy crime drama, Caesar, and his uber-corny catchphrase, “Crime waits for no man.” Brought out of hibernation when “scintillatingly irritating” fangirl DS Janie Mallowan (Gwyneth Keyworth) knocks on his door while investigating a nearby murder, he subsequently ingratiates himself into the inquiry, drawing upon his fictional experiences and celebrity ego to forge an unlikely — and often reluctant — buddy duo.

There are inevitable parallels with “Only Murders in the Building” where Steve Martin’s Charles, the similarly jaded star of a classic detective show, also finds a new lease of life by teaming up with a younger woman to solve very real crimes. Instead of an overarching mystery rooted within a swanky high rise in Manhattan’s Upper West Side, though. “Death Valley” is a case-of-the-week affair grounded in the humdrum of rural South Wales: murder scenes include a rugby club, fish and chip shop, and community service litter-picking session.

Furthermore, the forays into showbiz are hardly dripping with glamour. Chapel briefly returns to his old day job not in a prestige reboot of his biggest hit, but a local amateur dramatic staging of “Hamlet.” Meanwhile, the fantasy series he infiltrates while investigating the death of a production runner looks hokier than a Syfy original.

Of course, the dichotomy between Chapel’s overinflated sense of self and the humbling situations he finds himself in provides much of the comedy. Despite admitting that cozy crime isn’t his bag, Spall is clearly having a ball as a luvvie prone to grand soliloquies about his craft and unwarranted pats on the back about his “revelatory Tartuffe at the Almeida.”

Perhaps sensing the response from hardened critics scoffing at the absence of tortured souls and gritty visuals that leave you reaching for your remote’s contrast button, writer Paul Doolan also beats them to the punch with a string of self-knowing lines, whether Janie describing her partner’s performance as “hammy” or a prime suspect’s assertion that their whodunit reveal was “needlessly theatrical.”

“Death Valley” is undeniably ‘played to the rafters.’ However, its smart self-deprecation and popculture-spoofing ensures that, like its counterparts, it rises above what Chapel himself calls “the current level of banality in most mainstream TV drama.” Isn’t that better than cozy?

#3433. iFixit tears down touchscreen MacBook Pro, reveals light-up Apple logo details

iFixit published its teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display today, revealing interesting details about how Apple brought back its illuminated logo on the lid. Watch it below.

iFixit’s teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is now live, and it explores not only how the new illuminated Apple logo works, but also its tandem OLED and how Apple managed to trim its weight down to 3 pounds (1.38 kg) from 3.4 pounds (1.55 kg) on the standard 14-inch model.

The teardown opens with a close look at the tandem OLED, which stacks two light-emitting layers to deliver higher brightness than conventional single-layer OLED displays.

Under a microscope, iFixit found that the blue subpixels are larger than the red and green ones, which they say should help reduce strain on the materials and potentially extend the display’s lifespan.

Most of the teardown process is quite familiar from past models, though iFixit noted that replacing the USB-C ports or fans still requires removing the entire logic board, despite both components being independently replaceable.

iFixit noted that the headphone jack also requires logic board removal, while the HDMI port, SDXC port, RAM, and storage remain soldered to the board.

As with past teardowns, iFixit also tested what happens when swapping logic boards between two MacBooks.

While last year’s M5 MacBook Pro failed to complete Touch ID calibration through Apple’s Repair Assistant, iFixit noted that the new model successfully recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor after a logic board swap, with True Tone, brightness controls, and the touchscreen all working as expected.

iFixit was also able to enroll a fingerprint with the donor board installed from another MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

As for the illuminated Apple logo, iFixit had a bit of a rough time getting to it, destroying the OLED panel in the process and even asking whether anyone had managed to remove it intact.

Once inside, iFixit found that the Apple logo is illuminated by a strip of four LEDs, which work in conjunction with a reflective layer and a diffuser to distribute the light evenly.

The Apple logo itself, in turn, has a two-way mirror coating that gives it a shiny, reflective appearance when the LEDs are off, while allowing light to pass through when they’re on.

When it comes to weight, Apple shaved 92 grams off the chassis and 101 grams off the display assembly, despite adding touch and an illuminated logo. The battery is just 2 grams lighter, while the slightly smaller trackpad saves another 8 grams.

Finally, iFixit gave the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display a repairability score of 5 out of 10. That was one point higher than last year’s M5 MacBook Pro, but one point below the cheaper MacBook Neo.

#3432. ‘Lanterns’ Officially Shows What DC Stands to Lose After James Gunn’s Exit

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) is signing autographs at a taco stand when he gets word of possible alien activity in Nebraska. He flies out to investigate, leaving John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) to make his own travel arrangements, and winds up at a crime scene where Sheriff Kerry Kane (Kelly Macdonald) is rightfully in control. For Hal, the possibility of aliens explains why a Green Lantern should be there. For Kerry, there are dead people in her town, and the man who just showed up owes plenty of explanations of his own. The joy of Lanterns is how long it lets those two ways of seeing the same crime coexist. Hal knows things about the universe that Kerry couldn’t possibly know, and Kerry knows things about Rushville that Hal is going to have to earn the right to hear.

That balance is worth thinking about now that James Gunn and Peter Safran are exiting their roles as co-heads of DC Studios and Jeremy Latcham is taking over. Gunn and Safran will still be working on Man of Tomorrow, and there may be more for them with the studio in the future, but their most interesting contribution to DC was the room they gave other people to decide what a story in this universe could be. Lanterns took that freedom far enough to let a murder investigation change what it means for John Stewart to become a Green Lantern. There’s a big difference between signing off on a crime drama with a superhero in it and trusting that crime drama to have a say in who the superhero becomes.

The first time John sees Hal, he’s a kid watching him on television, and like any kid would, he's looking up to one of Earth's heroes. Years later, John gets to have the much less pleasant experience of working for somebody you grew up admiring. Hal has had the ring long enough to get comfortable testing whether John can handle himself, and there’s a particularly ugly echo of that in the way John’s father used to shoot apples off his head. The boy holds still, and the person pointing the gun gets to call him fearless. You can see how John would grow up believing that what somebody else sees you do under pressure tells them everything they need to know about what you felt.

Then Hal dies, and John has to look into the life of somebody he’s still grieving, without really knowing how to properly do so. Making him a detective under these circumstances is cruel, because every answer he wants as an investigator is something he might be happier never hearing as the kid who watched Hal on TV and has, albeit maybe reluctantly, grown to care about him as a person. By the time John gets one last conversation with a projection of Hal, the mystery has given him reasons to be angry with the man and just as many reasons to miss him. The finale can sit with both feelings because the show has spent enough time with the two of them for either one to hurt.

That’s why John’s new oath landed with so many viewers. Making room for fear is a meaningful choice in a mythology that has given fear an entire corps of its own, and it’s an even more meaningful one coming from somebody who spent his childhood being praised for how well he could hide it. A detective has to care what somebody is afraid of, especially when the answer might explain what they’ve done. By letting John take that understanding with him when he puts on the ring, Lanterns makes its murder mystery part of the kind of Green Lantern he’ll be in every story after this one.

Four teams, four completely different reasons to put yourself in danger for strangers. This is the roster you actually belong on, what they would want from you, and what it would cost you to stay.

You belong where the stakes are largest and the personalities are loudest. This is a team of people who are all used to being the most important person in the room, which is exactly why it works and exactly why it keeps nearly falling apart.

You have never had the luxury of being thanked for this. The X-Men protect a world that has never once been comfortable with them existing, and something in you understands exactly why they keep doing it anyway.

You do not want colleagues, you want your people. The Titans are the team where the friendship came first and the world-saving turned up afterwards as an inconvenient side effect.

You are not asking who to trust. You worked out the answer a while ago and it was nobody in a cape. This is where you go once you have decided the people in charge need watching, and that nobody else is going to do it.

It was wonderfully mean to make the first person to show us around the DCU’s live-action Gotham and an actor going through the worst time in his life, but it certainly let us see some of the ugliest parts of the city. Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries) has good reason to believe people will treat him differently once they see what’s happened to him. The prospect of getting his face back is so appealing that you can know exactly what kind of movie you’re watching and still find yourself hoping the treatment works.

James Watkins told Collider that Gunn gave him the freedom to reinvent Gotham, and the most consequential thing he does with that freedom is decide whose suffering the city is going to make us look at first. There are plenty of Batman stories where Matt’s transformation would be the awful thing that happened before the hero got involved, but instead, Clayface spends a movie with Matt while he can still imagine getting his old life back. That approach makes what happens to his body feel worse the longer you’ve spent hoping he might be right, until the movie reaches its tragic ending.

Those projects also give audiences two different ways to get invested in DC. A horror fan can walk into Clayface wanting to see what Watkins does with one of the superhero genre's best uses of body horror. A crime drama fan can come to Lanterns because they want to know what happened in Rushville. In exploring other genres first and superheroes second, both found a way to make those types of fans leave caring about a character they might not have sought out on their own. That’s a valuable thing for a shared universe to be able to do, especially when it has as many corners as DC does.

This Mike Flanagan-penned body horror is at its best when it dispenses with plot for gore.

Lanterns and Clayface can share a universe without asking the audience to watch them for the same reasons. I wanted to know what happened in Rushville because the show made me care about what the people there were keeping from each other. I wanted to know what would happen to Matt Hagen because I understood why he’d agree to something that looked like a terrible idea from the moment he heard it. There’s real value in a studio being able to earn both kinds of investment, especially when it has enough characters to spend decades making movies and television about them.

What I liked about getting Lanterns and Clayface from the same studio was that, after seeing both, I had less idea what the next DC project would be, and for the first time in my life that was a positive thing, not a negative. I knew more about the world they shared, and I could imagine more kinds of people living in it. I’d like the next filmmaker who comes in with a story about one of DC's characters to have as much say over what we get to see as the people who took Green Lantern to Nebraska.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3431. Robert Pattinson Is the Next James Bond: Denis Villeneuve Finds Star for His 007 Movie

Robert Pattinson is your new James Bond. Denis Villeneuve has cast Pattinson as the star in his 007 movie for Amazon MGM Studios. He will now be the seventh actor to officially star in the franchise and will lead what will be the 26th James Bond movie to hit the big screen.

Villeneuve is directing Bond 26 from a script by Steven Knight, and the franchise is being guided by mega producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman, who took over from the long-time stewards of 007, Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, upon the rights to Bond being acquired by Amazon following its acquisition of MGM.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime. I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team,” said Robert Pattinson. Related Stories Glenn Close Wipes Away Tears as She Gets Her Long Overdue Oscar While the Governors Awards Celebrate Indie Films Box Office: ‘Club Kid’ Scores Best Limited Expansion of the Year as Younger Audiences Embrace Jordan Firstman’s Oscar Hopeful

Pattinson this year starred in “The Drama” and “Primetime” at A24, and is currently in production on Matt Reeves’ “The Batman Part II.” Last year’s credits included “Die My Love” opposite Jennifer Lawrence and “Mickey 17,” from Bong Joon Ho.

“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond as we proudly introduce Robert Pattinson as the next 007,” said Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios. “This iconic character has captivated audiences around the world for more than six decades, and there’s no doubt that Robert’s remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice to carry that legacy forward. With Denis Villeneuve at the helm, Amy Pascal and David Heyman producing, Tanya Lapointe executive producing, and a brilliant script from Steven Knight, we have a world-class creative team in place to usher in a new era of Bond, and we couldn’t be more excited about the journey ahead.”

“Few films carry the kind of anticipation that comes with James Bond, and we have strived to honor the passionate fans, the legacy, and the future of this iconic character. We are thrilled to officially welcome Robert Pattinson as our 007 and are confident he will bring something truly special to this role. Robert, Denis, Amy, David, and Tanya are embarking on an amazing adventure together,” said Courtenay Valenti, head of film at Amazon MGM Studios.

“Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin,” said director Denis Villeneuve.

“James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic, and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies. The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit, and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times,” said producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman.

It’s been well over a year of fervent speculation as to whom would take up the mantle as Britain’s top super spy, as Villeneuve was announced to be taking the directing job way back in June 2025. Rumors abounded about who could star, with reports about a sprawling wish list and group of young Brits who had tested for the part. Film chief Courtenay Valenti teased the upcoming Bond movie at this year’s CinemaCon but said “it’s a responsibility we don’t take lightly” and would share more when the time was right. And with Villeneuve’s “Dune: Part 3” finally arriving this December, that time appears to be now.

The 26th Bond will be the first James Bond movie since 2021’s “No Time to Die,” which was the fifth and final entry for Daniel Craig as 007. That film, directed by Cary Joji Fukunaga, earned $774.1 million worldwide in its initial release (a UK re-release grossed another $132 million), putting it among the highest-grossing Bond movies ever, even when adjusted for inflation. The 25 films dating back to the ’60s have grossed $7.6 billion at the box office worldwide.

#3429. Legend Of Zelda: Majora's Mask Remake Teased By Industry Insider

It looks like a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask may be on the way from Nintendo. Less than two weeks after the Ocarina of Time remake launched on Switch 2 to critical acclaim, an industry insider is already teasing a follow-up via a Majora's Mask remake. While nothing has been officially confirmed by Nintendo yet, this insider has been known to have quite a few scoops, and was also one of the earliest people to suggest an Ocarina of Time remake was in the works.

This isn't the first time signs have pointed to a Majora's Mask remake. Speculation that it would follow Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2 has been around for a while, and even last week, an alleged leak of Ocarina of Time DLC seemed to suggest a remake of Majora's Mask was already in the works at Nintendo. Considering Majora's Mask is a direct sequel to Ocarina of TIme, it makes sense that it'd be the next Legend of Zelda video game to get an official remake, even if the original N64 classic remains a bit of a divisive entry overall.

The latest update on a potential Majora's Mask remake comes via Nash Weedle on YouTube. "I’ve received some information about this supposed remake,” Nash Weedle says in the video. “For now, I can only tell you that I’m looking into it. But I assure you that this one piece of information alone has made me believe that the Majora’s Mask remake is real.”

As with any leak, this should be taken with a grain of salt, especially considering Nash Weedle doesn't disclose what exactly the "one piece of information" is. It also contradicts earlier suggestions, including those from insider Nate the Hate, that said a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask was in development but not an immediate priority for Nintendo to release. Still, given Nash Weedle's past history with Nintendo scoops, there's at least some degree of credibility here. Perhaps the remake is further along than most people thought.

The original Majora's Mask, which launched on the N64 in 2000, proved to be a pretty divisive entry, mostly because to its timer system. People either hate this entry or consider it to be one of the greatest Zelda games of all time. There really is no middle ground. And a 3DS remake was equally divisive, mostly because of how many changes there were, particularly when it came to boss fight mechanics. Remaking Majora's Mask for Switch 2 would be a pretty bold move, even if the game has its legions of fans.

The real question might just be when a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask will release. Considering the Ocarina of Time remake just launched this month, it will likely be at least a year before the sequel arrives on Nintendo Switch 2. Given how past remakes have launched, though, a release year beyond 2028, and even as far away as 2030, all feel more accurate. Hopefully, Nintendo will share some official details soon.

A direct sequel to the iconic Ocarina of Time, The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask sets players loose in the parallel world of Hyrule, Termina, as they face a new impending disaster. Set months after Ocarina of Time, Link wakes up in a world similar to his own and discovers that the moon will crash into the planet in three days and bring about the end of days. Players will utilize a unique time travel mechanic that forces them to relive the same three days to try to avert catastrophe. An enhanced Nintendo 3DS version of Majora's Mask was released in February 2015.

Johnny Depp's return to the big screen landed at No. 1 at the international and domestic box offices this weekend years after his court drama ... despite a wide divide between critics and regular moviegoers.

While the movie has split critics down the middle -- with the film sporting a 54% Tomatometer -- audiences have raved over it.

While a jury awarded Johnny millions in damages after siding with him, Heard won one count in her countersuit.

All in all ... it seems that Scrooges aside, Johnny has done it all in one weekend, returning to screens all over the world in a triumphant way.

#3423. End of an era: Apple Support Community forums will permanently close on November 20

Users visiting the Apple Support Community tonight were greeted with a message informing them that the platform will permanently shut down on November 20. Here are the details.

If you have ever had a question or ran into a problem with an Apple product, chances are you have come across the Apple Support Community, the company’s official discussion forums where users from around the world help each other troubleshoot issues and share tips.

The platform has a history dating back to at least 1998, when it was known as Apple Tech Exchange. Since then, it was renamed Apple Discussions before relaunching as Apple Support Communities in April 2011, with a redesigned interface, personalized profiles, and a reputation system that rewarded users for helping others.

Tonight, however, users who tried to access the platform were greeted with the following message:

The AppleCare Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site.

We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.

Right now, the portal still shows a “Sign in” button, though it leads only to an AppleConnect login page labeled “AC Communities Web – Internal,” suggesting that access is now restricted to Apple employees.

Interestingly, Apple’s message refers to the “AppleCare Support Community,” rather than the “Apple Support Community,” which is how the platform is officially branded.

These forums were often far up when searching for Apple problems, but I’m not sure I ever found a real answer there. So often the threads went no where or someone would link an unhelpful Apple support page.

Still, the forums are already in read-only mode, with users able to browse existing discussions, search for answers, and interact with posts through the “Me too” and voting buttons, but no longer submit new questions or replies.

At the time of writing, the most recent post was published just 57 minutes earlier, suggesting that Apple only recently disabled new submissions.

9to5Mac has reached out to Apple for comment and clarification on the scope of the shutdown, and we’ll update this story if we hear back.

#3422. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3421. Reddit Reviews goes against the whole philosophy of the platform, say users

Many Redditors have expressed dismay at the launch of Reddit Reviews, a new AI-powered feature which aims to summarise posts about particular products.

Reddit is positioning the feature as a way to save time and effort when researching a potential purchase, but many Redditors say that replacing human interaction with AI summaries is antithetical to the whole philosophy of the platform – and is going to make the existing spam problem massively worse …

The value of customer reviews on ecommerce platforms like Amazon is becoming increasingly questionable thanks to practices like astroturfing by brands and offering people free products in return for five-star reviews.

That’s led to Reddit becoming one of the most trusted sources of feedback and advice on potential purchases, precisely because it’s a forum in which real people are free to express their true opinions. Indeed, many use a filter in their Google searches to draw content from Reddit specifically, adding the suffix ‘site:reddit.com’.

Reddit is increasingly a cesspool of maligned moderators (human and bot) and owners looking to make a bot. Posters on the platform are simply supplying free content with nothing to gain except bans when someone/somebot disagrees with them.

Reddit certainly isn’t immune to astroturfing – that is, fake posts by brands posing as ordinary users – but moderators put a lot of work into deleting spam and other inauthentic posts.

The platform yesterday announced the launch of Reddit Reviews, in which AI summarises the posts made about particular products and product categories. It’s being pitched as a way for people to save time when seeking the product opinions of Redditors.

Across Reddit’s communities, people discuss everything from hobbies and daily life to products they’re researching. By offering perspectives grounded in real experience, these conversations provide valuable context in every purchase decision journey […]

Today, we are starting to test Reddit Reviews, a new experience that organizes product conversations from across Reddit into dedicated reviews and highlights the most important takeaways from across our communities.

However, as CNET spotted, the move has led to a backlash by many Redditors and subreddit moderators.

“I’ve already seen this in practice and it is a nightmare. It turns a basic conversation into an ad-ridden distracting mess. It’s horrible to read and had me fleeing every thread I saw it in.”

“I am a moderator on a couple of health subs and we explicitly do not allow advertisements because most of them are bullshit slop and completely predatory for vulnerable and newly diagnosed patients. We do not want, or need this, on our subs!”

“Yeah, this definitely isn’t going to lead to even more fake account stealth marketing efforts across the site.”

“This is going to make our spam fighting even worse. This is horrible.”

“Every decision made by Reddit lately encourages spam and/or abuse that will make spam.”

“Not a single person who uses Reddit wants this.”

“You are incentivising existing spammers to continue or step up their activities, now that there’s a new well they can poison.”

I find it hard to disagree with the view that almost every monetization step the platform has made has degraded the user experience. This seems almost guaranteed to be another one.

Both are now considered classics of the heist genre, giving Jordan a lot to live up to.

In the trailer for the new Amazon MGM Studios film, Crown (Jordan) is a billionaire who's acquired his incredible art collection, including a priceless Vincent van Gogh painting, via somewhat unconventional means...like rappelling up an entire skyscraper to steal it from the top floor. However, he may have met his match in a brilliant investigator (Adria Arjona) who sees through his facade: but is she friend or foe? One person who's definitely a foe is Kenneth Branagh, playing a man who's determined to bring down Crown, no matter the cost. The film also stars Lily Gladstone (Killers of the Flower Moon), Danai Gurira (Black Panther), Pilou Asbæk (Game of Thrones), and Aiysha Hart (A Discovery of Witches).

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

In addition to starring, Jordan also directed the film; it's his second turn behind the camera after helming Creed III. The script is by Drew Pearce (The Fall Guy) and Jason Hall (American Sniper), based on the 1968 movie's screenplay by the late Alan R. Trustman; Kurt Wimmer and Leslie Dixon, who penned the 1999 remake, will also have screenwriting credits on the film. Oscar-winning musician Jon Batiste will score the film.

The Thomas Crown Affair will premiere in theaters on March 5, 2027. Stay tuned to Collider for future updates.

#3418. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3414. This video lets you actually see the ‘incredible’ new MacBook Pro cooling system

When Apple launched the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, the company said that it had completely redesigned the cooling system for “incredible sustained performance.”

That could sound like marketing hype, but a YouTuber has found a great way to let us actually see the new system living up to Apple’s claims …

The real-life performance of any electronic device depends not only on the power of the chip but a range of additional factors. A key one is the effectiveness of the cooling system, because when the device gets too hot, the performance will be throttled in order to avoid damage.

In the worst of cases, the theoretical maximum performance of a chip is only delivered for a very short time before it is throttled back to a much lower level. Thermal management is absolutely key in the case of a laptop like the MacBook Pro.

Apple said that the latest model has a completely new cooling system.

A completely redesigned thermal architecture enables […] incredible sustained performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max, even in a lighter design, while redirecting warm air away from the display.

As Macworld spotted, a YouTuber has found a simple but clever way to enable us to actually see the difference with our own eyes.

A YouTube video by Geekerwan compared the mini-LED MacBook Pro with the new PROLED XDR model using a fog machine. With each MacBook’s fans running, you can clearly see how the internal design disperses the heat: In the old model, heat goes both out and up through the display, while the PROLED pushes the heat toward the back of the device through the hinge.

Cooling is particularly challenging when the laptop is closed while connected to an external monitor, and the results of the testing show a dramatic improvement by the latest model. You can watch the video below, which links directly to the demo – but Geekerwan’s videos are always worth watching in full, so click here to watch the whole thing.

#3411. I feel a little nostalgic about the Apple Support Community forums, but it was time

Yesterday brought a surprise move by Apple when it abruptly ceased write access to the Apple Support Community and announced that it would be permanently closing in just over a week.

While the news does make me a little nostalgic, I do have to say that I think its time had long since come and gone …

As we noted yesterday, the community has a fairly long history. It started in 1998 as the Apple Tech Exchange before being renamed Apple Discussions and finally relaunching as Apple Support Communities in 2011. There were some paid community specialists working for Apple on the forum, while the majority of the responses came from volunteers.

The company’s statement was brief and didn’t give any official explanation for the shutdown.

The AppleCare Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

Interestingly, Verizon did exactly the same thing with its own Community Forum earlier this year, with an immediate switch to read-only access, followed shortly afterwards by closing it altogether. That too had a reasonably long history, having first launched back in 2008.

I suspect in both cases this was mostly about streamlining operations and reducing costs. CEO John Ternus does seem to be aiming to improve efficiency and eliminate what he views as unnecessary expenses. Additionally, community forums always run the risk of reputational damage when customers criticize decisions made by the company.

I’m old enough to remember the times when the forum was one of the first places I’d turn when troubleshooting an issue with an Apple product, but in all honesty, that hasn’t been the case for a very long time now. A lot of the suggestions were very basic steps any experienced user would already have tried.

There was sometimes also a snarky tone to some of the responses, essentially amounting to “Apple doesn’t promise you should be able to do X, so why are you expecting to do this?” or “Apple already provides a better way to do Y so use it.”

If you were very new to Apple devices and needed very basic help, then I’m sure it could sometimes prove useful, but I have to say that for a very long time now my own starting point has always been Reddit. I don’t think too many people are going to mourn the passing of ASC.

On one hand, the 1.5" height won’t require you to buy deeper sheets, however, it may not be thick enough for larger bodies. I should also mention that the topper didn’t quite cover my mattress from one edge to the other. The cover isn’t removeable, and thus washable, but at least it has an antimicrobial treatment to prevent mold and mildew growth.

Overall, I think it’s a solid topper for those who sleep hot or want to soften their firm mattress without making it too soft. Keep reading for my full breakdown of this topper to see if it’s a good choice for you.

The Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper starts out at $255 for a twin size, with a queen priced at $345. The premium price tag is not surprising, considering the topper is made with natural latex. However, we’ve seen more expensive natural latex toppers from Naturepedic ($399 for a queen at full MSRP) and Brooklyn Bedding ($587.07 for a queen on sale) so the Saatva is comparatively excellent value for money.

The price of the Natural Latex Topper includes free shipping, a one-year warranty, and a 180-night sleep trial with free returns.

The Saatva Natural Latex Mattress is 1.5" tall, which is a nice height because I can still use my regular sheets without any issue. Although natural latex is more breathable than memory foam, the perforations in this topper result in even better airflow. The cotton cover helps with breathability and has moisture wicking properties too.

Neither the latex nor the cotton cover is organic, but at least the latex foam is eco-INSTITUT® and Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certified. The only other drawback to the design was the extra fabric that was noticeable when I removed it from the packaging and at the end of testing. I couldn’t feel the fabric sticking up or bunching as I slept, but it’s quite noticeable when the sheets are off the mattress.

I slept on the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper for one week and tested everything from temperature regulation to comfort. Here’s what I found:

Setting the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper on my bed took five minutes to complete. It arrived vacuum-sealed and rolled up into a small box. The box was pretty damaged but thankfully that did not affect the topper.

Upon removing the plastic, the topper unraveled and expanded. I moved it onto the center of the mattress and noticed that there were a few inches on either side of the mattress, even when it was strapped into place with the corner straps. There was also a lot of extra fabric that bunched up from the cover. The topper had already expanded so I knew right away that the latex wasn’t going to fill out the cover and that for some reason there was just too much fabric.

Memory foam off-gasses and causes smells, but since this topper is made from latex, there were no smells. I slept on the mattress topper that night.

I sleep on an organic natural latex mattress, so when I placed the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper on my mattress to test, the topper was slightly softer than my mattress. After a week of testing, I’d say the topper offers a medium-soft feel that’s a 5.5 out of 10 on the firmness scale. The surface didn’t contour around my body, and I didn’t sink into the topper. Instead, it provided a hug-like feel, one that relieved pressure across the touch-points of the bed as I slept. My body felt supported and my spine was aligned no matter if I slept on my stomach, back, or side.

I’d suggest using this topper on a firm mattress that’s 7.5 or more out of 10 on the firmness scale, as the topper will provide a more cushioned and comfortable sleep experience, while maintaining the support you need. It could be used on a super soft mattress to extend its life. However, if you're paying $345 to provide extra comfort to a mattress that's lost its support, you could always consider picking up one of the best cheap mattresses instead for around the same price.

I tested the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper in Texas at the end of October and the beginning of November when the temperatures were in the high 70s or low 80s during the day and the low 70s and high 60s at night.

During this time, I turned my air conditioner off and used a fan to sleep at night, though it was still fairly warm in my house (about 70-76 degrees). I didn’t have to worry about overheating because the Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper was very breathable and maintained a temperature neutral sleep.

As someone who sleeps on a latex mattress, I expected to have this experience with the topper too, and I was glad to be right. No matter the time of year, I’m confident that the airflow through the perforated latex will ensure a sweat- and heat-free night of sleep.

At first glance, the Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper appears to have a 4.7-star rating out of 305 reviews on the Saatva site. However, a closer look shows that all the topper reviews are mixed together, so I wouldn’t trust that rating.

I was able to search the reviews for those who had specifically mentioned buying the Natural Latex Mattress Topper and found reviewers who liked the topper because of its pain-relieving qualities, especially when placed on firmer mattresses.

Because of how the reviews section is designed, it was not easy to find lower-star rating reviews of the Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper. Even so, I found a few customers who weren’t fans of the topper, with some stating that the 1.5" thickness flattened too quickly or that the topper developed creases.

✅ Your mattress is too firm: If you love the supportive aspects of a firm mattress but don’t want to wake up with aches and pains, the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper can help. The medium soft feel is comfortable and provides just enough cushioning, while also being supportive.

✅ You overheat at night: The cotton cover and the natural latex work well together to provide a temperature neutral sleep. You won’t get this kind of airflow with a memory foam topper.

✅ You and your partner have different sleep needs: The Saatva Latex Mattress Topper is ideal for any sleep type and those who sleep hot. If your partner likes a firm bed, but you don’t, this topper will provide some cushioning that you need, while maintaining the firm feel your partner likes.

❌ You are trying to firm up your mattress: If you’re trying to provide some more support to your soft mattress or firm it up a bit, the Natural Latex Mattress Topper has too much flexibility.

❌ You prefer a contouring topper or a sink-in feel: Natural latex is a somewhat bouncy material, so you aren’t going to sink into the Natural Latex Mattress Topper or feel the material contour around your body. This topper has more of a cloud-like feel that keeps your body lifted.

The Naturepedic Adagio Organic Latex Mattress is half an inch taller than the Saatva topper and one of the most comfortable toppers that Tom’s Guide has ever tested. Learn more in our Naturepedic Adagio Organic Latex Mattress Topper review.

The Birch Plush Organic Mattress Topper is expensive but it’s a good choice for those who want a latex topper to firm up their soft mattress. You’ll enjoy similar benefits to the Saatva Natural Latex Topper, like breathability and support, but at least the Birch Plush Organic Topper has a 10-year warranty.

#3409. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

#3408. WhatsApp may soon replace the Communities tab on iOS

Some WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are seeing a new option in the app’s bottom navigation bar that replaces the Communities tab. Here are the details.

Over the past few years, WhatsApp has increasingly focused on Communities as more people have turned to messaging platforms to interact in smaller, more private groups rather than through traditional social networks.

At the same time, WhatsApp has been testing several features that make it easier for users to see which of their contacts are online and available to chat.

Back in May, WABetaInfo found that WhatsApp was developing a new Contacts hub that would bring together users’ favorite contacts, as well as those who were currently online or had recently been active.

A few weeks later, WhatsApp began testing a new green dot indicator on iOS to make it easier to identify contacts who were online.

Now, WABetaInfo reports that WhatsApp is rolling out the new Contacts hub to some iOS beta testers, replacing the Communities tab in the app’s bottom navigation bar.

The new tab includes a section with favorite contacts and a full contact list. Users can see their favorite contacts at the top of the screen, making it easier to start a conversation with them. They can also sort the full contact list by activity, alphabetical, and birthdays. With alphabetical, the app organizes contacts by name. With activity, WhatsApp shows who is currently online at the top of the list. WhatsApp marks these contacts with a green dot, so users can easily distinguish them from offline contacts. WhatsApp also sorts recently active contacts by last seen, so users can quickly identify who was active most recently. With birthdays, WhatsApp sorts contacts by their upcoming birthday, so users can see who has a birthday coming up soon.

The site notes that the new tab also allows users to add contacts directly, with the option to sync them to their iPhone’s address book.

As for Communities, the feature itself isn’t going away, but rather being moved to a dedicated filter in the Chats tab.

WABetaInfo also notes that WhatsApp is experimenting with potentially replacing the Updates tab, rather than Communities, with the Contacts tab in a future configuration.

For now, the new Contacts tab is available to a limited number of beta testers running the latest WhatsApp beta for iOS via TestFlight, with a broader rollout expected over the coming weeks.

To read WABetaInfo’s full report, follow this link.

#3406. John Carpenter’s Zombie Apocalypse Is Officially Available for Free

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

A truck can get four people out of a zombie-infested town, provided somebody knows how to drive it. In one of John Carpenter’s latest forays into horror, taking a shortcut through the mud can leave the whole crew stuck while the infected close in. Somebody has to work the winch, while everybody else has to buy them enough time to use it. If there’s a better way to find out which of your friends you’d trust in a zombie apocalypse, it probably takes longer.

There’s as much Big Trouble in Little China in that setup as there is The Thing. Saber Interactive wanted the feel of a late ’80s or early ’90s action movie, and by the time the studio approached Carpenter, it already had the basics of its zombie outbreak. Saber’s Tim Willits told the Epic Games Store that Carpenter suggested additions to the story and composed music for the game. He also voiced a zombie in its animated trailer, which gives him a chance to enjoy the outbreak from the other side.

John Carpenter’s Toxic Commando joined Xbox Game Pass on November 12. It’s available on Xbox Series X|S, PC, and Xbox Cloud Gaming, with access through Game Pass Ultimate, Game Pass Premium, and PC Game Pass, depending on the platform. The first-person shooter originally launched in March and supports up to four players in co-op.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

Saber brought ideas from both World War Z and SnowRunner into the game. The studio’s Swarm engine can put enough infected on screen to make a fortified position feel temporary, while the driving gives the squad decisions to make before the shooting starts. There’s time to look for supplies and prepare for a siege, and there’s always a chance that getting to the next objective will turn into a rescue mission for the person who insisted the truck could make it through.

The campaign runs nine missions, which gives a group something to work through together over a few nights. Solo players can fill out the squad with bots, although it's definitely a challenge to handle objectives on your own, leaving a lot for one person to do once things go bad. With friends, even an ugly escape can be the part of the night everybody remembers, especially if the person who got the truck stuck is the one who has to get it moving again.

Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-new versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $152.99 for the Paperwhite and savings of $27 to $75 across five models that include the color-screen Colorsoft and the pen-equipped Kindle Scribe. All five are a generation behind Amazon's current lineup: The company introduced redesigned Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (plus accessories) in October, with the new Paperwhite now starting at $199.99, and replaced the 2024 Scribe with a third-generation model in December 2025. As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. Its seven-inch, 300ppi glare-free display is larger than the previous generation’s 6.8-inch screen, with faster page turns, an adjustable warm light, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. As PCMag notes in its review, it's a great option for readers who don't need color or handwriting features.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $190.99 from $224.99, making it just $38 more than the like-new Paperwhite (16GB). For that relatively small difference, you're doubling the storage to 32GB and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft (16GB) is down to $220.99 from $260.99 and offers something the Paperwhite models can’t: a color E-Ink display, which makes it well suited to comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, and travel guides. Its seven-inch screen shows that color content at 150ppi while keeping text at a sharp 300ppi, and you can mark passages in multiple highlight colors to keep your notes organized. That said, colors are noticeably more muted than on a conventional tablet, and battery life tops out at eight weeks, compared with 12 weeks on the Paperwhite.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $243.99 from $287.99, making it just $23 more than the standard like-new Colorsoft. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3404. HomeKit Weekly: SwitchBot’s Curtain Track 4 is the easiest smart curtain retrofit yet

The worst part of owning smart curtain motors is charging them, because it usually means taking the whole motor down from the track or running a really long USB cord to charge it. Today, SwitchBot has released the SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 aimed at solving that problem with a battery module that detaches on its own, so the motor stays in place, and you only take down the part that needs to charge.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is a retrofit motor for curtains that hang on a U-rail track. You hang it on the track between the curtain hooks, run a one-tap calibration in the SwitchBot app, and your existing curtains can then be motorized and used in your smart home. There’s no drilling, no rewiring, and no need to position magnets to stick to the rail, as earlier SwitchBot curtain motors required. SwitchBot claims the whole setup takes about 30 seconds.

One thing to check first: this version is for U-rail tracks only, not curtain rods.

The Battery+ version pairs a small built-in battery with a detachable 5,000mAh module for a total of 6,400mAh. SwitchBot rates it at up to 12 months of use for each charge, depending on curtain weight and movement frequency. When it needs charging, you pull the module off, charge it via USB-C, and clip it back on. SwitchBot also sells a Solar version that uses a small panel to keep the battery topped off if the window gets enough sun.

The motor itself connects via Bluetooth, so getting it into Apple Home requires a compatible SwitchBot Hub, which brings it there via Matter. Once it’s there, the curtains work like any other window covering in your Home app. You can add them to scenes, control them with Siri, and include multiple windows in a single automation. It’s always nice to time smart curtains/shades with dusk/dawn as well.

SwitchBot’s built-in QuietDrift mode opens the curtains slowly in the morning, at about half a centimeter per second, so the room fills with daylight gradually rather than all at once. SwitchBot says it runs at around 25 dB in that mode. You can also give the curtain a gentle tug by hand and the motor takes over, which is great if you don’t have your iPhone with you or someone doesn’t have access to your Apple Home setup.

SwitchBot built it in a way to correct drift over time, so you shouldn’t need to recalibrate it if it gets off.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 turns the U-rail curtains you already have into Apple Home window coverings without replacing anything. The detachable battery is the best feature here, as it lets you charge it without a long cord.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is available now on Amazon and directly from SwitchBot.

#3403. If you bought an iPhone Duo, have you kept or returned it? [Poll]

When Apple announced the iPhone Duo back in September, the company called it “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original,” and there’s no doubt that it generated a huge amount of excitement.

But a new report suggests that for some buyers the novelty quickly wore off, and they ended up returning their devices. Is this just a handful of people, or is it more common … ?

It’s been a very long time since any smartphone launch has generated quite so much buzz. Apple called it a breakthrough in iPhone design.

iPhone Duo features a breakthrough foldable design that’s beautiful, versatile, and durable, opening up possibilities that feel entirely new yet remarkably familiar […]

“iPhone Duo is the most transformational change to iPhone since the original. With an entirely new design and intuitive experiences, it shows what’s possible when hardware and software are engineered together and redefines what it means to use a foldable phone,” said John Ternus.

Despite not really being the target market for the phone, I was still wowed by the launch video and remained incredibly impressed when I got some hands-on time with one.

Many couldn’t resist buying one despite the price – but The Verge notes that not everyone has ending up keeping the device. Apple allows you to return any product within 14 days for a full refund without having to give any reason. That window has come to an end for some of the first buyers and the site’s Alison Johnson spoke with some of those who’d decided to take advantage of it.

The iPhone Duo replaced both my iPhone 15 Pro Max and my iPad Mini 6. It now is my phone and iPad mini in my pocket. This is the dream phone I never knew I wanted.

And for the lack of Face ID, Touch ID works perfect with my Apple Watch. And even without wearing it, I don’t see the big deal of the ‘huge’ effort of bringing my finger to a button.

For the lacking 5x zoom that I had on my Pro Max, I haven’t had a moment yet that I wanted to use it to be honest. Those moments will definitely arise, but the lack of that camera cannot go up against the amazing overall experience of the iPhone Duo.

But the more fundamental reason for some is that it hasn’t really lived up to their hopes for a multifunctional device.

“If I can have an iPad in my pocket, that would be great.” So thought Ben Seligson, a content creator, photographer, and now former iPhone Duo owner […] “Usually I’d throw a YouTube video on the iPad or throw a podcast up. And then I start cooking dinner and leave my iPad in one spot, but I’d have my phone in my pocket if I got a text, or I needed to set a timer or something like that.” With the Duo, the phone was also the iPad on the counter, so a quick reply became much more of an interruption.

I’m curious as to whether this is just a small minority of buyers or a more common phenomenon. If you bought a Duo early enough to have hit the end of the return window, please take our poll to let us know whether you decided to keep it or return it – and do share your reasons in the comments (which are now back).

Oh, and the good news for anyone buying one now is that you’ll have a lot longer to make up your mind, with the extended return window for the holidays in place. You can now return anything bought today through January 8.

#3402. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.
